verdict:
DOES NOT SURVIVE. The diagnosis is excellent and the core mechanism (positions over a durable log; postgres_changes deleted; private channels) is right. But three things are fatal as written, and each is load-bearing.

(1) The design's headline invariant — "THE TRANSPORT CARRIES POSITIONS, NEVER STATE" — is violated by its own inline-payload optimisation. Section D/F apply the inline entity row and then advance the cursor. Once the cursor passes pos N, branch 2 ("pos <= local_cursor -> discard idempotently") makes N permanently unfetchable, and `resync_required` only fires in the opposite direction. A single wrong, truncated, stale or forged inline copy is silent permanent divergence with no repair path. The one mechanism contains a hole exactly the shape of the class of bug it exists to remove.

(2) The RLS story that is supposed to make (1) unreachable does not work. Realtime computes the policy verdict once at join and caches it for the connection lifetime — the design's own invariant #7 — so a per-topic verdict cannot be conditioned on a per-message `event` name. Verified in realtime_client 2.8.0: `sendBroadcastMessage` pushes over the already-joined channel with no per-message authorization, and the REST fallback posts `{topic,payload,event,private}` under the same bearer. Write access is all-or-nothing per topic. "The doorbell is DB-originated only, so a client cannot forge a position advertisement" is false. Anyone who may send `typing` on `couple:{id}` may send `{stream,pos,<inline row>}`.

(3) Stage 1 — named "the highest value-per-risk change" and the sole reason the 10k ceiling is claimed to fit — cannot be shipped. Verified: `RealtimeClientOptions` (supabase 2.13.0) exposes only `eventsPerSecond` (deprecated, ignored), `logLevel`, `timeout`, `transport`; `SupabaseClient._initRealtimeClient` forwards none of `reconnectAfterMs`/`heartbeatIntervalMs` even though `RealtimeClient` accepts them. Full Jitter is not injectable through `Supabase.initialize`. Stage 1 also calls `sync_head`, which Stage 2 creates — so it is not "no schema change" and cannot be first.

Beyond those: the liveness probe is unfalsifiable when the partner is quiet and degenerates into the reconnect storm it replaced; Stage 5 deletes ServerClock's only feed (verified: one caller, presence_service.dart:206) while Section F rule 6 gates every join on it, so a 3-minutes-slow phone joins with a dying token — the exact "silently unauthorized" shape the design calls worst-case, made *more* likely than today; the compaction floor `min(both partners' cursors)` has no source in the stated schema and the reinstall re-bootstrap has no checkpoint boundary; WebRTC signalling is parked on `rt:`, which carries no positions, so the design's correctness argument explicitly does not cover ICE — and it adds two private-channel joins plus an HTTP sync_head to a ring path that inventory/calls.md already says "routinely does not fit" inside the caller's 35s timer.

The scale ceiling is optimistic at 10k: it is computed against msg/s and joins/s and ignores Realtime's `DB_POOL_SIZE=5` authorization pool, which at ~9ms per policy eval caps private joins near 550/s against a ~1,000/s correlated-reconnect burst. The cost model has two errors that move real money: the "don't subscribe the sender to its own doorbell, flat 33% cut" lever is unachievable on a shared topic, and the 100k escape hatch (move `rt:` to the WebRTC data channel) is priced at zero while routing 75% of the message volume onto metered Cloudflare TURN relay for exactly the users the brief names — two strangers, different carriers, symmetric NAT.

Stage 7 is a big bang in disguise. It rewrites all 29 `.channel(` sites and 6 hand-rolled resubscribers at once, cannot be half-done (the whole point is that features stop calling `.channel()`), and is where the *live* data leaks finally close — `call:<coupleId>` carrying SDP/ICE, `capsule_proximity:<coupleId>` carrying raw GPS every 4s, `mood_burst:<coupleId>` carrying message plaintext all stay public through Stages 1-6, in a design that calls that class "already breached".

Four invariants depend on the client behaving: cursor-after-apply, the token-freshness gate (whose input is a device clock after Stage 5), the outbound rate limiter (the SDK removed its own — `eventsPerSecond` is deprecated and ignored — and `TENANT_MAX_BYTES_PER_SECOND` is project-wide, so one stale APK disconnects other couples), and single-owner channel lifecycle (which collides with `MilesApp.showRealApp = false` on paused/hidden/detached unmounting the entire real tree on every background — the design never says where the transport component lives).

Verification does not reach four of these: nothing tests the inline path, re-bootstrap, compaction, or glare, and the reconnect-storm test will hit the self-host `TENANT_MAX_JOINS_PER_SECOND=100` default before it measures jitter.

Fixable, and worth fixing — the skeleton is sound. Minimum to make it survive: drop inline-payload-advances-cursor; split the DB doorbell onto a topic no client may write; reorder Stages 1/2 and own the reconnect loop above the SDK; make `sync_head` emit a probe broadcast so liveness is decidable; feed ServerClock from `sync_head` *before* Stage 5; add a server-side per-device cursor table and define the bootstrap checkpoint; move call signalling into the stream; make the existing topics private in Stage 1 rather than Stage 7.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The inline payload optimisation violates the design's own headline invariant. Section D permits the entity row inline; Section F applies it when pos == local_cursor + 1 and then advances the cursor. Socket-carried state becomes committed local truth. Once the cursor is past pos N, branch 2 ('pos <= local_cursor -> already applied, discard idempotently') permanently prevents re-fetching N. There is no checksum, no confirming read, and no repair path — `resync_required` only fires when the cursor falls BELOW the retained floor, which is the opposite direction. So a dropped/duplicated/reordered broadcast is indeed a latency bug, but a WRONG one is permanent silent data loss.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Partner A sends a message at pos 105. The doorbell arrives with an inline copy that is stale, truncated by a payload cap, mangled by the trigger's row-to-json construction, or forged (see flaw 2). B's client sees pos == cursor+1, applies the inline copy, commits, advances cursor to 105. The real row 105 is now <= cursor forever. B renders content that exists in no database; the three-branch reconciler will never fetch it; no error is raised on either side; no resync is triggered. This is the exact class of bug the design claims to have removed 'by construction'.
fatal_flaws.repair: The inline copy must never advance the cursor. Two acceptable shapes: (a) delete inline entirely — the doorbell is `{stream, pos}` and the client always reads the durable row, costing one round trip you were paying anyway; or (b) keep inline as a render-only hint that paints an optimistic bubble but leaves the cursor untouched until a read of couple_stream/entity confirms pos, with the fetched row authoritative on any mismatch. Do not attempt to validate the inline copy client-side — validation requires the fetch, so the honest answer is that positions come from the database and payloads are decoration.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Section E claims the write policy can exclude the `stream` event on `couple:` so 'a client cannot forge a position advertisement'. RLS on realtime.messages cannot express this. Realtime computes the verdict once at join (insert -> read -> rollback under the joiner's JWT) and caches it for the connection lifetime — the design's own invariant #7 states this. A cached per-topic verdict cannot be conditioned on a per-message event name. Verified in realtime_client 2.8.0: `sendBroadcastMessage` -> `send()` pushes over the already-joined channel with no per-message authorization round trip (realtime_channel.dart:608-700), and the REST fallback posts `{topic, payload, event, private}` under the same bearer token (:633-668). Broadcast write access is all-or-nothing per topic.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A malicious signed-up stranger cannot join `couple:{X}` — RLS holds there, and profiles.couple_id is genuinely locked down (verified: hardening_2026_08.sql revokes table-level UPDATE and re-grants every column except couple_id, plus the guard_couple_id trigger). But the partner can, and so can anyone holding a partner's token, or any modified/stale build. Because the design gives clients write access to `couple:` for `typing` and `screen`, the same principal can emit `{stream:'chat', pos: cursor+1, <arbitrary inline row>}`. Combined with flaw 1 that is arbitrary content injection into the partner's UI plus permanent loss of the real message at that position. No server-side check exists anywhere in the path.
fatal_flaws.repair: Separate the doorbell from client-writable traffic by topic, not by event. `couple:{id}:stream` — read-only to `authenticated`, no INSERT policy at all, written only by the SECURITY DEFINER trigger via realtime.send. `couple:{id}:live` — client-writable for typing/screen/presence. That is 3 always-on channels, not 2; say so and re-price (it does not change billable messages, only join count). Do this together with the inline fix — either one alone leaves the hole open.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Stage 1 — explicitly 'the highest value-per-risk change in the list', and the sole justification for the 10k-user ceiling ('At 2,500 joins/s that fits *only because of jitter*') — cannot be implemented on this SDK. Verified: RealtimeClientOptions in supabase 2.13.0 has exactly four fields — eventsPerSecond (deprecated: 'Client side rate limit has been removed. This option will be ignored.'), logLevel, timeout, transport. SupabaseClient._initRealtimeClient (supabase_client.dart:337-352) forwards only logLevel, httpClient, timeout, customAccessToken, transport. RealtimeClient itself does accept `reconnectAfterMs` (TimerCalculation?) and `heartbeatIntervalMs`, but neither is reachable through Supabase.initialize. Separately, Stage 1 replaces the forced disconnect with the `sync_head` probe, and sync_head reads couple_cursor, which Stage 2 creates — so Stage 1 is neither first nor 'no schema change'.
fatal_flaws.scenario: An engineer takes Stage 1 as written, opens supabase_service.dart:14, and finds there is no reconnectAfterMs to pass. The likely outcome is that the disconnect deletion ships and the jitter does not — which is strictly worse than today: app_shell.dart:66-80's own comment documents that doze kills the socket with no close event, and realtime_client's heartbeat is a Timer.periodic that Android throttles while backgrounded, so recovery moves from ~1s (forced reconnect) to up to two heartbeat intervals (~50s, realtime_client.dart:524-612) of silent non-delivery after every resume. Meanwhile the un-jittered 1s/2s/4s/8s/10s ladder is still in place for the correlated-reconnect case the 10k ceiling depends on.
fatal_flaws.repair: Pick one and price it as a dependency change, not a one-commit client change: (a) own the reconnect loop above the SDK — never let it auto-reconnect; catch the close, `realtime.disconnect()`, sleep random(0, min(30_000, 1000 * 2^n)), `connect()`; (b) fork realtime_client / patch RealtimeClientOptions to forward reconnectAfterMs and heartbeatIntervalMs, and pin the version; (c) upstream the field. Then reorder: Stage 2 (couple_cursor/couple_stream) ships before any probe, and the probe must force disconnect/connect when sync_head succeeds but no doorbell follows — otherwise you have traded a reconnect storm for up to 50s of silent non-delivery on every resume, a regression the design never acknowledges.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The liveness probe is unfalsifiable when the partner is quiet, and its failure mode is the storm it was built to replace. Section F rule 1: 'If head_pos > local_cursor, drain the gap over HTTP *and* verify a doorbell arrives; if no doorbell arrives within the probe window, the socket is silently dead -> replace it.' A doorbell fires only on a NEW append. Backlog drained over HTTP produces none. So absence of a doorbell is evidence of nothing.
fatal_flaws.scenario: User offline 3 days, opens the app on a train. head_pos >> local_cursor. The client drains 3 days of backlog over HTTP, waits its probe window, and no doorbell arrives — because the partner is asleep, not because the socket is dead. The client concludes the socket is dead and replaces it: 1 close + 1 open + 2-3 joins. 30 seconds later the train enters a tunnel and the socket really drops; on the next resume the same false-negative repeats. Every 30s gap now costs a socket teardown and a join burst, per user, in a carriage of users, against a joins/sec quota that refuses (`too_many_joins`) rather than queues — which the design itself names as a documented cause of manual project suspension.
fatal_flaws.repair: Make the probe self-answering. Have `sync_head` itself call `realtime.send({probe: <nonce>}, 'probe', 'couple:'||couple_id, private => true)` before returning, so a doorbell is guaranteed to fire and its absence within the window is genuine proof the socket is dead. Cost is one extra billable message per probe (~8 probes/user/day x 3 = 24/user/day; add it to the event budget). The nonce also gives you a real round-trip latency sample for the telemetry the plan wants.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Stage 5 deletes the only feed for ServerClock, and Section F rule 6 gates every channel join on ServerClock. Verified: `ServerClock.observe` has exactly one caller in the entire codebase — presence_service.dart:206, inside the presence upsert. Stage 5 deletes the 30s heartbeat (main.dart:191-209), the 5s chat_last_read write (chat_screen.dart:495) and the 15s poll, leaving ~2 presence writes per session. On cold start zero writes have happened, so `_known == false` and `_offset == Duration.zero` (server_clock.dart:24-28) — ServerClock.now() is the raw device clock. The design asserts ServerClock is 'already correctly designed' and changes nothing about its feed.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Phone with a clock 3 minutes SLOW, cold start after a long close. ServerClock offset is 0, so `session.expiresAt - ServerClock.now()` reads 3 minutes longer than reality. A token with 2 minutes of real life left appears to have 5, the freshness gate passes, and the client joins `couple:` with a token that expires during or just after the join. Because the authorization verdict is cached for the connection lifetime, the channel is silently unauthorized until the next reconnect — precisely the failure the design calls 'the worst possible failure shape', and which the SDK will not surface because supabase_client.dart:375-394 swallows FormatException: InvalidJWTToken. Stage 5 makes this MORE likely than the status quo, because today the 30s heartbeat keeps the offset warm.
fatal_flaws.repair: Two changes, and the ordering matters. First, `sync_head` already returns `server_now` — make feeding ServerClock from it mandatory, and ship that BEFORE Stage 5, not after. Second, and better: stop measuring. A gate whose input is a device clock is not a gate. On cold start, call `auth.refreshSession()` unconditionally before the first join and gate on the refresh succeeding, so the server asserts the token's validity rather than the client inferring it from arithmetic on a clock it does not control.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The compaction floor is unimplementable with the stated schema, and the re-bootstrap path has no consistency boundary. Section F says retention is 'compacted by pg_cron gated on min(both partners' cursors)'. The schema is `couple_cursor(couple_id, next_pos)` — the head — and cursors are local to the device (invariant 5). No server-side per-user or per-device cursor exists anywhere in the design, so `min(both partners' cursors)` has no source. Separately, 'the client re-bootstraps that stream' never defines what cursor the client adopts afterwards. The design cites PowerSync's rule that data is made visible only at a consistent checkpoint boundary and then does not apply it to the one path that needs it.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Partner reinstalls. local_cursor = 0, below the retained floor, so sync_head returns resync_required and the client re-bootstraps by paging the entity tables (the stream rows for those positions were compacted away). If it reads head_pos AFTER the bootstrap it silently skips every message appended during the paging — the bootstrap of a long history is minutes on a train. If it reads head_pos BEFORE, it replays the overlap, which is fine and idempotent — but nothing in the design says which. Compounding it: open_decisions #2 mandates per-device topics, so a user with two devices has two cursors; add a per-USER server cursor to feed compaction and device A's advance moves the floor past device B, giving B resync_required on every second launch. That is Matrix's documented two-readers bug, which delivery.md flags as an invariant ('ONE CONSUMER PER QUEUE, ENFORCED').
fatal_flaws.repair: Add `couple_member_cursor(couple_id, user_id, device_id, applied_pos)`, advanced by an RPC using greatest() (the repo already has this shape in ack_delivered/ack_read). Gate compaction on min(applied_pos) across devices seen in the last N days, with the 90-day hard cap as the backstop. Define bootstrap explicitly: read head_pos -> set cursor := head_pos -> page the entity tables -> any doorbell arriving during the bootstrap is a normal forward gap and is drained afterwards. State that this reintroduces a cursor-report write per device per session and price it (~2 writes/device/session, negligible).

fatal_flaws.flaw: WebRTC signalling is placed on `rt:`, which carries no positions, no gap detection, no ordering and no durability — so the headline invariant ('a dropped, duplicated, reordered broadcast is a latency bug, never a correctness bug') explicitly does not cover it, and the design never says so. research/calling.md's own invariant is the opposite: 'Signalling is serialized: one message in flight per call, a FIFO queue behind it... This is what lets trickle ICE satisfy RFC 8838's exactly-once, in-order delivery requirement without sequence numbers on the wire.' The design also specifies `rt:` as living 'only while an interactive surface is open' — which is exactly when a ringing call's surface is not open.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Two strangers, different carriers, both behind symmetric NAT. The only viable ICE pair is relay-relay, so the TURN candidate is the single indispensable frame. Lose it on at-most-once unacknowledged broadcast and ICE never gathers a viable pair; the caller sits on its 35s timer with no error. Today's code at least re-sends the entire `_localCandidates` list on receiving the answer (inventory/calls.md:42); the proposal deletes nothing and adds nothing there, it relabels the topic. Worse for the killed-callee path: the callee must now learn session_id from the stream, then join a SECOND private channel (`rt:{couple}:{session}`) before it can send the answer — each private join is an RLS round-trip through Realtime's DB_POOL_SIZE=5 pool — on top of a token refresh, a `couple:` join, an HTTP sync_head and a gap drain, all inside a caller timeout that inventory/calls.md already states 'routinely does not fit'.
fatal_flaws.repair: Put call signalling in the stream where the one mechanism actually applies: `stream='call'`, one couple_stream row per signal, entity_id -> a `call_signals` table carrying kind/sdp/candidate. ICE then inherits commit-ordered positions, arithmetic gap detection and durability for free, and a cold-started callee gets the full candidate set from the catch-up query rather than hoping the caller re-sends. Keep `rt:` for gestures and game state only. Drop the session_id topic for calls entirely — Section E's own policy admits `topic LIKE 'rt:'||couple_id||':%'`, so a member can join any session and the secrecy buys nothing while adding a rendezvous requirement with no glare rule. Resolve glare the way calling.md prescribes: a total order over a value both peers already have — you have one, it is `pos`. Then publish the ring latency budget.

fatal_flaws.flaw: 'POSITION ORDER IS COMMIT ORDER' holds only if no write path can create an entity row without appending, and the design never states the enforcement mechanism or revokes direct writes. Section C says allocation happens 'inside the same transaction as the entity write' without saying by what. The repo's precedent is SECURITY DEFINER RPCs (ack_delivered/ack_read, create_couple, unlock_capsule), while chat_repository.dart writes messages via a plain PostgREST insert. Relatedly, 'one trigger to review instead of ~28' is true of the doorbell only — it silently omits that you now need ~28 APPEND triggers (or ~28 rewritten write paths), which is the bulk of the work and does not appear in the stage plan.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Allocation is implemented as an RPC (the path of least resistance, matching the repo's existing style). One of the ~28 tables — or one of the four insert call sites in chat_repository.dart at lines 228/249/279/309, or a screen shipped after the migration — keeps using the direct PostgREST insert. The row commits, RLS allows it, no error is raised, and it is never advertised and never appears in a gap fetch. The partner never sees it, on any device, forever. Both users' clients report 'caught up' (local_cursor == head_pos) because the row has no position. This is undetectable by every check in the verification plan.
fatal_flaws.repair: Enforce it structurally, not by convention: BEFORE INSERT triggers on each streamed entity table that allocate the position and write the couple_stream row, so no write path can bypass regardless of whether it comes from an RPC, PostgREST, or the SQL editor. Where an RPC is used instead, revoke INSERT on that table from `authenticated`. Add to Stage 8's CI: for every table in the stream vocabulary, assert an append trigger exists — the same mechanically-checkable-invariant argument the design already makes for the empty publication.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The 10k ceiling is computed against msg/s and joins/s and ignores Realtime's authorization pool, which the design itself cites and then never uses. research/supabase.md records DB_POOL_SIZE=5 — five connections gate every private-channel join for the entire project. Every private join is an insert-read-rollback against realtime.messages under the joiner's JWT, evaluating a policy that calls `current_user_couple_id()`, a subquery on profiles. The design's own best-case figure for a wrapped policy is ~9ms.
fatal_flaws.scenario: 10k users, ~800 peak devices, a Supabase restart or a regional carrier event drops everyone. Full Jitter spreads socket reconnects over ~1s, then 2 joins each jittered over the specified random(0,500)ms: ~1,600 joins arriving at roughly 1,000/s. Authorization capacity is 5 connections / 9ms ~= 550 evals/s. Joins queue behind the pool, hit the client's 10s channel timeout, and are retried — amplification on top of the original burst, then too_many_joins, then the RealtimeDisabledForTenant suspension the design names as its own honest ceiling. The stated '~2x headroom' is measured against the 2,500 msg/s quota, which is not the binding limit. The verification plan's 'assert p99 join spread > 400 ms' is calibrated to the same wrong number.
fatal_flaws.repair: Three things, all cheap. Raise DB_POOL_SIZE in the dashboard and put the chosen number in the design as a named dependency. Make the join policy a single indexed equality with zero table access — put couple_id into the JWT via a custom access token hook so the policy reads `realtime.topic() = 'couple:' || (auth.jwt() ->> 'couple_id')`, which also removes profiles from the join hot path entirely. Size the join jitter window from the authorization pool rather than the quota: at 1,600 joins against ~550/s the spread needs to be >= 3s, not 500ms, and the test assertion should follow.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Two cost levers are wrong in ways that move real money, and two cost lines are missing. (a) 'Do not subscribe the sender to its own doorbell — a flat 33% cut' is unachievable in this topology: the doorbell is a DB broadcast to a topic both partners are joined to, and Realtime has no per-recipient suppression on a shared topic. Getting it requires per-user topics, which contradicts the 2-channel design. (b) The 100k escape hatch — 'Move rt: onto the WebRTC data channel... at zero new infrastructure' — is priced at zero, but inventory/calls.md:35 records Cloudflare Realtime TURN as billed on relayed bandwidth with no server-side quota, no per-user cap and no per-call credential scoping. (c) couple_stream storage growth and the compaction job are absent from the cost model. (d) Section G correctly identifies TENANT_MAX_BYTES_PER_SECOND=100_000 as the binding limit, then sizes the token bucket 'under the plan's msg/s' and plans for 12,000 msg/s at 100k users.
fatal_flaws.scenario: The brief's own scenario — two strangers, different carriers, both behind symmetric NAT — is 100% relayed. Executing the recommended exit routes the entire gesture/game/watch-together stream (the ~500 of ~660 daily events that constitute 75% of the message bill) through metered TURN relay for exactly those users, with 24h credentials cached in plaintext SharedPreferences and no server-side minting limit. The '$7,487 -> ~$1,800' line is not a saving until relay bandwidth is priced, and per inventory/calls.md the app's own fallback banner when TURN acquisition misses its 3s budget reads 'calls only work when both of you are on the same wifi' — so the primary cost and scale exit depends on the single most broken subsystem in the app.
fatal_flaws.repair: Delete lever (a) or change the topology and re-price honestly. For (b), price Cloudflare relay GB at the 100k gesture volume and add a server-side per-user credential mint cap plus per-call scoping before making the data channel load-bearing; if TURN cannot be made reliable first, the honest 100k exit is self-hosted Realtime, not the data channel. Add couple_stream rows/GB and the pg_cron job to the cost table. Size the token bucket in BYTES per second against the 100 KB/s tenant ceiling, since that is the limit the design itself identified as binding, and either confirm what the hosted plan enforces project-wide or flag it as unverified.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Several defects that only appear under the brief's 'implemented literally' rule, plus a mis-sequenced security fix. Section E lists the device predicate as `realtime.topic()` EQUALS `'device:' || (select auth.uid()) || ':%'` — `=` against a string containing `%` never matches, so every device-channel join is rejected. Section G's 'one outbound send path' is defeated by the SDK: `send()` silently falls back to an HTTP POST to /api/broadcast when the channel has not joined (realtime_channel.dart:633-668) — per inventory/calls.md:68 that is already how the callee's answer leaves today, one POST per ICE candidate. And Stage 3 writes policies for `couple:`/`device:`/`rt:`, topics that do not exist until Stage 4/7.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Implemented literally: ringing and session revocation are dead from day one because device: joins are rejected, and the failure is a silent authorization denial rather than an error. Separately, the token bucket sits inside the transport's send path while the SDK routes around it whenever a channel has not finished joining — precisely during the reconnect burst when rate limiting matters most. And through Stages 1-6 the live leaks stay open: `call:<coupleId>` carrying SDP and ICE, `capsule_proximity:<coupleId>` broadcasting raw GPS every 4 seconds, `mood_burst:<coupleId>` carrying message plaintext, and `mood_lamp:` — all joinable by anyone with the anon key and a couple UUID, which the design correctly notes is public (first path segment of every couple_media URL). The design calls this class 'already breached' and then schedules the fix last, behind the largest client refactor.
fatal_flaws.repair: Use LIKE for both the device and rt predicates and say so. Put the token bucket ABOVE sendBroadcastMessage in the transport component, and either disable the REST fallback or make it an explicit, separately-budgeted path. Most importantly, flip the security sequencing: add `private: true` plus RLS policies keyed on the CURRENT topic names (`call:<id>`, `capsule_proximity:<id>`, `mood_burst:<id>`) in Stage 1. It is a small diff — one config flag per channel plus one policy — and it is the only change on the whole list that closes a live data leak rather than preparing for one. Consolidation to `couple:`/`device:`/`rt:` can then stay last, where it belongs.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Stage 7 is a big bang in disguise, and the design says so in the same breath it denies it. It is described as 'the largest client refactor and the smallest correctness win', deferred to last — but it rewrites all 29 `.channel(` call sites and all 6 hand-rolled resubscribe implementations simultaneously, changes the topic of every ephemeral feature (touch, touch_trace, heartbeat, watch, games, together, proximity, mood lamp) at once, and cannot be half-done, because the entire mechanism is that features stop calling `.channel()`. There is no incremental path and no revert story. Related: the design never says where the single lifecycle-owning component lives, and the app's disguise architecture forces `MilesApp.showRealApp.value = false` on paused/hidden/detached (main.dart:210-231), which unmounts AppShell and everything beneath it on every background.
fatal_flaws.scenario: An engineer reaches Stage 7 with Stages 1-6 shipped and must land a single PR touching 29 subscription sites across chat, closer, games, touch, capsule, call and shell, with no dual-path fallback available (unlike Stage 4, which explicitly keeps the old leg for a week). If the transport component is mounted under AppShell it dies with the disguise cover on every background — taking the socket, the resume probe and Presence with it. If it is mounted above, it is a process-lifetime singleton that outlives sign-out, which is the exact non-autoDispose leak the inventory already flags for `call:` and `screen_presence:`.
fatal_flaws.repair: Split Stage 7. Introduce the transport component in Stage 1 owning only the socket, the resume probe and the reconnect loop, explicitly rooted ABOVE MilesApp as a singleton with a stated sign-out teardown — say in the design that it must survive showRealApp flipping false, and how sign-out unsubscribes without leaking. Then migrate features onto it one per ship, leaving each feature's old `.channel()` in place behind a flag for one release, exactly as Stage 4 does for chat. Consolidation should be N small reverts, not one large one. Also extend the verification plan: nothing currently tests the inline-payload path, the re-bootstrap checkpoint, compaction, glare, or the REST broadcast fallback — four of the findings above are invisible to the stated suite — and the 200-instance reconnect test will hit the self-host TENANT_MAX_JOINS_PER_SECOND=100 default long before it measures jitter, so it will fail for the wrong reason.

verdict: The core mechanism is right and I could not break it: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on chat_streams taken before the dedup check genuinely makes cseq order equal commit order (a second writer cannot acquire the lock until the first commits, so any snapshot that sees N sees everything below N), `unique(couple_id, sender_id, client_msg_id)` genuinely makes a timeout unambiguous, and rejecting Broadcast Replay, per-recipient queues, and SERIALIZABLE are all correctly argued. Two strangers behind symmetric NAT is a non-event here — messaging has no P2P path. What fails is everything around the mechanism. Three things are fatal as written. First, "process-scoped singleton with a re-entrancy guard" is not implementable in Flutter: the FCM background handler runs in a separate isolate with separate globals (verified in this app at reach_notifications.dart:227-295), so the design's own inherited "one consumer per queue" invariant is violated by the design's own "FCM wake" trigger, producing concurrent sync workers on one SQLite file. Second, `clear_conversation_everyone()` already hard-DELETEs every row for a couple (clear_chat_everyone.sql L22-23), which destroys row contiguity permanently and turns the receive-path assert into an infinite resync loop — the design discusses hypothetical future deletes and misses the destructive one that ships today. Third, the flagship claim that the phantom-seen bug is structurally impossible is false: `ack_read_cseq(max_observed)` is perfectly expressible, the server clamp only bounds the future, and the only guard is a debug-build assertion. That is correct-by-convention in a codebase where the identical convention already failed. Beyond those: the sync state machine has no failure exit from CATCHING_UP and no timeouts anywhere, so one tunnel wedges delivery until process restart; a newly-paired couple has no chat_streams row so both exit conditions are NULL and the new-user path wedges the same way; `outbox.next_attempt_at` is a device wall clock, directly contradicting the design's own "no inequality with a timestamp on either side" invariant; and reinstall pins delivered/read watermarks at their pre-reinstall value until a full history backfill completes, which for an active couple with a year of history is effectively never. Seven of the fourteen invariants are client conventions, not server-enforced properties, and the document does not say so. On numbers: the cost model's dominant line is ~2x low because it bills 6 events per message where the design's own cited rule gives 9+ (events × recipients+1, three broadcast events minimum), which pushes 100k from "at the 2,500 msg/s wall" to 1.5-2x past it — the honest ceiling is ~50k. pg_net's ~200 req/s bound is evaluated at daily mean rather than evening peak, so the rebuilt push path breaks at scale in the same window Realtime does, and the "benign degradation" story assumes FCM still works when it does not. DB disk, provisioned IOPS, and push_outbox retention are absent from the cost model entirely. On migration: stage 2 is a rewrite of the chat client with a non-clean rollback, stage 1's backfill races live inserts and can produce NULL cseq rows that are invisible to every future catch-up, partitioning is scheduled last in the plan and "now" in the open decisions, and stage 3 increases write pressure on chat_receipts while it is still on the 30-changes/sec postgres_changes poller. Verdict: the mechanism survives, the specification around it does not. It is repairable without changing the core idea — the fixes are concrete and small — but implemented literally as written it will fail in production in ways the stated verification plan cannot see, which is the exact failure mode the brief was written to prevent.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The 'process-scoped singleton with a re-entrancy guard' does not exist in Flutter. `firebaseMessagingBackgroundHandler` (verified at reach_notifications.dart:227-295, `@pragma('vm:entry-point')`, per inventory/realtime.md L111) runs in a SEPARATE Dart isolate with a separate heap and separate globals. The sync worker's boolean guard and the outbox drainer's singleton live in the main isolate's memory and are simply absent in the background isolate. So the design's 'FCM wake' trigger starts a second, concurrent sync worker on the same SQLite file. The design explicitly inherits Signal's 'ONE CONSUMER PER QUEUE, ENFORCED' (close code 4409) as an invariant and then implements it with the one construct that cannot enforce it across isolates. Compounding: push.md L205 documents that in the Rare/Restricted standby bucket NETWORK ACCESS IS DISABLED, and push.md L201 that the background handler gets 'several seconds' — so the background isolate's sync worker will routinely be killed mid-page.
fatal_flaws.scenario: MIUI phone, app backgrounded. Partner sends 3 messages. FCM wakes the background isolate; it reads applied_cseq=100 and calls sync_messages(100,200). The user taps the launcher at the same moment; the main isolate starts, reads applied_cseq=100 (the background isolate has not committed), and issues the same sync. Both write rows 101-103 and set applied_cseq=103. One transaction aborts on the messages PK; the other commits. If the page boundaries differ (background got 101-103, foreground got 101-250 because more arrived), the lost update leaves applied_cseq at 103 with rows 104-250 already stored — the CURSOR invariant now describes a state the client is in and cannot detect, and the design's own contiguity assert on the next sync sees rows above the prefix and triggers a full resync loop.
fatal_flaws.repair: Do not run the sync worker in the background isolate at all. The background handler's only jobs are: post the local notification, and write a 'sync due' row to SQLite. The main isolate drains on next foreground — this is precisely Signal's model (push is a doorbell) and removes the concurrency entirely. If a background drain is genuinely wanted later, the guard must be a lease row in SQLite (owner id + expiry on a MONOTONIC clock, taken with an atomic conditional UPDATE), never an in-memory flag.

fatal_flaws.flaw: `clear_conversation_everyone()` hard-DELETEs every message row for the couple — verified at E:/LDR/supabase/clear_chat_everyone.sql L22-23: `DELETE FROM public.messages WHERE couple_id = v_couple_id;`. That permanently destroys CONTIGUITY over stored rows while `chat_streams.last_seq` keeps advancing. `unique(couple_id, cseq)` does not prevent a hole; it only prevents a duplicate. The design's receive step 4 asserts 'rows are exactly applied+1..applied+n with no holes; if not, the server invariant is broken: log loudly, full resync' — and the full resync returns the identical gapped set. Open decision 7 discusses deletes as a hypothetical future stream event and never notices the destructive delete that already ships and is one confirm dialog from the sweep icon in chat_input_bar.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Partner A taps 'clear conversation'. All 8,000 rows for the couple are hard-deleted; chat_streams.last_seq stays at 8000. Partner B's client has applied_cseq=8000, so nothing happens yet. A sends one message: cseq=8001. B receives the hint, calls sync_messages(8000,200), gets one row — fine. Now B reinstalls, or any client starts from applied_cseq=0: sync_messages(0,200) returns rows starting at 8001. The assert 'rows are exactly 1..n' fails, the client declares the server invariant broken and full-resyncs, which returns the same thing. Infinite loop, pinned to that couple, with no exit state in the state machine.
fatal_flaws.repair: Define contiguity over ISSUED cseq (chat_streams.last_seq), never over rows present. sync_messages must return the issued range it covered alongside the rows, so the client can distinguish 'missing because deleted' from 'missing because lost'. Re-implement clear-for-everyone as a tombstone that itself consumes a cseq (which also gives the partner the live signal chat.deletion currently lacks), and never let a row physically leave the table without the range being declared. Until that ships, the assert must not be a resync trigger.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The phantom-seen bug is relocated, not eliminated. `greatest(existing, least(incoming, stream.last_seq))` bounds the ack from above but says nothing about what the client actually stored. `ack_read_cseq(max_observed_cseq)` is trivially expressible and reproduces today's exact failure — the recipient reports read=106 while 105 was never received, and the sender renders 105 as SEEN. The design's WATERMARK SOUNDNESS invariant claims the current bug 'has no expressible equivalent'; that is false. The only thing standing between the new system and the old one is verification item 5, which is a DEBUG-BUILD assertion. The flagship claim of the whole architecture — 'correct by construction' — is here correct by convention, in a codebase where the identical convention already failed (chat_screen.dart:344 `_messages.fold(0, (a,m) => m.seq > a ? m.seq : a)`, then `ackDelivered(_maxSeq)` immediately followed by `_ackRead()`, both verified on disk).
fatal_flaws.scenario: Any future refactor, or any partner on an older/forked build, passes the wrong integer to ack_read_cseq. Server accepts it (it is ≤ stream.last_seq). Sender's tick goes blue over a message the recipient never received. Nothing in production detects it — the stage-0 canary only checks server-side contiguity, and the client-side check is compiled out of release builds. This is the exact bug that has survived every previous fix, surviving again.
fatal_flaws.repair: Make the ack self-verifying on the server: send `ack_read_cseq(applied_cseq, local_row_count)` and have the RPC reject unless `local_row_count = applied_cseq`. One extra bigint on the wire and one comparison; a bug cannot produce a matching pair by accident, only deliberate lying can. Ship verification item 5's assertion in RELEASE builds, downgraded to 'refuse to ack + log' rather than crash.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The sync worker state machine has NO failure transition out of CATCHING_UP. The table lists CATCHING_UP → {CATCHING_UP, CAUGHT_UP, BACKFILLING} and nothing else. Combined with the re-entrancy guard, an error mid-catch-up leaves the worker permanently in CATCHING_UP and the guard then rejects every subsequent trigger (foreground, connectivity, socket open, FCM wake, 60s timer). Delivery is dead until process restart. Separately, the design specifies no timeout on any network operation anywhere; supabase_flutter's PostgREST calls have no default request timeout, so a half-open TCP socket hangs for the OS timeout (minutes). The same hazard sits on the outbox drainer's `await upload` in the UPLOADING state.
fatal_flaws.scenario: User offline 3 days, opens the app on a train. Catch-up needs 5 pages. Page 3 is issued as the train enters a tunnel: the socket is half-open, the request neither returns nor errors for ~2 minutes, then throws. The worker is stuck in CATCHING_UP with the guard held. The train exits the tunnel; connectivity fires, FCM wakes, the 60s timer ticks — all three are swallowed by the guard. The user stares at a chat that is 3 days stale with a live network, and the only fix is force-quitting the app. This is precisely the 'passed on wifi, dead in production' class the brief names.
fatal_flaws.repair: Explicit timeout on every network call (send_message, sync_messages, uploads, acks). Replace the boolean guard with a lease carrying a monotonic expiry so a wedged worker self-releases. Add CATCHING_UP → STALLED(backoff) → CATCHING_UP, and surface STALLED in the UI so the failure is visible rather than silent.

fatal_flaws.flaw: A newly-paired couple has no `chat_streams` row. The design never specifies who creates it. `sync_messages` returns `stream_last_seq` = NULL, and BOTH exit conditions from CATCHING_UP are NULL-valued: `stream_last_seq > applied_cseq` is NULL, `stream_last_seq == applied_cseq` is NULL. Neither transition fires. Same wedge as the previous flaw, on the path a brand-new user hits first — a path E:/LDR/supabase/newuser_fixes.sql shows has already been a repeated source of breakage.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Two users pair. Neither has sent anything, so send_message has never run and no chat_streams row exists. First app open: sync worker enters CATCHING_UP, gets {rows: [], stream_last_seq: null}, cannot exit, holds the guard. The couple's chat never syncs for the entire process lifetime, and the first message either partner sends is delivered only by the broadcast hint — which the design correctly forbids from advancing any cursor. First-run experience is a chat that appears to work and silently never catches up.
fatal_flaws.repair: Create the chat_streams row in the couple-creation path (and defensively upsert it in send_message and sync_messages). Have sync_messages return `coalesce(last_seq, 0)`, never NULL. Add a CI test for the zero-message couple — it costs nothing and this class of NULL-comparison wedge is invisible in any test that starts from seeded data.

fatal_flaws.flaw: `outbox.next_attempt_at` is a device wall clock, which directly contradicts the design's own stated invariant: 'CLOCKS ARE PAYLOAD, NEVER CONTROL... There is no inequality anywhere in the delivery path with a timestamp on either side.' The drainer's due-check is exactly such an inequality (`next_attempt_at <= now()`), and it sits in the send path. This is the same failure shape receipts_v2.sql's own header describes as having caused a two-month invisible outage.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Phone with a 3-minute-fast clock queues a message and sets next_attempt_at = now+30s. The phone then syncs time from the carrier (NITZ) and jumps back 3 minutes. next_attempt_at is now ~2.5 minutes in the future; the drainer skips the row on every wake. Worse case: a phone crossing a timezone boundary on a train, or a MIUI time correction, can park the whole outbox for hours. The user sees a clock icon and 'the app is just slow'; nothing distinguishes it from being offline, and no telemetry fires.
fatal_flaws.repair: Back off on attempt count plus a monotonic base (`Stopwatch`/`elapsedRealtime`), not wall time. Store `attempts` and `queued_at_monotonic`; recompute the delay relative to process start on each app launch, treating any row as immediately due after a restart. Zero timestamps in the drainer's predicate.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Reinstall/new-phone is the worst-supported common case and silently kills the product feature the whole design exists to fix. On a from-scratch install applied_cseq=0. Above the 2,000 threshold the design enters BACKFILLING and explicitly 'leaves applied_cseq where it is' while backfilling downward. But delivered_cseq/read_cseq are 'only ever written from applied_cseq' (stated invariant). So during backfill the reinstalled partner cannot advance either watermark at all. server-side greatest() pins them at the pre-reinstall value, and every message sent after the reinstall shows the sender one grey tick until the ENTIRE history has been re-downloaded and the prefix closed. Additionally, receive step 8 ('post local notifications for anything that arrived while backgrounded') applied literally to a from-zero sync posts one notification per historical message.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Couple with 14 months of history (~30,000 messages). Partner B gets a new phone. B installs, signs in, backfill starts at 200 rows/page = 150 sequential round trips, and B only ever opens the app for 90 seconds at a time. Every session the backfill advances a few pages and is killed; the prefix never closes. Meanwhile A sends 40 messages a day and every single one sits on one grey tick indefinitely. A reports 'delivered receipts are broken again' — and by the design's own rules they are working exactly as specified. On the first sync, B's phone also fires thousands of local notifications.
fatal_flaws.repair: Split the watermark base from the history base. On a from-scratch install, fetch the newest page and set applied_cseq := (stream_last_seq - page_size), recording an `install_floor`; treat everything below install_floor as display-only backfill that never participates in the prefix or the watermark. Gate notification posting on `cseq > install_floor` AND `cseq > session_start_watermark`. This is Telegram's differenceTooLong resolution done correctly — discard local state and restart from the server's head, not from 1.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The cost model's dominant line is ~2x optimistic, and correcting it moves the 100k ceiling from 'at the wall' to past it. '~6 billable per user-message' is wrong on the design's own cited billing rule (research/supabase.md: billable = events × (recipients + 1); a couple topic with both subscribed bills 3 per broadcast). The design has at minimum three broadcast events per message — the message, the delivered ack, the read ack — so 9 billable, plus typing. Also uncosted anywhere: database DISK for 1.46B message rows (~900 GB at 100k, ~$110/mo at $0.125/GB, plus provisioned IOPS, plus a working set no Large/XL holds in RAM); push_outbox, which the design gives no retention policy and which grows at the same rate as messages; and net._http_response / cron.job_run_details, which research/supabase.md explicitly flags as having no documented retention.
fatal_flaws.scenario: At 100k users the corrected figure is 1.08–1.44B Realtime messages (~$2,700–3,600, not $1,787) and peak ~3,600–4,800 msg/s against Team's hard 2,500/s. That is not 'no headroom', it is 1.5–2x over a ceiling whose documented consequence is `tenant_events` disconnects and, on sustained overage, manual `RealtimeDisabledForTenant` suspension requiring a support ticket. The honest ceiling for this design on Supabase is ~50k users, not 100k.
fatal_flaws.repair: Restate the ceiling as 50k. Recompute billable events with the ×3 fan-out applied to every broadcast event, not just the message. Coalesce delivered+read into a single receipt broadcast (they are already written by the same RPC). Add lines for DB disk, provisioned IOPS, push_outbox retention, and the two Supabase system tables with no documented cleanup.

fatal_flaws.flaw: pg_net's documented ~200 req/s reliable ceiling breaks the rebuilt push path at scale, and the design hides this by averaging over a 24-hour day ('~1.7 req/s'). An LDR couples app's traffic is concentrated in evening hours in two or three timezone clusters. research/supabase.md documents pg_net as ~200 req/s with a 2s default timeout, NO retry, and responses garbage-collected after 6 hours.
fatal_flaws.scenario: 100k users, 21:00 in the dominant timezone. 8,000 concurrent users, most in active conversations. The 5s pg_cron tick has several thousand recipients with pending watermarks, so it issues them through pg_net in one burst — thousands of requests in a tick against a 200 req/s bound. Requests are dropped or time out silently. The design's benign-degradation story ('Realtime refuses connections → falls back to FCM wake + foreground catch-up') assumes FCM works at the ceiling. At the ceiling both legs fail together and the real fallback is 'next time the user opens the app' — hours, not minutes.
fatal_flaws.repair: Rate-limit the cron drain to a fixed budget per tick (e.g. 500 rows) with rows carried forward, so pg_net is never presented with a burst. Model push volume at PEAK, not at daily mean. Above ~10k users the sender should be an Edge Function invoked once per tick with a batch, not one pg_net call per recipient — one invocation can hold the cached bearer and issue the FCM calls with proper concurrency control.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The push design specifies neither a collapse key nor a TTL, and both are load-bearing per research/push.md. With no collapse key, a bursty couple hits FCM's 100-pending-per-app-instance cap, at which point ALL stored messages are discarded and the device gets the onDeletedMessages tickle (push.md L40). With a collapse key — the obvious choice for a watermark, and what the coalescing design begs for — collapsible messages are throttled to 'a burst of 20 per app per device, refilling 1 every 3 minutes'. Separately, the suppression rule (`delivered_cseq >= max cseq`, evaluated at the 5s tick) races the recipient: a foregrounded recipient who acks after the tick still gets a high-priority push that produces no user-visible notification — the documented trigger for Android 13+ `priorityLowered`, which also silently removes the ability to start a foreground service for the CALL path.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Active couple, 60 messages in 20 minutes, recipient's phone in Doze. With a collapse key: the first 20 wake-ups land, then the device gets one wake every 3 minutes for the rest of the evening. Latency for the design's headline '~100ms' path becomes up to 3 minutes for exactly the couples who use the app most. Meanwhile the recipient who IS foregrounded but on the Home tab generates a steady stream of notification-less high-priority pushes, and over days FCM downgrades the sender — at which point the calling feature's ring stops working too.
fatal_flaws.repair: State the choice: one collapse key per couple ('msg:<couple_id>'), accepting the 20-burst/1-per-3-min bound, with a long TTL (not 0, not 30s) so nothing is discarded. Budget the 4-distinct-collapse-keys-per-device limit against the reach/care/call keys. Suppress at SEND time using a server-visible 'recipient socket is joined' signal, not only the 5s-later delivered_cseq check, so foreground recipients never receive a notification-less high-priority push.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Stage 2 is a rewrite of the chat client presented as one incremental step, and it is not cleanly revertible. It introduces a local database, a new send path, a new receive path, a new cursor, and a transport change in a single release, across chat_screen.dart (which per inventory/chat.md owns catch-up, receipts, the send queue, typing, deletion, selection, replies and themes in one object), chat_repository.dart and chat_send_queue.dart. The design's own criterion — 'a design requiring a big-bang rewrite is a failed design' — is violated at its largest stage.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Stage 2 ships and a crash-on-launch appears on some Android version in the Drift migration. Rolling back the APK does not roll back state: the previous build recomputes _maxSeq as a fold over a 300-row `created_at DESC` fetch (verified at chat_screen.dart:344 and chat_repository.dart fetch), which lands exactly on the bug the migration existed to remove, on devices whose SQLite now holds an applied_cseq nobody reads. The rollback is a regression, so the team ships forward under pressure instead — which is how the previous point-fixes got validated on two phones on one wifi.
fatal_flaws.repair: Split into four independently shippable releases: 2a outbox for TEXT ONLY (closes chat.send.text, the highest-risk inventory item, with the existing cursor untouched); 2b prefix cursor + sync_messages with the existing send path untouched; 2c media onto the outbox (also fixes the video duplicate-bubble bug); 2d delete the client-sent 'msg' broadcast. Each is revertible on its own and 2a alone removes silent send loss.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The migration plan and the open decisions contradict each other on partitioning, and the plan schedules the single irreversible step last. Stage 5 says HASH-partition messages; open decision 4 says 'decided now and applied at the first migration that touches the table'. Postgres cannot convert an existing table to partitioned in place — it is create-new, copy, swap, under a lock, on the largest table in the system. The design itself identifies this as 'the only step here that gets materially harder with data volume' and then puts it at the end.
fatal_flaws.scenario: The team follows the migration section (which is what people follow) rather than the open-decisions section. Stages 0-4 ship over some months while the table grows. Stage 5 arrives with 100M+ rows and now requires a genuine maintenance window on a live product — the one thing the design promised there would be none of. It gets deferred, and the app carries an unpartitioned messages table permanently.
fatal_flaws.repair: Move partitioning into stage 1, executed BEFORE the cseq backfill while the table is smallest, and delete the contradicting sentence from stage 5. If it cannot be done in stage 1, say plainly that it will require a window and size it.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Stage 1's backfill races the live fleet. `cseq = row_number() over (partition by couple_id order by seq, id)` plus 'set chat_streams.last_seq to each couple's max' is not atomic with respect to old clients still doing direct PostgREST inserts, and the design states no lock and no ordering between installing the BEFORE INSERT trigger and running the backfill. Every ordering has a hole: trigger-first means new rows get cseq from a chat_streams whose last_seq is still 0 and collide with the backfill; backfill-first means rows inserted in the window get NULL cseq.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Backfill runs at 03:00 and takes 40 seconds. Three couples send messages during it. Those rows land with cseq NULL. sync_messages filters `cseq > after_cseq`, and `NULL > n` is NULL — so those messages are invisible to every future catch-up, forever. That is silent permanent message loss introduced by the migration whose entire purpose is preventing silent permanent message loss, and the stage-0 canary (which checks contiguity of assigned cseq) does not detect a NULL.
fatal_flaws.repair: Install the trigger first, seeding chat_streams.last_seq per couple to `count(*) + safety_margin` so live inserts allocate above the backfill range; backfill below it; then close the gap or accept a one-time offset (contiguity from 1 is not actually required, only contiguity of the issued range). Add `cseq IS NOT NULL` to the stage-0 canary before starting, and make cseq NOT NULL as the last step of stage 1.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The migration's intermediate states are more fragile than the starting state, which the staging narrative does not acknowledge. Stages 0-4 leave postgres_changes on both `messages` and `chat_receipts` (the swap is stage 5), while stage 3 INCREASES chat_receipts write volume: today the app writes one ack per 5s per open chat; the new design writes delivered and read acks debounced to 1/s each. research/supabase.md documents the postgres_changes ceiling at 30 changes/sec with RLS, PROJECT-WIDE across all ~28 published tables, and unimprovable by compute (40/s even on a 16XL).
fatal_flaws.scenario: Stage 3 ships to make the double-grey tick reachable. At 1,000 users with ~60 concurrent open chats, chat_receipts alone now generates up to 120 changes/s against a 30/s project-wide poller shared with presence, messages, reach_events and the Closer tables. The poller falls behind, receipt updates arrive minutes late or not at all, and the visible symptom is 'the new delivered tick is broken' — the exact conclusion that gets the redesign reverted.
fatal_flaws.repair: Move stage 5's transport swap for chat_receipts ahead of stage 3, or coalesce delivered and read into a single ack RPC and a single broadcast (they are already written by the same function). State explicitly in the plan that stage 3 must not ship while chat_receipts is still on postgres_changes.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The outbox introduces a new storage leak with no cleanup path. If a media upload succeeds and send_message then goes BLOCKED (RLS denial, unpaired, rejected payload) or the user deletes the queued message, the uploaded object sits in `couple_media` with no row referencing it — exactly the flung-GIF leak class the design itself flags in its cost section as 'nothing can ever delete them'.
fatal_flaws.scenario: User photographs something, the send fails deterministically (partner unpaired mid-send), user taps the X on the failed bubble. The 1200px JPEG stays in a PUBLIC bucket at a permanent unauthenticated URL whose first path segment is the couple_id. At 10k users this accumulates silently and is also a privacy exposure, not just a cost one.
fatal_flaws.repair: Record the uploaded remote path on the outbox row (the design already does this) and delete the storage object when the outbox row is discarded without committing. One statement in the BLOCKED-discard path.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Verification is the strongest part of the document and meets the no-two-phones constraint, but it has three holes that map exactly onto the fatal findings. (a) Nothing tests that the value passed to ack_read_cseq is applied_cseq rather than a max — the property test covers apply(), not the ack call site, so flaw 3 ships untested. (b) Item 3 names 'socket dies mid-catch-up, page 2 of 4' as a regression test for a transition the state machine does not contain, so the test either fails on day one or is written against a state machine different from the one specified. (c) An in-process single-isolate harness structurally cannot exhibit the two-isolate race in flaw 1 — 'FCM wake with the app process killed' is listed but cannot be simulated by a fake transport in one isolate.
fatal_flaws.scenario: CI goes green on every listed item, the team ships stages 1-3, and the three failures that reach production are precisely the three the harness cannot see: a wrong ack value, a wedged catch-up on a flaky network, and duplicated/lost cursor advances from the background isolate. That is the same shape as 'passed on two NTP-synced phones, failed for everyone else'.
fatal_flaws.repair: Add: a test asserting ack_read_cseq is called with applied_cseq and never with any other integer (make it a compile-level constraint if possible — the ack function should take the cursor object, not a bigint). A named state-machine test for CATCHING_UP failure that must fail until the transition exists. And a real two-isolate integration test on a single device (main isolate + background isolate against one Drift file) — that needs one phone, not two, and it is the only device test that is a correctness test rather than a plumbing check.

verdict:
Does not survive. The skeleton is right — a durable ordered log with an in-transaction seq counter, server-owned freshness, and push-as-doorbell is the correct answer, and it is faithfully derived from research/calling.md and research/delivery.md. But five things are fatal as written, and four of the five are in the ten lines of RPC semantics between an FCM push and a ringing phone, which is precisely the code path every previous fix died on.

The worst is that the design makes the ring MORE network-dependent than the broken system it replaces: §3 puts a catch-up query and a `ring_ack` RPC in front of posting the notification, so on the killed-app / Doze / cold-radio path — the only path that matters — a failed round trip means the phone never rings at all. Today's code at least posts from the push payload first. Second, `ring_ack` and `accept_call` gate on exact state equality (`= 10`, `= 20`) while `end_call` correctly uses `greatest()`; the design's own duplicate-push coalescing therefore guarantees a second drain that returns `expired` and cancels the ring, and a fast Answer tap races into `accepted_elsewhere` on a single-device couple. Third, `start_call`'s glare table is copied from RingRTC, which classifies RECEIVED offers, and has no branch for "the live call's caller is me" — so a caller whose process was killed mid-dial (the design's own primary scenario) gets `glare_lost` on a coin flip and is told to attach to an offer whose PeerConnection no longer exists. Fourth, `unique (couple_id) where state_ord < 90` converts an abandoned dial into a permanent per-couple calling outage, because the only three things that clear it all require someone's process to be alive and networked, and the sweeper's interval is never specified. Fifth, the `broadcast_changes` trigger runs inside the durable insert's transaction, so a Realtime-layer failure aborts `start_call` — which falsifies the headline invariant that the socket is never required for a call to ring, and falsifies the 100k "degrades to rings 1–3 s slower" claim with it.

On the brief's explicit checks: yes, several invariants depend on the client behaving — 9 (seq-cursor reconciliation), 12 (relay bitrate clamp, whose failure mode is money with no error code, as the design itself admits), 13 (priority hygiene, enforced nowhere), 14, and 15 (all three cancellation owners are client-side and one of them reads the device clock). Invariant 5 ("no device clock decides whether a phone may ring") is contradicted by §5.4's absolute-instant timer, and invariant 10's ServerClock fallback is provably unavailable in the FCM background isolate — `_offset` is an in-memory static fed from exactly one call site in presence_service.dart. Invariant 6 is contradicted by its own mechanism, since SECURITY DEFINER RPCs bypass the RLS that is claimed to make injection impossible. Yes, a migration step is a big-bang in disguise: S3's dual-read safety rests on legacy messages participating in a seq-cursor rule they structurally cannot, so the unkeyed-hangup bug survives to S6 — and S6, not S4, is the second step needing both peers upgraded, with no capability gate. The scale ceiling is honest in its Supabase arithmetic and optimistic in its framing, because the binding constraint is a per-handset ring-success rate present at n=2 that no amount of scale changes. The cost estimate omits `call_events` volume and retention entirely, prunes `call_signals` by DELETE where Supabase's own realtime.messages uses partition drops, and under-counts relay egress ~15–20% by applying a video-only send cap to total billed bytes.

Two smaller things worth fixing before anyone writes SQL: `expires_at` as a STORED generated column will not create (`timestamptz + interval` is STABLE, not IMMUTABLE), and `device_id` — which S2, S3, S5 and S7 all key on — does not exist anywhere in the codebase today.

Fix the five fatals and this becomes a strong design; the repairs are all local and none requires abandoning the log.

fatal_flaws.flaw: `ring_ack` gates on `state_ord = 10` exactly, so the SECOND drain of the same call cancels the ring. The design itself guarantees a second drain: §3 Layer C copies Signal's `SerialMonoLifoExecutor` (1 running + 1 queued, newest wins) and states 'N duplicate pushes collapse into ≤2 drains'. Drain 1 calls ring_ack, moves state 10→20. Drain 2 calls ring_ack, the `for update` select matches 0 rows (state is 20), and the only documented non-happy return is `expired` — for which the design's own rule is 'the client logs a missed call and NEVER RINGS'. FCM redelivers routinely; the fast path (private broadcast) plus the push path are two independent triggers for the same drain. `accept_call` has the identical shape: it requires `state_ord = 20` exactly, so a user who taps Answer from the full-screen intent before drain 1's ring_ack has committed gets 0 rows, and the RPC then writes `accepted_elsewhere` to 'the losing devices' — which on a single-device couple is the device that just answered. The design preaches `greatest(state_ord, incoming)` monotonicity and then uses strict equality on the only two RPCs that stand between a push and a ringing phone.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Callee's phone gets two copies of the call push 400 ms apart (normal FCM behaviour). Drain 1 rings. Drain 2 gets `expired`, writes a missed-call row, and cancels the notification via the `call_ended` cancellation owner in §5.4. The phone rings for half a second and stops. Caller sees `ringing` for 60 s. Reproduces on one phone, no network variation needed.
fatal_flaws.repair: Make ring_ack and accept_call idempotent and monotone like end_call. ring_ack: `update calls set state_ord = greatest(state_ord, 20) where id=$1 and callee_id=auth.uid() and state_ord < 30 and now() < expires_at returning offer_sdp, video, signal_seq, now() as server_now` — and return the offer for any state < 30, not only 10. Distinguish three return codes, never two: `ring` (offer returned), `already_ended` (state 90), `expired` (past expires_at). Only `expired` and `already_ended` may cancel a notification; 'no rows' must never be collapsed into `expired`. accept_call: `state_ord = greatest(state_ord, 30)` guarded by `answered_by_device is null or answered_by_device = p_device_id`, so the same device re-accepting is a no-op success rather than a loss.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Redial by the same caller is misclassified as glare, and the `glare_lost` branch tells the caller to attach to a call it cannot service. `start_call`'s decision table is copied from RingRTC's `check_for_collision`, which classifies RECEIVED OFFERS. It has no branch for 'the live call's caller_id is me'. Branch 2 fires on 'Live call, same peer, state_ord < 30' — which is exactly what a caller's own abandoned dial looks like — and resolves by 128-bit order over call_id. That is a coin flip. When the new call_id loses, the RPC returns `glare_lost` plus the surviving call id 'so the client attaches to the call already in flight'. The caller cannot attach: the surviving call's offer SDP belongs to an RTCPeerConnection in a process that no longer exists, with dead ICE credentials it cannot reconstruct a local description for. It hangs until the 60 s expiry. Signal never hits this because its UI blocks a second outgoing dial while one is active; here the caller is a cold-started app with no memory of the first attempt, which is the exact scenario the whole architecture is built for.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A dials B. B's phone is force-stopped by MIUI, no push, no ring. A backgrounds the app; Android reclaims the process (the design targets battery-optimising ROMs, so this is the norm). A reopens and dials again. `start_call` sees the live 60-second-old row, same peer, state 10, and roughly half the time returns `glare_lost`. A's screen shows a call connecting to nothing. A hangs up and redials; the same coin flips again against the new stale row.
fatal_flaws.repair: Branch on caller identity before the tie-break. If the live call's `caller_id = auth.uid()`, this is a redial, not glare: terminate the live row with `end_reason='superseded'`, emit no hangup signal, and insert the new call unconditionally — the caller is the only party who could have been servicing it. Reserve the 128-bit tie-break for `live.caller_id = the partner` (true glare). Add `superseded` to the end_reason enum. This also makes the caller-side recovery deterministic instead of 50/50.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The ring is gated on a successful server round trip. §2 states ring_ack 'is the only path that returns the offer to a callee' and performs the freshness transition; §3 Layer C states the wake sequence is 'drain the log for that call_id, then call ring_ack'. Implemented literally, the notification cannot be posted until a catch-up SELECT and an RPC have both completed. That is 2+ network round trips plus Supabase session restore plus a possible token refresh, executed in the FCM background isolate, on a cold radio, inside FlutterFire's documented ~30 s process-kill window and `onMessageReceived`'s 'short execution window'. If any of it fails or is slow, THE PHONE DOES NOT RING AT ALL. The current broken design at least posts the notification from the push payload first and fetches the offer only after the user taps. This design makes the ring strictly MORE network-dependent on the one path — killed app, Doze, App Standby Rare bucket — that the architecture exists to fix, and it violates the brief's own constraint that nothing may depend on a reachable network at ring time.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Callee is in Doze in the Rare bucket. High-priority FCM grants the documented temporary network window. The isolate cold-boots Firebase, restores the Supabase session (a refresh round trip because the access token expired hours ago), runs the catch-up query, then ring_ack. On a 3G-fallback radio that is 4–8 s. FlutterFire kills the isolate at 30 s or the temporary network grant lapses first. No notification is ever posted. `push_outbox` says `sent`, `call_events` records `push_received` but never `ring_shown`, and the caller waits 60 s.
fatal_flaws.repair: Invert the order. Post the CallStyle ring immediately from the push payload alone — it already carries `call_id`, which is all §3 Layer C says it carries. Then drain and ring_ack in the background. ring_ack becomes a two-way advisory: a definitive `expired` or `already_ended` CANCELS an already-showing ring (that is the correct use of a server-owned freshness gate); a network failure leaves the ring standing and the offer is fetched on Answer. Move the offer SDP fetch onto the Answer path where the user has demonstrably granted attention and the app is being launched anyway. The freshness invariant survives intact — a stale ring is cancelled within a round trip instead of never being shown.

fatal_flaws.flaw: `unique (couple_id) where state_ord < 90` converts an abandoned dial into a total calling outage for that couple, and nothing in the design reliably clears it. Only three things move a row to 90: `end_call` (client-initiated, requires the caller's or callee's process to be alive and networked), `ring_ack` past expiry (requires the callee to receive the push at all), and 'cron sweeps to no_answer' in §9 — whose interval is never specified anywhere in the design. The dominant failure case has none of the three: caller dials, callee is force-stopped so no push and no ring_ack, and the caller's process is killed by the OEM ROM before its 60 s client timer fires. The row sits at state 10 forever, and the partial unique index then rejects every subsequent `start_call` from either partner. The headline structural invariant is also the app's newest single point of total failure, and its only recovery mechanism is an unspecified cron.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A dials B. B is force-stopped (MIUI). A locks the phone; OxygenOS kills A's process at ~40 s. Nobody calls end_call. The `calls` row is live at state 10 forever. Both partners now get a unique-violation on every dial. Neither has any UI affordance to clear it. Calling is dead for that couple until an operator notices.
fatal_flaws.repair: Do not let the index be the only gate. Make `start_call` self-healing: inside the same transaction, first `update calls set state_ord = 90, end_reason = 'no_answer' where couple_id = $c and state_ord < 90 and now() >= expires_at`, THEN evaluate the live-call branches against what remains. An expired row can never block a dial, because the dial itself reaps it. Keep the pg_cron sweeper for telemetry hygiene at 30 s and name its interval in the design, but never make correctness depend on it. State explicitly that `expires_at` is the reaping authority and `end_call` is only an optimisation.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Layer B runs inside Layer A's transaction, so a Realtime-layer failure aborts the durable write. §3 specifies `AFTER INSERT on call_signals` → `realtime.broadcast_changes(...)`, which per research/supabase.md:85 INSERTs a row into `realtime.messages`. An AFTER INSERT trigger runs in the writer's transaction: if that insert raises — missing daily partition, permission drift on the `realtime` schema, a `realtime.messages` write error, a restore where the extension is out of step — the trigger aborts the whole transaction and `start_call` fails. The offer is never committed and no push_outbox row is ever written. This directly contradicts the design's headline invariant ('The signalling socket is never required for a call to ring... a Realtime outage degrades calling to rings 1-3 seconds slower') and the claimed scale property at 100k ('tenant_events throttling degrades to rings via push'). The design asserts the layers are independent and then couples them with a trigger.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Supabase's partition-maintenance job for `realtime.messages` misses a day (or a project restore leaves the current partition absent). Every `start_call` and every `send_signal` now raises. Calling is 100% down, not 'slower', and the failure presents as a Postgres error on dial with the push path never reached — the exact inversion the design warns about elsewhere.
fatal_flaws.repair: Make the notification path unable to fail the durability path. Either wrap the `broadcast_changes` call in a `begin ... exception when others then null; end` block inside the trigger (broadcast is best-effort by definition, so swallowing is correct here and only here), or drop the trigger entirely and have the writing RPC emit the broadcast after commit — the clients already reconcile from the log via the seq-cursor rule, so a lost broadcast costs latency only. Add a Layer-1 SQL test that revokes INSERT on `realtime.messages` and asserts `start_call` still commits and still writes push_outbox.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The ring's self-cancel timer is armed at an absolute wall-clock instant, so a skewed device cancels its own ring. §5.4: 'a local AlarmManager/coroutine timer set to `expires_at`'. AlarmManager RTC and Dart DateTime comparisons both read the device clock. Invariant 5 claims 'no device clock participates in any decision about whether a phone may ring' — §5.4 is that decision, and it is on the device clock. Separately, the fallback the design leans on is broken on the wake path: `ServerClock` (verified at E:/LDR/mobile/lib/core/services/server_clock.dart) holds `_offset` in a static in-memory field with no persistence, and `ServerClock.observe` is called from exactly one site, presence_service.dart:206. In an FCM background isolate `_known == false` and `now()` returns the raw device clock. So invariant 10 ('the client's expiry check compares client_expires_at against ServerClock') is false in the cold-start case, which is the only case that matters, and it is fed by the presence heartbeat the brief declares broken.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Callee's phone clock is 3 minutes fast. Push arrives, notification posts, the timer is armed at `expires_at` = server now + 60 s, which on this device is 2 minutes in the past. The timer fires immediately and cancels the notification. The phone flashes and goes silent. On a 3-minute-SLOW phone the mirror case: cached TURN credentials past their real expiry are trusted, ICE gathers no working relay candidate, and the call fails cross-carrier while working on one wifi — the exact two-month bug the design cites as its founding evidence.
fatal_flaws.repair: Never arm a timer at an absolute remote timestamp. Have ring_ack return `server_now` (it already does) and arm on the DURATION `expires_at - server_now`, using `SystemClock.elapsedRealtime`-based scheduling, which no clock change can move. Ship the same duration in the FCM payload as `ring_ms_remaining` so a notification posted before any RPC (per the fix above) can arm correctly with zero round trips. Persist the ServerClock offset to SharedPreferences on every observation and rehydrate it in the background isolate, and feed `observe` from every server response that carries a timestamp — not only the presence heartbeat.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Both TURN recovery mechanisms require an ICE restart the design claims to avoid. §8: 'late credentials are applied with `setConfiguration()` plus a regather, which Cloudflare documents as the supported mid-session path.' That conflates Cloudflare's SFU documentation with libwebrtc PeerConnection semantics. Changing `iceServers` via setConfiguration affects only the NEXT gathering phase, which on a PeerConnection means an ICE restart — a new ufrag and therefore a full offer/answer round trip. The same applies to §9's `RELAY_ESCALATION`: 'renegotiate with `iceTransportPolicy: relay`' also takes effect only on a new gathering generation. So the design's flagship claim that 'acquisition never blocks a dial' silently converts into 'the first call after a cold start costs a full renegotiation' — on the killed-app path, where the callee's cached credentials are also cold. And `setConfiguration` appears nowhere in E:/LDR/mobile (verified by grep), so this is an unproven API on the exact code path that produced the two-month outage.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Callee cold-starts from a push after 3 days offline. Cached TURN is 3 days old and rejected. The design says create the answer immediately and apply credentials late. The answer's ICE generation contains only host and srflx candidates. Both peers are on carrier-grade NAT, so no pair ever becomes writable.
