At 8 s the client escalates to relay-only — which needs a new offer/answer that the design's §7 explicitly says is unnecessary. Nothing in the FSM covers a renegotiation during setup, and MEDIA_DEADLINE fires at 20 s with `media_failed`.
fatal_flaws.repair: State the round trip instead of denying it. Add an explicit `ice_restart` signal kind to `call_signals` (it is a durable log; a restart is one more row) and specify the setup-time renegotiation path in the FSM: on RELAY_ESCALATION the CALLER (impolite, role already durable in `calls.caller_id`) issues the restart offer, the callee answers, the seq cursor orders it. Separately, remove the incentive to ever hit it: since the client must be online to call `start_call` anyway, fetch TURN in the SAME round trip — have `start_call` return the ICE servers from the server-side cache in `turn_grants` alongside the call row. Then late credentials stop being a case that exists.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Migration S3 is a big-bang in disguise, and S6 is a second coordinated step the plan does not label as one. S3 says the client 'reads the log IN ADDITION to the broadcast, preferring whichever arrives first (both are idempotent under the seq-cursor rule)'. Legacy broadcast messages have no `call_id` and no `seq` — the design's own current_design section makes that the headline defect, and S6 is what adds them. A message with no seq cannot participate in a seq-cursor rule, so the stated safety property of the dual-read window is simply false. Consequence: through S3, S4 and S5 an unkeyed legacy `hangup` from a dead attempt still tears down the live call. That bug — the one the whole design is organised around — is not fixed until S6, and S6 requires BOTH peers upgraded (a legacy peer keeps emitting unkeyed hangups) yet is given no capability gate, unlike S4 which gets `profiles.client_caps`. Additionally, during S3/S4 a legacy client's call creates no `calls` row, so 'at most one live call per couple' is false for the entire dual-write window while the partial unique index is nonetheless live and rejecting new-path dials.
fatal_flaws.scenario: S3 ships behind a flag. A is on the new client, B is on the old one. B's previous call ended 30 s ago; B's client emits a trailing unkeyed hangup on the couple topic. A's new client cannot key it, applies it, and the live call dies. The team concludes the durable log did not help and rolls back — the rollback is correct, because S3 as specified genuinely does not fix it.
fatal_flaws.repair: Move `call_id` on the wire out of S6 and into S3, as a pure additive field on the existing envelope: `{from, kind, data, call_id?}`. New clients ignore any signal whose `call_id` is absent or does not match the active call; old clients ignore the extra field. Then gate S6's remaining behaviour (batching, end_of_candidates, ReCall) on the same `client_caps` bitfield S4 uses. Also drop the 'both are idempotent' claim from S3 and state the real rule: during dual-read the log wins and the legacy broadcast is accepted only for a call_id the client itself is currently servicing.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Invariant 6 is contradicted by the mechanism that implements it. The invariant states that call injection is impossible because `call_signals` RLS carries an explicit `WITH CHECK (from_user = auth.uid() AND exists(...))`. But §2 states 'All transitions go through SECURITY DEFINER RPCs. Nothing writes calls.state_ord directly; table-level UPDATE is revoked', and `send_signal` is the only documented write path for signals. SECURITY DEFINER functions execute as the owner and bypass RLS on the tables they touch. So either (a) the RLS policy is dead code and the real guarantee is 'the RPC body checks correctly' — a code property that a future edit can silently break, exactly the class of thing the brief says an invariant must not be — or (b) direct INSERT is granted and the RPC is optional, in which case the seq assignment is bypassable and holes become possible again. The design cannot have both. This matters because invariant 6 is the entire answer to the 'malicious stranger who knows a couple UUID' threat.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A later change adds a convenience RPC that inserts a signal for a call the caller is not party to (say, an admin repair function, or a copy-paste of send_signal that forgets the party check). RLS does not catch it because SECURITY DEFINER bypasses it. The Layer-1 RLS test in verification passes, because it tests direct table access — which is revoked and therefore untested-in-practice.
fatal_flaws.repair: Pick one and say so. Preferred: keep the RPCs but make them enforce the same predicate the RLS policy states, and additionally run the RPC bodies with `SET row_security = on` plus an explicit `security_invoker`-style party check as the FIRST statement, so the check is unmissable. Then make the RLS policy real by granting INSERT/SELECT on `call_signals` to `authenticated` — belt and braces, and the Layer-1 test then exercises the path that actually runs. Restate invariant 6 as 'every signal write executes one party-membership predicate, asserted identically in RLS and in the RPC preamble, and the Layer-1 test drives the RPC path, not the table path.'

fatal_flaws.flaw: There is no rate limit on `start_call`, in an app whose threat model explicitly includes the partner. The design adds a mint quota for TURN and closes the unauthenticated ring endpoint, then leaves the authenticated ring endpoint unbounded. Any couple member can dial-and-end in a loop. Each dial writes N push_outbox rows and sends N HIGH-priority FCM messages. Two documented ceilings get burned: FCM's per-device limit of 240 messages/min and 5,000/hour, and — far worse — Android 13+'s rule that an app whose high-priority pushes do not consistently produce a user-visible notification is downgraded HIGH→NORMAL over a 7-day assessment window. The design correctly identifies this cliff in §4 and in the 10k scale ceiling ('the scariest undocumented cliff'), then leaves the one mechanism that can trigger it deliberately wide open. A downgraded message cannot start a foreground service, so one abusive week disables calling on that device for the following week.
fatal_flaws.scenario: An abusive partner (or a compromised account, or just a stuck retry loop in a future client build) dials 300 times in ten minutes. The callee declines or the calls expire; most produce no ring because the notification is suppressed while the app is foregrounded. FCM's 7-day heuristic downgrades the app. Calls now arrive minutes late on that handset, and the only signal is `originalPriority != priority` in `call_events` — which S7 ships four steps after S2.
fatal_flaws.repair: Enforce a dial budget inside `start_call` in the same transaction: reject with `rate_limited` if the caller has more than N rows in `calls` for this couple in the last M minutes (6 in 5 minutes is generous for a two-person app and stops every loop). Cheap to implement — the index on `(couple_id, state_ord)` plus a `created_at` range scan. Separately, enforce the priority-hygiene invariant in the SENDER, not as client policy: push_outbox rows carry `priority`, and only `kind='call'` may be high; make it a CHECK constraint so a future feature cannot spend the calls budget.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The push_outbox retry cadence is a chat mechanism applied to a 60-second deadline. §4: pg_net fast path, then 'a pg_cron job every 10 s drains pending rows... retryable → exponential backoff'. Inside a 60 s ring window, the first retry lands at up to +10 s (one sixth of the window gone), the second with exponential backoff at ~+30 s (half gone), and the third is past `expires_at` and will be sent with `ttl = floor(expires_at - now())` clamped to ≥0 — i.e. `ttl=0`, which FCM documents as now-or-never. So of the three retries the outbox promises, roughly one is useful. The design presents the outbox as what 'makes failures survivable and visible' for calls; for calls specifically it is neither, because the deadline is shorter than the retry schedule.
fatal_flaws.scenario: pg_net's documented 2 s default timeout trips on a slow FCM response (its own docs state no automatic retry). Cron picks the row up 9 s later, FCM 429s under a burst, backoff schedules +20 s, the call has 30 s left, the third attempt is past expiry. The user never rings and `push_outbox` ends at `dead` after the call is already gone.
fatal_flaws.repair: Give calls their own drain. A dedicated pg_cron job at 1 s for `kind='call'` with fixed 1 s / 2 s / 4 s / 8 s retries and a hard stop at `expires_at` — and never send a `ttl=0` call push, just abandon and record `push_abandoned` in call_events. Keep the 10 s exponential-backoff drain for chat and nudges. Also note that pg_cron's documented guidance is 'no more than 8 concurrent jobs, each under 10 minutes'; budget for that when S2 routes all app pushes through the same outbox.

fatal_flaws.flaw: `expires_at` as a STORED generated column will not create. The design specifies `expires_at timestamptz generated (created_at + interval '60 seconds')` and builds five invariants on it ('the ring deadline, the offer freshness window and the push lifetime are three readings of one column'). Postgres requires generation expressions to be IMMUTABLE; `timestamptz + interval` resolves to `timestamptz_pl_interval`, which is STABLE — interval carries day/month components whose meaning depends on the TimeZone setting. The DDL fails with 'generation expression is not immutable'. This is the single column the design's clock story rests on, and it does not compile.
fatal_flaws.scenario: S3's migration fails on the first statement, in CI or worse in production, and the obvious quick fix under pressure is to make it a client-supplied column — which reintroduces the device clock into the freshness gate and silently deletes invariant 5.
fatal_flaws.repair: Use a plain column with a server default: `expires_at timestamptz not null default (now() + interval '60 seconds')`, and revoke INSERT of that column from clients (the RPC is the only writer, so this is free). Assert in a Layer-1 test that a client-supplied expires_at is ignored. Verify before writing the migration: `create table t(a timestamptz default now(), b timestamptz generated always as (a + interval '60 seconds') stored);` against `supabase start`.

fatal_flaws.flaw: `device_id` does not exist anywhere in the app. Grep across E:/LDR/mobile/lib for `device_id`/`deviceId` returns zero hits. Yet `device_tokens(user_id, device_id, ...)`, `calls.answered_by_device`, `call_events(device_id)` and `turn_grants(user_id, device_id)` all key on it, spanning S2, S3, S5 and S7, and the TURN mint quota is enforced per `(user_id, device_id)`. research/delivery.md flags this exact gap ('No stable device identity. Supabase Auth gives you a user, not a device. Mint a UUID on first run, persist it in SECURE STORAGE'). The design never says where device_id comes from or what its persistence guarantees are. If it is minted into SharedPreferences — which is where this app already keeps `fsi_can_use` and the TURN cache — it resets on reinstall and on 'clear data', which is the same action a user takes when the disguised app misbehaves.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Partner reinstalls. New device_id, new FCM token. The old `device_tokens` row survives (the design's uniqueness is on `token`, not on `(user_id, device_id)`), so every subsequent call fans out a high-priority push to a dead token until FCM eventually returns UNREGISTERED — spending the device's high-priority budget on nothing. The old `turn_grants` rows are orphaned, so the per-user mint quota silently drifts. Reinstall loops make a user un-mintable.
fatal_flaws.repair: Add device identity as an explicit S1 prerequisite: mint a UUID on first run, store it in `flutter_secure_storage` (Android Keystore-backed, survives app data clear on most ROMs, and this app already ships crypto_core), and make `device_tokens` unique on `(user_id, device_id)` with the token as an updatable attribute — so a token refresh updates a row instead of creating one. Enforce the TURN quota on `user_id` alone with `device_id` as an attribute, so a device_id reset cannot reset the quota.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The cost model omits `call_events` and mis-models relay egress. (a) `call_events` is specified as the telemetry spine with seven event types per call per device plus a jsonb meta blob, and no retention is stated anywhere. At 100k users that is 3M calls × 2 devices × 7 = 42M rows/month with jsonb payloads, on the order of 10–15 GB/month, against a cost table that says 'Postgres ~60k live rows, negligible, ~$0' (which counts only call_signals). Supabase disk grows and is billed at $0.125/GB beyond 8 GB, and disk does not shrink. (b) `call_signals` is pruned by hourly DELETE of 42M rows/month, producing dead tuples and autovacuum load on a table that also serves the latency-critical catch-up query — the design's own source (research/supabase.md:87) points out that Supabase avoids exactly this for `realtime.messages` by using daily partitions with DROP TABLE, 'no bloat, no vacuum debt', and the design does not copy the pattern. (c) The 15 MB/min relayed-video figure derives from the 1 Mbps cap, but RELAYED_MAX_SEND_RATE is a VIDEO send cap; Opus audio, RTX/NACK retransmissions, RTCP, TURN ChannelData/Send-indication framing and IP/UDP headers ride on top — realistically +15–20%. That is ~$290 rather than $240 at 10k, and ~$3,400 rather than $2,850 at 100k.
fatal_flaws.scenario: At 100k the invoice is ~15% above the projected relay line and Postgres disk has quietly grown by 150 GB of telemetry over a year, which cannot be reclaimed by deleting rows. Meanwhile autovacuum on call_signals competes with the catch-up query during the evening call peak, and the symptom is 'rings are slower in the evening' with no obvious cause.
fatal_flaws.repair: Partition `call_signals` and `call_events` by day with a pg_cron partition-drop sweeper (copy Supabase's own realtime.messages shape), never DELETE. State a retention for call_events explicitly — 30 days is enough for the OEM latency dashboards S7 needs. Add +20% to the relay egress line and say it is protocol overhead on top of the video cap. Also add a Supabase realtime EGRESS line ($0.09/GB uncached beyond 250 GB) — SDP-bearing broadcasts are ~8 KB each and the cost table only counts message quota.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Layer B delivers no benefit on the path the design exists to fix, and the verification plan cannot test the path that broke before. (a) The per-call private topic is created at dial and joined by the callee — but a cold-started callee must establish a websocket, present a JWT, and have Realtime evaluate the `realtime.messages` RLS join, all inside the ring window on a cold radio. That is 1–3 s, so Layer B is pure overhead on the killed-app path and a benefit only for a foregrounded callee — the case that was never broken. §3's claim that 'the happy path costs no extra round trip' is true only for the case that already worked. (b) Verification Layer 3 specifies 'both RTCPeerConnections in the same Dart test process'. flutter_webrtc has no Dart-VM implementation; RTCPeerConnection requires platform channels, so this is an `integration_test` on a device — and two peer connections on one emulator connect over HOST candidates, which is structurally the same worthless evidence as two phones on one wifi that the verification section opens by condemning. (c) The specific historical bug was a RESPONSE SHAPE change (Cloudflare returning `iceServers` as an object, not a list). No layer in the plan pins Cloudflare's live response shape; a test double would have had to already know the bug to reproduce it.
fatal_flaws.scenario: S5 ships with the symmetric-NAT harness green because the harness uses a Cloudflare stub built from the current client's assumptions. Cloudflare changes a field name or nesting six months later. Every cross-carrier call fails; every same-wifi test passes; the harness stays green because it never talks to Cloudflare. This is the two-month outage recurring with more tests than before.
fatal_flaws.repair: (a) Say plainly that Layer B is a foreground optimisation and that killed-app ring latency is a Layer C number; measure and publish push→ring p50/p95 from `call_events` for backgrounded devices only, and do not let a Layer B improvement mask a Layer C regression. (b) Split Layer 3: the FSM/signalling half runs headless in the Dart VM against a fake channel with NO real PeerConnection (that is where the reorder/duplicate/delay adversary belongs); the media half runs in the NAT harness. (c) Add a CI contract test that hits the LIVE turn-credentials function daily, asserts the parsed result contains at least one `turn:`/`turns:` URL plus username and credential, and fails the build on a shape change. That single test is the one that would have caught the bug that motivated this entire document.

fatal_flaws.flaw: SDP now sits at rest and is replicated, which is a privacy regression for this specific product. Today the offer lives in an ephemeral broadcast plus a `call_invites` row. The target design writes every offer, answer and ICE batch into `call_signals` as plaintext jsonb, and the AFTER INSERT trigger copies each one into `realtime.messages`, retained 72 hours to 4 days per research/supabase.md:87. SDP and ICE candidates carry both partners' LAN addresses and public IPs — i.e. approximate location and ISP, per call, for both parties. For an app whose entire premise is a disguised launcher and whose research corpus includes a dedicated e2ee.md, the design never mentions this and never states what threat model it is accepting. §3 correctly strips `from_name` from the push for exactly this reason, then puts a far more identifying payload in a durable table.
fatal_flaws.scenario: The Supabase project is compromised, or a support/service-role credential leaks, or a future contributor adds a permissive view. The attacker gets a 72-hour rolling history of both partners' public IPs with per-call timestamps — location and daily-routine inference for a couple who chose this app specifically to avoid being observed.
fatal_flaws.repair: Prune `call_signals` on call END, not hourly — the log's only consumer is the two parties of a live call, so a row's useful life is at most 60 s plus the call duration. Have `end_call` delete the call's ICE and SDP payloads in the same transaction (keep the row skeleton for ordering if needed, null the payload). State the retention as a documented invariant: 'no SDP or ICE payload outlives its call by more than one sweeper interval.' If Layer B is kept, use `realtime.broadcast_changes` with a payload of `{call_id, seq, kind}` only and make the client fetch the payload from the log — the seq-cursor rule already forces a fetch on any gap, so this costs a round trip only on the SDP-bearing signals.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The scale ceiling measures the wrong axis and is optimistic in its framing. The section concludes 'Calling is not the thing that breaks' at 100k and names Realtime concurrency as the wall. But the design's own §5 states the truth: on Samsung/Xiaomi/Oppo/Vivo/OnePlus there is no fix, force-stop is an absolute platform wall, and the honest sentence is 'if you swipe this app away on this phone, calls will not ring.' The three named target handsets — IN2015, OnePlus 7, Vivo — are all on the worst or near-worst dontkillmyapp tier. So the real calling ceiling is a per-device success rate that is present at n=2, does not improve with scale, and is unaffected by every table, RPC and index in this document. Stating a 1k/10k/100k ceiling in terms of Supabase quotas, when the binding constraint is a fixed fraction of handsets on which the architecture cannot ring at all, is honest in the body and optimistic in the summary.
fatal_flaws.scenario: The team ships S0 through S8, every Layer-1 SQL test is green, and the two actual users still report that calls do not ring when the app has been swiped away — because both own worst-tier handsets. The architecture is correct and the product is still broken, and the scale_ceiling section gave no warning that this was the expected outcome.
fatal_flaws.repair: Lead the scale ceiling with the device axis: 'Calling's ceiling is not user count. It is the fraction of handsets on which a killed app can be woken — currently 0 of 3 target devices without user-granted autostart exemptions. Supabase quotas do not bind until ~600k users on calling's own traffic.' Then make S7's diagnostics screen a S1 deliverable, not a S7 one — it is the only thing in the plan that addresses the actual ceiling, and it is scheduled last. Add the per-OEM ring success rate from `call_events` as the domain's single headline metric, above p50 latency.

fatal_flaws.flaw: S0's authentication change breaks care reminders. S0 step 2 adds a Bearer header to `notify_call`'s `net.http_post` and re-enables `verify_jwt` on the `reach-notify` function. But E:/LDR/supabase/20260628_care_call_push.sql defines TWO triggers posting to the same function — `notify_care` on `care_nudges` and `notify_call` on `call_invites` — and fcm_push.sql/message_push.sql route other kinds there as well. Turning on `verify_jwt` for the function silently kills every caller that was not updated. S0 is presented as the safest, ship-today step with 'risk: near zero'.
fatal_flaws.scenario: S0 ships. Calls ring fine. Care reminders and message pushes stop entirely, and the failure is invisible because `net.http_post` is fire-and-forget and the function 'always returns HTTP 200 to avoid webhook retry storms'. Nobody notices for days.
fatal_flaws.repair: Make S0 step 2 update every trigger that posts to `reach-notify` in the same migration — grep `functions/v1/reach-notify` across E:/LDR/supabase/*.sql first and enumerate them in the migration header. Add a Layer-1 assertion that no trigger function body contains a `net.http_post` to that URL without an Authorization key, so a future trigger cannot regress it.

verdict: The core move — online = membership of a live authorized socket, last-seen = a server-computed integer age, ephemeral state off the WAL — is correct and is the right one mechanism. The write-path invariants (no timestamp parameter, `greatest(existing, now())`, the 240s anchor predicate) are genuinely structural and I could not break them. But the design is written entirely from the tracked user's point of view and never asks what the OBSERVING client does when its own socket is dead, which is the exact bug the app has today and which this design would reproduce while deleting the accidental workaround that currently masks it. Three fatal items, eight serious. Not shippable as written; shippable after F1-F3 and F7.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The presence fold has no socket-liveness gate on the READING side, and the design simultaneously deletes the only thing in the app that currently forces a fresh socket. Invariant 1 says every failure converges on OFFLINE — that is true for the tracked user, and false for the observer. When the observing client's socket is silently dead, `presenceState()` keeps returning the last-known set forever, and §5's 'pure fold over the current set' faithfully renders the partner as ONLINE. There is no leave event, so the 12s flap grace never arms. Supabase documents this exact case (research/mobile.md source: backgrounded apps get heartbeat timers throttled, the socket 'can silently drop' and 'your application then stops receiving events without any explicit error message'). I grepped: `heartbeatCallback` has zero hits in mobile/lib. The ONLY reason this is survivable today is app_shell.dart:77-78's unconditional `realtime.disconnect()` + `connect()` on every resume — which §7 of this design explicitly removes ('do not disconnect; debounce lifecycle bursts to 1 action / 400 ms'). This violates hard constraint 2 (nothing may depend on a reliable socket) at the one place the design never looked.
fatal_flaws.scenario: MIUI freezes the app, or the phone sits in Doze for 40 minutes. Android throttles the 25s heartbeat timer; the server drops the socket at 60s; the client's Dart timer never fires so it never notices. User opens the app. Resume no longer forces a reconnect. The fold renders from the pre-background CRDT snapshot: partner shown ONLINE with a green dot. Real state: partner has been asleep for six hours. The stale window is bounded only by (time to foreground) + 25s heartbeat + 10s timeout ≈ 35s after resume, and it renders the single most damaging wrong answer in a couples app ('she was online and didn't reply'). Two phones on one wifi never background-freeze, so this passes every test you can run on your desk.
fatal_flaws.repair: Make socket health an explicit input to the fold, not an assumption. Three parts: (1) the observer renders `unknown` (a third state — no dot, show last-seen only) until a `presence_sync` has arrived on a socket whose last heartbeat ACK is within 2x the interval; a stale snapshot must never render as `online`. (2) Register a `heartbeatCallback` (Supabase's own documented fix) that calls `connect()` on status `disconnected`/`timeout` — this is the client-side half of Signal's `GET /v1/keepalive` zombie eviction, which research/presence.md §1 cites and this design cites but does not adopt. (3) On resume, do not trust the socket: issue `presence_last_seen()` (plain HTTP, fails fast, needs no socket) and render from that until a fresh sync lands. This also fixes the resume path for free — you get the debounced no-disconnect behaviour you wanted AND a correctness gate, instead of trading one for the other.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The `seq` ordinal is specified as 'a per-session monotonic integer starting at 0' with receiver-side drop of `seq <= lastSeenSeq`, but the design never states what `lastSeenSeq` is KEYED BY, and `session_id` is regenerated on every channel join. Implemented literally with a per-user `lastSeenSeq` — the obvious reading, since the receiver renders per-user state — every reconnect resets the sender's seq to 0 while the receiver's watermark is at 40, so every subsequent typing/room/geo event from that user is dropped permanently for the life of the receiver's process. Invariant 11 claims 'a stuck typing indicator is impossible in both directions'; the literal implementation makes a permanently-dead typing indicator certain. Separately, the spec uses one counter for three event types (`typing`, `room`, `geo`) — if `lastSeenSeq` is also single, a `room` at seq=7 suppresses a `typing` at seq=6 that was merely delivered second.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Train, 30-second network gaps. Partner A rejoins `couple:<id>` six times in ten minutes; each join mints a new session_id and resets seq to 0. Partner B's receiver holds lastSeenSeq=40 from the first session. From the second reconnect onward, A types and B sees nothing — forever, until B restarts the app. This is indistinguishable from the current bug and would be reported as 'the typing fix didn't work again'. It cannot be caught by the property test in verification §1, which only covers the presence fold, not the broadcast receiver.
fatal_flaws.repair: State it explicitly and test it: `lastSeenSeq` is keyed by `(session_id, event_type)`, and a session_id never seen before starts at -1 (accept everything). Drop the map entry when the session's presence key leaves. Add a property test alongside §1: generate random session rotations with seq restarting at 0 and assert every event from a NEW session is accepted regardless of prior watermarks. Better still — since Phoenix already delivers in order per topic per sender, and the 3s pause / 15s receiver expiry already bound staleness — consider deleting `seq` for `typing` entirely and keeping it only where you can name a reordering that the expiry does not already cover. One mechanism (receiver expiry) beats two (expiry plus a watermark you have to key correctly).

fatal_flaws.flaw: Invariant 7 is not an invariant — it is a client convention with no defined failure behaviour, and its 'reservation' has no mechanism. 'Every discretionary track() call passes through a token bucket of capacity 2 refilling 1 per 15 s... The cap cannot be exceeded regardless of navigation speed.' A token bucket in the Dart client cannot constrain anything: an older build, a crashed timer, or any code path that calls track() outside the bucket exceeds it. The platform's answer to exceeding `CLIENT_PRESENCE_MAX_CALLS=5 / CLIENT_PRESENCE_WINDOW_MS=30000` is to REJECT the call — and the design specifies no behaviour for a rejected track(). A rejected track on JOIN means the user has an open, authorized socket and is not in the presence set: rendered offline while actively using the app, with no leave event and no timer to retry. The design also never establishes whether the 5-call window is per-socket (resets on reconnect) or per-client-identity (does not) — the whole 'reserve 2 for join+leave' argument depends on which, and it is asserted rather than measured.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Commute. Radio flaps every 30s: 2 joins/minute, each needing a mandatory track(). Between flaps the user navigates Home to Chat to Vault to Chat — 4 zone changes. Bucket capacity 2, refill 1/15s: the zone changes drain it, the next join's track() is either deferred by the client (invisible until a token refills) or issued and rejected by the server (invisible with no retry at all). Either way the partner sees offline while the user is typing to them. This is the current production symptom, reproduced by the fix.
fatal_flaws.repair: Split the paths and make the failure loud. (1) The join track() is MANDATORY and bypasses the bucket entirely; only zone updates are discretionary. (2) A rejected or deferred join-track must retry with Full Jitter and must surface as a counter — 'track_rejected' alongside the flap rate in §7 telemetry — because a silent failure here is exactly the class of bug that survived five fixes. (3) Stop asserting the cap and measure it: verification §4(b) already drives zone changes at max rate; extend it to drive JOIN/LEAVE churn at max rate against a real project and record whether the window resets on reconnect. Until that number exists, the 'cannot be exceeded' claim should be labelled INFERRED. (4) Demote invariant 7 to a design rule; the only true invariant here is 'a user with no accepted track() renders offline', which is safe — the bug is that it is also wrong.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Stage 0 delivers none of its claimed standalone security value, and it is the stage the design tells you to ship 'first regardless of the rest of the plan'. Creating a NEW private topic `couple:<couple_id>` does not make the EXISTING topics private. `screen_presence:<coupleId>`, `mood_burst:<coupleId>`, `call:<coupleId>`, `capsule_proximity:<coupleId>` and `mood_lamp:none` are separate topic names, joined by clients with no `private` flag, and Supabase bypasses `realtime.messages` RLS entirely for public channels. I grepped: `private: true` has zero hits in mobile/lib and there is no `realtime.messages` policy in supabase/*.sql. So after Stage 0 ships, the room-by-room surveillance feed described in open decision 3 is still fully open to anyone holding a couple UUID — which the app's own hardening_2026_08.sql notes is 'the first path segment of every never-expiring couple_media URL'. Closing it requires migrating the CONSUMERS of those topics, which crosses into the chat and calling domains.
fatal_flaws.scenario: You ship Stage 0 on its stated rationale, believe the hole is closed, and deprioritise Stages 3/5. A stranger with a leaked couple_media URL continues to receive a live room-by-room feed of a partner moving through an intimate app, plus raw GPS every 4s from capsule_proximity, plus SDP/ICE from call:<id> — for however many release cycles the rest of the plan takes.
fatal_flaws.repair: Rename Stage 0 honestly: it is 'stand up the new private channel', with zero security value on its own. Then add a real Stage 0.5 that IS independently shippable and DOES close the hole: flip the existing `screen_presence:` and `capsule_proximity:` topics to `private: true` and add the matching `realtime.messages` policy, in one client change plus one SQL statement, with no dependency on the presence rework. That is a two-line client diff per topic. If you want the surveillance hole closed first, close it — do not close a different hole and claim credit.

fatal_flaws.flaw: On a hard kill, last-seen jumps from 'Online' straight to 'about 5 minutes ago' with nothing in between, because the two mechanisms are tuned independently but rendered on the same surface. The anchor runs at 300s +/- 30s with a 240s predicate, so `last_confirmed_at` is up to ~300s behind reality at the moment of death. The CRDT holds the user online for another 35-72s. When the leave finally lands, the client renders the server-computed age — which is now ~360s. The design's own defence ('5 min is below any human-meaningful last-seen granularity') is contradicted by open decision 4, which coarsens display to 1-MINUTE granularity: at that granularity a 5-minute error is five buckets wrong, and it is wrong in the direction that reads as a lie.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Partner is chatting. Android LMK kills the app at 14:00:00; last anchor was 13:55:10. At 14:01:00 the socket times out, at 14:01:12 the grace expires, and the UI flips from 'Online' to 'last seen 6 minutes ago' — claiming she left before the message you just watched her read. In a couples app this reads as the app covering for her, which is worse than either honest answer.
fatal_flaws.repair: Floor the age with what the observer measured itself, which requires no clock and no extra write: the observer SAW the partner in the presence set until the leave, so `displayed_age = min(server_age, monotonic_elapsed_since_observed_leave)`. That is a `Stopwatch`, consistent with invariant 4, and it makes the hard-kill case render 'last seen just now' -> '1 minute ago' -> ... correctly. Keep the 300s anchor as the cold-start/never-observed backstop it actually is. State the contract as 'last-seen is exact when the observer was connected at the moment of departure, and accurate to +/-5 minutes otherwise'.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The 'clean background' path is counted as the reliable common case but contains a PostgREST round-trip initiated at the exact moment Android is taking the process away. §6 collapses `untrack() + presence_mark('offline')` into one LEAVING transition, but they have completely different reliability: untrack() is a frame on an already-open socket (usually lands), while presence_mark is a fresh HTTPS request that must resolve, connect, round-trip and commit during onPause — with App Standby and MIUI freezing the process within milliseconds. When it does not land, `state` stays 'online', `ended_at` stays null, and `last_confirmed_at` is up to 300s stale — i.e. the clean case silently degrades into the hard-kill case, and does so on exactly the aggressive-OEM devices the app targets (memory: IN2015/Vivo/OnePlus7).
fatal_flaws.scenario: User taps Home on a Xiaomi. untrack() lands, partner correctly sees offline in ~12s. presence_mark never completes. Partner opens the profile 20 minutes later, gets `state='online'` and an age derived from a 5-minute-old anchor. The durable row now contradicts the CRDT, and the durable row is what a partner on a train (no socket) sees.
fatal_flaws.repair: Stop treating a durable write at lifecycle-pause as reliable. Either (a) derive the durable last-seen from the leave rather than the client: have the anchor be the ONLY durable write and accept +/-5 min, dropping presence_mark('offline') entirely — one mechanism instead of two; or (b) keep presence_mark but make the read path never trust `state`: `presence_last_seen()` should return only the age and let the caller decide online-ness from the CRDT, so a stale `state='online'` cannot be rendered. (b) is one line of SQL and removes a whole class of contradiction between the two stores. Do not rely on onPause completing an HTTP request — that is the same category of assumption as 'the client sends an ack'.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Internal contradiction on offline latency: §7 states 'Clean background -> offline <=2 s (explicit untrack(); the common case)' while §5 arms an unconditional 12s flap-suppression grace on 'when the last key for a user disappears'. The observer cannot distinguish a clean untrack from a socket death — both arrive as a leave — so the grace applies to both and the real clean-background latency is ~12s, not <=2s. The <=2s figure is then carried into open decision 4 as the product contract.
fatal_flaws.scenario: You publish '<=2s' as the internal contract, then field-test: partner backgrounds the app, tester counts twelve seconds. Reported as 'the presence fix is slow'. Or worse, someone 'fixes' it by skipping the grace on the first leave — which reintroduces the wifi/LTE-handoff flicker the grace exists to kill.
fatal_flaws.repair: One number, honestly derived: clean background = 12-14s (grace-bound), hard kill = 47-72s. If <=2s matters for the clean case, buy it explicitly — send a broadcast `bye {session_id}` immediately before untrack(), and let the observer skip the grace only for a leave whose session_id was explicitly announced. A forged or replayed `bye` can only accelerate the offline transition for the session that sent it, which is the safe direction, and it keeps the grace for every unannounced disappearance. Then <=2s is a real number instead of a contradicted one.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Moving every user onto a private channel introduces a brand-new Postgres serialization point that the design never prices, never names, and tests for the wrong failure. Realtime evaluates private-channel RLS at join against `realtime.messages` using its OWN connection pool, which research/supabase.md documents as `DB_POOL_SIZE=5` by default — 'Five connections gate every private-channel join for your entire project'. The proposed policy calls a SECURITY DEFINER helper doing a subquery on `profiles`. Today the app pays zero join-time RLS (public topics and postgres_changes). The scale section counts joins only against the 2,500/s `too_many_joins` quota and concludes '13 joins/s, comfortably under' — but the binding constraint at a correlated reconnect is 5 concurrent RLS queries, and its failure mode is join TIMEOUT, not `too_many_joins`. Verification §4(c) measures the wrong signal for the same reason.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Supabase restarts a Realtime node, or a regional carrier flaps at 18:00. Several thousand of the 8,000 concurrent devices rejoin within a second. Each join queues behind a 5-connection pool for a `profiles` subquery. Joins time out rather than being refused; clients retry; the design's Full Jitter helps the spacing but not the pool depth. Every user in the storm renders their partner offline (correctly, per invariant 1) — which means a network blip becomes a fleet-wide 'everyone appears offline' event, and the retries look exactly like the 'rapid reconnection loops' Supabase names as a top cause of manual project suspension.
fatal_flaws.repair: Three things. (1) Name `DB_POOL_SIZE` in the design and raise it in the dashboard before Stage 1 — it is a settable number and the default of 5 was chosen for projects with no private channels. (2) Make the policy cost O(1) with no join: the SECURITY DEFINER helper should read `couple_id` from the JWT claim if you can put it there at pairing time, or at minimum be a single indexed lookup with `(select auth.uid())` wrapped per the documented 179ms->9ms pattern. (3) Change verification §4(c) to measure join LATENCY distribution and timeout rate under a 200-client storm, not just `too_many_joins` count. `too_many_joins` is the failure you will not get.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The privacy design contradicts its own verification step, and the resolution is bad either way. §8 gates `presence.read` / `presence.write` — which in Supabase's model disables PRESENCE on the channel while leaving broadcast working. Verification §4(d) instead asserts 'the channel join is refused server-side'. These are different mechanisms with different blast radii. If §8 is right, 4(d)'s test fails and the assertion is wrong. If 4(d) is right, then turning off `share_presence` — a last-seen privacy toggle — also silently kills typing, room and live location for BOTH partners, because §1 puts all of them on the same `couple:<id>` channel. That product consequence is nowhere acknowledged. Separately, multi-device is declared to 'work with no change', but only `last_confirmed_at` is guarded by `greatest()`; `state`, `session_id` and `ended_at` are blind last-writer-wins on a row keyed by `user_id`, so a phone going offline stamps `state='offline'` while the tablet is still connected.
fatal_flaws.scenario: (a) A user turns off last-seen sharing for privacy. Typing indicators and live location stop working in both directions with no explanation, and the bug report is 'typing broke again'. (b) Multi-device: user is on the tablet, closes the phone app. `presence_mark(session_phone,'offline')` sets state='offline', ended_at=now(). Partner, on a train with no socket, falls back to `presence_last_seen()` and is told 'offline, just now' while the user is actively on the tablet.
fatal_flaws.repair: (a) Commit to the §8 mechanism (gate presence.read/write only, leave broadcast alone), delete the 4(d) assertion about join refusal, and add the real test: with share_presence=false, assert the peer receives zero presence frames AND still receives typing frames. If you actually want typing suppressed too, that is a second predicate on the broadcast policy and should be stated as such. (b) Either key `presence_session` on `(user_id, device_id)` and let the read path aggregate, or — cheaper and honest for now — drop `state` and `ended_at` from the durable row entirely and derive online exclusively from the CRDT, leaving `last_confirmed_at` as the only durable field. Open decision 6's claim that multi-device 'works with no change' is false as written and should say so.

fatal_flaws.flaw: `presence_last_seen()` is called 'once per chat/profile open and once on resume. Not on a timer' — with no retry policy, no backoff, and no defined render for the failure case. Deleting the 15s poll is right; replacing it with a single unretried request is not. The design also deletes the cached `presence` row that today at least gives the UI something stale to show, and `ServerClock` along with it, so a cold start with no network has literally nothing to render.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Offline for 3 days, opens the app on a train. Resume fires `presence_last_seen()` into a 200ms window of signal; it times out. Nothing retries it because it is not on a timer and the next trigger is the next resume. The socket is also flapping so the CRDT is empty. The user sees neither an online state nor a last-seen, for the whole journey, with no error and no spinner — and the design has no specified behaviour for this, so whatever the implementer does becomes the contract.
fatal_flaws.repair: Give it the same treatment the rest of the app's reads need: coalesce by couple_id (singleflight), retry with Full Jitter on failure up to a cap, refetch on socket reconnect as well as on resume, and persist the last (age, monotonic_receipt_instant) pair to disk so a cold start renders 'last seen ~3d ago' rather than blank. Define the empty state explicitly — 'unknown', not 'offline' — so it composes with the socket-health gate from F1 instead of contradicting it.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Two cost assumptions are wrong in the same direction. (1) 'Broadcast self:false ... means a couple channel bills 2 per event, not 3 — this is already assumed in the numbers above' — but presence is not broadcast. Presence diffs are batched by the server at PRESENCE_BROADCAST_PERIOD_IN_MS=1500 and delivered to every subscriber on the topic including the originator; there is no `self:false` for presence. Presence events bill 3, not 2. (2) The 100k scale ceiling concludes 'Presence is not what breaks' from a quota (1,000 presence msg/s) that research/presence.md explicitly flags as unvalidated: Supabase publishes broadcast benchmarks and 'publishes no Presence benchmark at all', and their architecture doc states that on connect 'the state of that user is sent to all connected Realtime nodes' — presence is a per-TENANT cluster-wide replicated CRDT, so the load scales with churn x cluster size, not with your 2-member topic. The design notes this once as a caveat and then uses the confident '14x headroom' number in the summary.
fatal_flaws.scenario: You budget 470M messages/month at 100k users. Presence's share bills at 3x rather than 2x, and the 8,000-key CRDT with a 20-minute permdown behaves in a way no published benchmark covers. The first symptom is not a bill — it is presence sync latency degrading under churn, which is unobservable until users report it, because there is no presence benchmark to compare against.
fatal_flaws.repair: Correct the presence line to 3 billable messages per event and re-run the three totals (the change is small — presence transitions are only 2 of the 26 events — but the stated assumption is wrong and will be copied). More importantly, downgrade the 100k verdict from 'Presence is not what breaks' to 'unknown above a few thousand concurrent presence keys, evidence: absence of a published benchmark', and make the concurrent-presence-key count a metric you ship at Stage 1 alongside the flap rate. An honest unknown is worth more than a confident number derived from a quota nobody has validated.

fatal_flaws.flaw: 'Revert = one boolean' is not true for this app. mobile/lib/core/feature_flags.dart holds `static const bool` values — build-time only — and there is no remote config anywhere in the repo (grepped: no remoteConfig/app_config/kill_switch). This is a deliberately non-Play-Store, sideloaded private app, so reverting Stage 2 means rebuilding an APK and manually reinstalling on every device. The migration's central safety claim — that each stage is 'independently revertible in one commit or one SQL statement' — holds for the SQL stages (0, 9, 10) and is false for the client stages (1-8), which are the ones that flip user-visible behaviour.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Stage 2 flips the read to the presence fold. A device-specific bug appears on the Vivo. Rolling back is: revert commit, rebuild, transfer APK, uninstall/reinstall on each phone — hours to days, during which presence is broken. The design's own diagnosis is that five previous fixes 'passed then failed in production'; a revert path measured in days is what turns a failed stage into a multi-week outage, which is the exact history being designed against.
fatal_flaws.repair: Before Stage 1, add the one thing that makes every later stage genuinely revertible: a server-read config row (a `couple_settings`/`app_config` table with a `presence_source` enum, read on resume, cached locally, defaulting to the old path). It is one table, one read, and it converts every client stage from 'rebuild and reinstall' to 'one UPDATE'. It also makes the Stage 1 shadow mode and the Stage 6 dual-write comparison controllable per user rather than per build. Without it, do not describe stages 1-8 as independently revertible.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Two smaller specification gaps that will be implemented literally. (a) `presence_mark(p_session uuid, p_state text)` is an upsert on `user_id` but takes no `couple_id`, and `presence_session.couple_id` is declared NOT-NULL-in-spirit ('for RLS only') — the INSERT branch has nothing to write there. (b) Stage 4's premise is wrong in a way worth knowing: it says "'Actively in chat' becomes `zone == chat` from the presence payload", but presence_service.dart:120 already reads `isActivelyInChat => typingInChat && isTrulyOnline`, and `chatLastRead` (parsed at line 73) has zero consumers in mobile/lib. The 12 writes/min are pure write-only waste today.
fatal_flaws.scenario: (a) A user's first-ever presence_mark on a fresh install inserts a row with a null couple_id; the RLS policy on presence_session then excludes their partner from reading it, and last-seen silently returns null for that user forever. (b) An implementer builds the zone plumbing as a prerequisite for Stage 4, delaying the single largest steady-state cost reduction in the app behind work it does not need.
fatal_flaws.repair: (a) Resolve couple_id inside the SECURITY DEFINER function from `(select auth.uid())` rather than taking it as a parameter — same pattern as the existing `current_user_couple_id()` helper, and it keeps the 'client supplies no fields the server can derive' discipline that makes invariant 2 work. (b) Re-scope Stage 4 to what it actually is: delete `setChatLastRead` and its 5s timer outright, no replacement needed, shippable today, independent of every other stage. That makes the highest-value change in the plan also the cheapest one — move it to Stage 1.

verdict: The design is the best-argued document in this set and it still fails, in the same way the code it replaces fails: it fixes one instance of a bug class and reinstalls the class in a different currency. Three fatal breaks. (1) It gives a collapse_key to all four classes, which makes every push in the app collapsible and therefore subject to FCM's per-app-per-device 20-burst / 1-per-3-minute refill (research/push.md:42, :124, :199) — so chat volume now burns the ring's *delivery* budget exactly as it previously burned the ring's *priority* budget, and the design's own rate guard plus its own 45s call deadline convert that into a phone that does not ring. Worse, `call` gets `ttl:"0s"`, which means FCM never stores it, which means the collapse key buys the call literally nothing while costing it the throttle. (2) The watermark that licenses the entire "nothing is lost, it's just late" promise is `messages.seq`, which already exists (receipts_v2.sql:28-31) as a plain `nextval` — assigned at INSERT, not at commit. The live catch-up is `.gt('seq', _maxSeq)` (chat_repository.dart:183, chat_screen.dart:343). Two same-couple inserts that commit out of assignment order permanently skip the lower one. Telegram's `pts` has commit-order assignment; a bare sequence does not, and the design cites the analogy to license a property the mechanism lacks. It also never mentions `seq` exists and never builds `stream_seq` in the migration. (3) `stream_seq` is declared "message class only" and there is no cursor for reach/care/call anywhere in the design or the codebase — so with `reach ttl=600s`, a Reach missed during a 3-day absence is *gone*, which is the precise failure the design opens by diagnosing. The headline invariant is true for one of four classes. Beyond those: the `unique(token_hash)` steal is a cross-user push-takeover primitive that is exploitable through the `profiles.fcm_token` leak the design itself documents, and stays exploitable for stages 1-3 because the column is not dropped until stage 4; quarantine cannot distinguish force-stop from the RARE standby bucket (where the app's network is disabled but the notification still displays — push.md:55), so its flagship product output tells a partner a lie about a working phone; the latency SLI measures ack-buffer-flush delay, not delivery; "duplicate notification is impossible" is false at the worker-dies-after-FCM-200 boundary; and the Level-4 canary needs a second phone and cannot detect the outage it exists to detect, because probe enqueue, drain and alert-write all ride the chain under test. The outbox core (row trigger + SKIP LOCKED lease + dead-letter as a queryable state) is right and should be built. The parameter table, the watermark story, the quarantine product feature and the canary are not shippable as written.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Every class gets a collapse_key, which makes every push in the app collapsible and subjects the whole app to FCM's per-app-per-device collapsible throttle: burst of 20, refill 1 per 3 minutes (research/push.md:42, :124, :199 — 'a chatty collapse key starves the others'). The budget is per app per device, not per key, so priority_rank in the outbox buys nothing: FCM's bucket is already empty by the time the call row is claimed. The design's own per-device rate guard then does the worst possible thing — 'defer rather than send' — and the call's 45s class deadline fires, marking the row `superseded`, 'never sent'. Compounding it: `call` is specified `ttl:"0s"`, which per push.md:38 means FCM never stores the message; collapse only ever replaces a *stored* pending message, so the `c:<couple_id>` key cannot help a ttl=0 ring under any circumstance. It is pure cost. The design correctly identifies that chat volume is burning the ring's priority privilege (fcm_service.dart:139-146 + push.md:36) and then reinstalls the identical coupling in the collapsible-quota currency.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Partner B is backgrounded (walking, phone in pocket) — the exact case push exists for. A and B exchange messages for ten minutes. The design's own message rate guard permits one push per device per 30s = 20 pushes, draining the entire 20-token burst; refill is 1 per 3 minutes, so the bucket now holds ~0. A calls B two minutes later. The `call` outbox row is claimed at rank 0, ahead of everything — and the per-device rate guard sees zero collapsible tokens and defers. At created_at+45s the row is marked `superseded, never sent`. B's phone does not ring. If the guard is instead skipped, FCM throttles the send and a ttl=0 message that cannot be delivered immediately is discarded (push.md:38). Both branches: no ring, no error, `state='superseded'` in a table nobody is paging on.
fatal_flaws.repair: Collapse keys only for the `message` class. `call`, `reach` and `care` are low-volume, time-critical and must stay non-collapsible so they are governed only by 240/min and 5,000/hr, not 20-burst/1-per-3-min. That leaves one collapse key (`m:<couple_id>`), well inside the 4-key budget, and it is the only class where coalescing is worth anything. Then make the per-device rate guard class-aware: it may defer `message`, and must never defer `call` — a rank-0 row bypasses the guard entirely, because a deferred ring is a failed ring. State the corrected invariant: a collapse key is only ever attached to a class whose TTL is long enough for FCM to store the message, since collapse is meaningless on a message that is never stored.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The 'monotone watermark' the design builds three invariants on (#4 superseding is safe, #9 push is a hint / cursor is delivery, and the user-facing promise 'nothing is lost, it's just late') is not monotone in the sense required. It already exists as `messages.seq`, defined at E:/LDR/supabase/receipts_v2.sql:28-31 as a plain `nextval('public.messages_seq_seq')` default — assigned at INSERT time, not at commit time. The live catch-up query is `.eq('couple_id',…).gt('seq', afterSeq).order('seq').limit(500)` at E:/LDR/mobile/lib/features/chat/chat_repository.dart:183-189, with the cursor computed as `max(seq)` of what is locally visible (E:/LDR/mobile/lib/features/chat/chat_screen.dart:343). A row whose seq was assigned earlier but whose transaction commits later becomes visible *below* a cursor that has already passed it, and `.gt` never returns it again. The design cites Telegram's `pts` as the precedent, but `pts` is assigned in a serialized per-dialog apply step precisely so that assignment order equals visibility order; a bare Postgres sequence has no such property. The design also never notices `seq` exists, refers to `stream_seq` as if it were part of the new schema, and the migration plan (stages 0-5) never builds or repairs it — so the load-bearing artifact of the whole design is assumed, not delivered. The `.limit(500)` with no continuation loop is a second, independent truncation of the same query.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Both partners act simultaneously — the brief's glare case, and routine in a couples app. A's insert takes seq=1041 and B's takes seq=1042; B's transaction commits first. B's client (or A's, on reconnect) runs catch-up, sees 1042, sets its cursor to 1042. A's transaction commits 40ms later. The next catch-up asks for `seq > 1042`. Message 1041 is now permanently invisible: it is not in the list, not re-emitted by postgres_changes (live-only, cursor = join moment — the code comment at chat_repository.dart:176-181 says exactly this), and not reachable by any later catch-up. This is 'she never texted me', reproduced by the mechanism advertised as its cure. Separately: 3 days offline with >500 queued messages returns 500 rows, advances the cursor to the 500th, and `_catchUp()` is not looped — the remainder waits for an unrelated future trigger.
fatal_flaws.repair: State which of these you are buying, because the design must pick one. (a) Bounded-lookback read: query `seq > cursor - K` and dedupe on `id` client-side, where K bounds the concurrent-commit window; cheap, and correct as long as K exceeds the longest same-couple transaction. (b) Commit-ordered assignment: a BEFORE INSERT trigger takes `seq` from a per-couple counter held under a row lock on `couples`, so assignment order is serialized with commit order for that couple; costs a row lock per message, trivial at 2 writers. (c) Snapshot-safe advance: never advance the cursor past `min(backend_xmin)` at read time. Whichever you choose, it belongs in Stage 0 or Stage 1, before anything depends on it — and the catch-up must loop until a page returns fewer than `limit` rows, advancing the cursor per persisted page so a 30-second network gap costs one page, not the whole backlog.

fatal_flaws.flaw: 'Push is a hint whose loss costs latency, never data' is stated as a global invariant and used to justify the honest user-facing promise, but the design's own schema restricts the watermark to one class: `stream_seq bigint (message class only)`. There is no cursor, no catch-up and no resync path for `reach`, `care` or `call` anywhere in the design — and none in the codebase (a grep of E:/LDR/mobile/lib for catch-up/cursor logic returns hits only in features/chat). So the design simultaneously assigns `reach` a 600s TTL — a deliberate, bounded window after which FCM discards the message (push.md:38) — and provides no mechanism to recover a Reach that expired in that window. Three of the four classes are 'push is the only delivery', which is exactly the property the design correctly condemns in the current system ('31 seconds in a tunnel means FCM discards it and never mentions it again — designed data loss') and then reproduces at 600 seconds instead of 30.
fatal_flaws.scenario: User is offline for 3 days (the brief's case). Day 1: partner sends a Reach. The outbox row is claimed, sent, FCM accepts it, `state='sent'`. FCM holds it for 600s and discards it. Day 3: user opens the app on the train. The message catch-up runs and recovers every chat message. Nothing recovers the Reach — there is no `reach_events` cursor to consult. The user never learns it happened; the sender was shown no failure because FCM returned 200 and the outbox says `sent`. The design's quarantine detector also stays silent, because a `sent` row with no receipt is exactly what an expired TTL looks like and exactly what a healthy-but-quiet device looks like.
fatal_flaws.repair: Either make the cursor multi-stream — one persisted cursor per class, catch-up on foreground fetching `reach_events`, `care_nudges` and unanswered `call_invites` above their cursors — or, better, replace four cursors with one: a per-couple `events` log carrying (seq, class, row_id) that every class writes to, so there is exactly one cursor, one catch-up query and one watermark for the whole app. Until that exists, `reach` cannot have a 600s TTL; it needs the same 86400s as `care` and `message`, because a TTL shorter than the recovery interval is data loss whenever no recovery path exists.

fatal_flaws.flaw: `push_devices` is specified with `unique(token_hash)` *globally, not per user*, plus the explicit requirement that a token appearing on a new row 'must be *stolen* from the old row', plus owner-only RLS. No possession proof is specified. The token is obtainable: `profiles_select_self_or_partner` (E:/LDR/supabase/schema.sql:117-120) is `for select using (id = auth.uid() or couple_id = current_user_couple_id())` with no column restriction, and `fcm_token` lives on `profiles` (fcm_push.sql:7) — the design documents this leak itself. The migration then keeps `profiles.fcm_token` alive and partner-readable through stages 1, 2 and 3, dropping it only in stage 4. So the entire cutover window ships a table whose uniqueness rule converts a read-only leak into a write primitive. The mechanism chosen to prevent 'a user's messages go to someone else's phone' is the mechanism that causes it.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Partner A reads B's `fcm_token` with one PostgREST GET on `profiles` (allowed today, allowed through stage 3). A inserts a `push_devices` row with `user_id = A`, `token_hash = hash(B's token)`. The global unique constraint fires; the steal-on-conflict rule reassigns the row to A. B now has zero `push_devices` rows: every send targeting B expands to an empty device set and is marked `sent` with nothing attempted. B receives no calls, no reaches, no messages, silently and indefinitely. Meanwhile A's own notifications are delivered to B's handset. When B complains, the design's quarantine detector reports B's phone as unreachable and the OEM diagnostics screen tells B their phone stopped the app — the design's own tooling actively misattributes the attack.
fatal_flaws.repair: Never reassign a row across `user_id`. Make uniqueness `(user_id, token_hash)` and tolerate a transient cross-user duplicate: the stale holder's token stops being valid for that install and FCM returns `UNREGISTERED` on the first send, which is the only authenticated signal of ownership transfer available, and which the error classifier already handles as terminal-for-that-device. Move the `profiles.fcm_token` column revoke (or the whole column drop) from stage 4 to stage 1, so the leak closes when `push_devices` opens rather than three stages later.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Quarantine is defined as three consecutive sends with no matching `push_receipts` row spanning >10 minutes, and its product output is telling the *caller* that the partner's phone may not be receiving alerts. But the receipt is a network write from the background isolate, and the design's own cited table (push.md:55-56, power-details) states that in the Rare and Restricted standby buckets **network access is disabled** for the app — while the local notification still posts fine, because `plugin.show()` needs no network. The design also chooses `normal` priority for `message`, forgoing the only documented escape from that state ('high-priority FCM's temporary network grant is the escape hatch, and it is the only one', push.md:58). So quarantine fires hardest on the case where push is working. It also cannot distinguish four conditions with four different remedies: force-stop (no fix), RARE/RESTRICTED bucket (working, cannot ack), POST_NOTIFICATIONS denied (fixable in one tap), and a genuinely dead token. Separately, the same buffering corrupts the design's headline SLI: `push_receipts.received_at` is `default now()` at *ack-insert* time, so `p50/p95(received_at − fcm_accepted_at)` on a buffered ack measures hours of buffer-flush delay and reports it as push latency. The design presents this as the number that 'replaces argument with a number' and claims it is correct on a phone whose clock is a year off — it is clock-independent and it is not latency.
fatal_flaws.scenario: B's phone drops to the RARE bucket after 8 days of light use (push.md:119). A sends three messages over 12 minutes. All three are delivered by FCM, all three post notifications on B's screen, none can ack because B's app has no network in that bucket; the acks buffer to SharedPreferences. Quarantine fires. A is shown 'their phone may not be getting alerts right now' while B is reading the messages. In an app whose premise is concealment, the design has just made a false claim about a partner's device state. Two hours later B opens the app, the buffer flushes, and the three receipts insert with `received_at = now()`, producing a p95 push latency of 2 hours in the dashboard that is supposed to settle arguments.
fatal_flaws.repair: Compute quarantine only from `high`-priority sends (call/reach), which are the only ones granted temporary network, and require the absence to persist across a foreground event — a late-flushing ack must retroactively clear the quarantine. Have the client stamp `SystemClock.elapsedRealtime()` at receive and at ack-attempt and send the delta: it is a monotonic interval, not a wall clock, so it obeys the design's own no-device-clock rule, and it lets the server compute a true `received_at` and exclude buffered acks from the latency percentile. Report the four conditions separately: quarantine is a symptom, not a diagnosis, and only one of the four is worth telling the partner about.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The row-level trigger writes the outbox row inside the domain transaction — the correct core of the design — but the consequence is never stated: any failure in the push path is now a failure of the user's message send. Today a pg_net failure costs a push; after this change a unique violation without ON CONFLICT, a lock held by the retention job, a check constraint on `event_class`, or a full disk aborts `INSERT INTO messages` and the user is told their message did not send. The design's phrasing — 'the notification obligation commits with the domain row or not at all' — read literally by an implementer means 'let the trigger raise', and its Level-1 test ('insert the same domain row twice → assert the unique constraint absorbs it silently') is the only place the correct behaviour is implied, in a test rather than in the invariant.
fatal_flaws.scenario: The stage-5 retention job runs `DELETE FROM push_outbox WHERE state='sent' AND ...` and takes locks on the partition being written. Concurrently a user sends a message. The row trigger's INSERT blocks, then fails or times out, and the whole transaction aborts. The user sees 'failed to send' on a message that Postgres was perfectly capable of storing. Chat outage caused by the notification system — a strictly worse failure than the one being fixed.
fatal_flaws.repair: State it as an invariant, not a test: the outbox trigger must be write-only, `ON CONFLICT (dedupe_key) DO NOTHING`, with no foreign keys out of `push_outbox` into hot tables and no constraints that can fail on well-formed input. Run retention as a partition DROP (daily partitions on `created_at`, the pattern Realtime itself uses for `realtime.messages`) rather than a DELETE, so the reclaim path never takes a lock that a writer can block on.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Invariant #3 asserts 'Duplicate notification on retry is therefore impossible, not merely unlikely.' It is not. The design's own state machine has an unprotected boundary: the worker POSTs to FCM, receives 200, and dies (isolate eviction, the 2s CPU cap, a 150s idle 504) before persisting `delivered_to` and `state='sent'`. The sweeper finds `lease_until < now()`, returns the row to `pending`, and the next claim re-sends to the same device — `delivered_to` records the first success only if the write survived, and it did not. FCM is independently at-least-once. The client contract has six numbered items and none of them specifies a stable notification id; the only existing precedent in the code is `reachId.hashCode & 0x7fffffff` (reach_notifications.dart:71), which is stable by accident and is not stated as a rule for the call, care or message classes.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A calls B. The worker sends, FCM returns 200, the isolate is evicted mid-response-handling. 20 seconds later the sweeper requeues, the row is re-claimed, and the ring is sent again. B's phone rings twice for one call, or — worse, if the call class starts a foreground service on each — two full-screen intents contend and the second cancels the first mid-answer. The stated invariant told the implementer this could not happen, so no dedupe was written.
fatal_flaws.repair: Restate honestly: delivery is at-least-once at the transport and exactly-once at the display, and the mechanism that makes it so is client-side, not server-side. Mandate the notification id as a stable function of `rid` for all four classes, and mandate that the call handler treats a second wake for an already-ringing `call_id` as a no-op. Server-side, write `delivered_to` and `fcm_message_id` before returning, and accept that a crash between the FCM 200 and that write is a duplicate the client must absorb.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The Level-4 production canary is presented as 'the direct answer to "the fix passed and then failed in production"', but it is structurally incapable of detecting the class of outage that matters most, and it violates the brief's own constraint. It requires 'one dedicated internal device' — a second phone, which must stay alive, un-force-stopped and charged forever, on a fleet the design itself rates 5/5 for OEM killing. And the probe's enqueue (pg_cron), its drain (the worker), and its alert write (`push_alerts`) all ride the exact chain under test. Related: 'Correctness depends only on Path B' is asserted while Path B is pg_cron → `net.http_post` → Edge Function — pg_net, the mechanism disqualified two paragraphs earlier. It is self-healing across ticks, which is the real argument, but the design never makes it, and a project-wide pg_net failure stops both paths at once. Nobody is specified to read `push_alerts`, which reproduces the invisibility being fixed.
fatal_flaws.scenario: pg_net degrades project-wide, or the `push-drain` deployment is broken by a bad secret. No wake fires, no cron invocation lands, no probe row is drained, no `push_alerts` row is written. The monitoring output is identical to a perfectly healthy system: silence. Every push in the app stops, rows pile up in `pending`, and the design's stated failure mode ('it fails by getting slower') is only true if someone happens to run the `p95(claim_time − created_at)` query — which nothing schedules and nothing alerts on. Separately, the canary phone is a OnePlus in a drawer; MIUI/OxygenOS force-stops it after a week and it alarms continuously until someone disables the alarm, at which point the canary is gone and nobody notices.
fatal_flaws.repair: Split the health check in two. A pure-SQL pg_cron job with no HTTP in it — `insert into push_alerts select ... where (select max(now()-created_at) from push_outbox where state='pending') > interval '2 minutes'` — detects a dead chain because it depends on nothing the chain depends on. Then split the probe SLI into `fcm_accepted` and `device_acked` so a dead canary handset is distinguishable from a dead pipeline. Run the canary on an emulator with Play Services on a CI box rather than a physical OEM phone, and give `push_alerts` a reader — an out-of-band pinger or an in-app 'last successful push N hours ago' banner — or it is another table nobody queries. Also set `timeout_milliseconds` explicitly on every `net.http_post`: with pg_net's 2000ms default against a ~20s worker budget, every one of 8,640 daily drain calls records `timed_out=true`, poisoning the one table operators are being told to trust.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Outbox rows can outlive their domain rows, and nothing in the design re-validates existence at claim time. `clear_conversation_everyone` (E:/LDR/supabase/clear_chat_everyone.sql) is a hard `DELETE FROM public.messages WHERE couple_id = ...` with no tombstone. With `message` at `ttl=86400s` and retries 'for hours', the design widens a race that is currently ~1 second into a 24-hour one. There is also no FK from `push_outbox.domain_row_id` and no cascade, so account deletion and couple dissolution leave orphan rows the worker will faithfully attempt. Relatedly, the design's diagnosis that '`clear_conversation_everyone` or any bulk insert fires one pg_net POST per row' is simply wrong — it is a DELETE, and all four triggers are AFTER INSERT — which means the statement-level wake trigger, presented as fixing a real bulk problem, addresses a case this app does not have.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A sends five messages while B is backgrounded. The first push 503s and is scheduled for retry. A then clears the conversation for both sides. B's phone wakes on the retried push, posts a notification, runs the catch-up fetch, finds nothing above its cursor, and shows a notification for a message that no longer exists anywhere. B taps it and lands in an empty chat.
fatal_flaws.repair: Re-check domain-row existence in the claim RPC (join `push_outbox` to the source table on `domain_row_id` and mark missing rows `superseded` in the same statement), or partition-by-class with an ON DELETE CASCADE FK where the source table permits it. Drop the statement-level bulk-insert justification or replace it with the real reason for a statement-level wake, which is invocation-count economics, not bulk inserts.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The cost model omits the largest storage line and the largest client-request line, and the scale ceiling omits a latency cost it deliberately buys. `push_receipts` is specified at 30-day retention but only the outbox is sized: '~600 MB live at 24 h retention'. At 100k users and the design's own 15 pushes/user/day, receipts are 45M rows over 30 days; with the `(device_id, fcm_message_id)` PK index that is ~9-12 GB, against Pro's 8 GB included disk — off by roughly 20x, plus 1.5M inserts and 1.5M deletes per day of vacuum load on a compute tier the design already calls tight. The client ack is a PostgREST write per push — ~45M requests/month at 100k users, plus its egress — and appears nowhere in the '$5-15/mo all-in' figure. Money stays small; the arithmetic does not survive. Separately, the decision to fire the pg_net wake only for `call` and `reach` (to fit Free's 500k invocations) makes the 10-second pg_cron tick the delivery floor for `message` at every scale, which is a designed p50 of ~5s and p99 of ~10s on the app's highest-volume, most emotionally load-bearing event. That is presented purely as a safety net and never as the latency it costs.
fatal_flaws.scenario: At 100k users, disk crosses the Pro allowance on `push_receipts` alone and autovacuum on a 1.5M-delete/day table starts competing with the 52 writes/s the design budgeted, on Nano's 250 baseline IOPS which the design already flags as too tight. Nobody notices until write latency climbs, because the storage line in the design says 600 MB. Meanwhile at 1k users a chat message buzzes 8 seconds after it was sent, which is the complaint that started this project, and the design contains no statement that this was chosen.
fatal_flaws.repair: Size receipts explicitly (daily partitions, DROP not DELETE, 7 days not 30 — the debugging question is always 'last night'), count the ack as a first-class request line at each scale, and state the message-class latency floor as a declared tradeoff with its own SLI. If the 10s floor is unacceptable, fire the wake for `message` too and budget the invocations honestly rather than discovering the latency in production.

verdict: The core idea — wrap content keys instead of deriving them — is correct and removes the n=2 catastrophe. But the design as written does not survive literal implementation. Six things are fatal. (1) Stage 1 has an unguarded CRK-mint race: both devices mint a different CRK at epoch 1, and the AEAD associated data `(couple_id, epoch, key_kind, key_owner, recipient_id)` is byte-identical for both, so the design's slot-binding invariant cannot disambiguate them; the stated primary key on key_wraps then forces a choice between silent divergence (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) and violating the additive-only invariant (DO UPDATE). (2) The DELETE policy on key_wraps is never stated, while invariant 2 forbids deletes and invariant 12 requires them for revocation — and the only stated write scope is couple-wide, which hands either partner an irreversible remote wipe of the other's key access. That is a weapon in an app whose threat model includes a hostile ex. (3) Stage 2 gates the one-way removal of the legacy path on a client-decremented counter, which two devices double-decrement — the exact "watermark moves on an unreliable client message" bug class the brief forbids. (4) The stage ordering ships that one-way cliff (Stage 2) before any recovery credential exists (Stage 3), so between them CRK's only copies are the two device keys and the original total-loss bug is reconstructed under a new name. (5) `key_requests.expires_at` defaults to `now()+15min`, which cannot survive the MIUI/backgrounded partner the same paragraph claims to be designed for, and partner-assisted is the tier recommended to ship first. (6) The partner-assisted handshake is described as CPace over a code shown on both screens, which is not CPace, and it backs its 3-attempt limit with `key_requests.attempts int` — a Postgres guess counter, which invariant 12 explicitly forbids and research/e2ee.md:210 calls worthless. Separately, the cost section misquotes its own source by 5-6x (research says $500-560/mo at 10k and $5,000-6,500/mo at 100k; the design cites $70-110 and $700-1,100), omits Realtime messages entirely (85-90% of the bill per supabase.md:282), and misses the largest egress term the encryption decision itself creates: encrypted objects cannot be transformed server-side, so there are no thumbnails and every list view pulls full-resolution bytes. The scale ceiling is optimistic in one specific way that matters: the headline "1,000/mo -> 2/mo" counts couple history only and silently excludes PK_u, which under the recommended ship order is destroyed at approximately the full phone-replacement rate. Two scenarios the design genuinely defeats: symmetric NAT (no P2P anywhere, every exchange is a row) and the stranger with a couple UUID (post-Stage-0, subject to the unspecified `devices` RLS). Repairable — every fatal is a missing constraint or a wrong ordering, not a wrong architecture — but not shippable as specified.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Stage 1 CRK minting has no election, and the AEAD associated data cannot distinguish two CRKs that both claim epoch 1. The AD is `(couple_id, epoch, key_kind, key_owner, recipient_id)` — the epoch NUMBER, not the key's identity — so it prevents moving a wrap between slots but not two distinct valid keys occupying the same slot. The stated `pk(couple_id, epoch, key_kind, key_owner, recipient_id)` then makes the second device's wrap insert collide: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING silently leaves a device holding a CRK nobody else can obtain, and ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE directly violates invariant 2 ('never UPDATEs a key_wraps row'). Either branch breaks a stated invariant.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Both partners update the app the same evening (the normal case — store auto-update) and both open Closer within the same minute. Device A derives the legacy key, mints CRK_A, inserts couple_epochs(epoch=1) and wraps CRK_A to both devices. Device B does the same with CRK_B, concurrently. A writes two vault items under CRK_A; B writes one under CRK_B. Whichever wrap rows lost the PK race are absent, and the items encrypted under the losing key are unreadable to the winner — a partial, silent, permanently-unreadable slice of history, which the design's own scale_ceiling section calls out as 'more confusing to a user than total loss'.
