fatal_flaws.repair: Make the epoch's identity a property of the key, not a counter: `epoch_id uuid` minted with the key (or `HKDF(EK_n,'epoch-id')`), carried in the AD, and stamped on every item row and every DEK wrap so a reader knows which key opens which row instead of trial-decrypting. Then elect the CRK server-side: mint via a SECURITY DEFINER RPC that does a single INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on `couple_epochs(couple_id, epoch)` and RETURNs the winning row; the loser reads the winner's epoch_id, discards its own CRK, and refuses to write any item until it holds a wrap of the winning key. No client may write a Closer row before it has read back a committed epoch_id.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The DELETE policy on `key_wraps` is never specified, and the two invariants that touch it contradict each other. Invariant 2 says registration 'never UPDATEs or DELETEs a key_wraps row, and no server code path is granted permission to'. Invariant 12 says 'Revoking one is deleting its wrap rows'. So DELETE must be granted. The only stated write scope is couple-wide ('a user inserts wraps only for a recipient_id belonging to their own couple'), and if DELETE mirrors it, either partner can delete every wrap row belonging to the other partner's devices and recovery credentials.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A relationship ends badly. Partner B, from an ordinary unmodified session, issues `DELETE FROM key_wraps WHERE couple_id = <ours>` through PostgREST. Every wrap of CRK and of A's PK_u to A's devices and to A's Recovery Key is gone. A's phone still has the keys cached in memory until the next cold start, then A has nothing: no wrap, no way to re-derive (the whole point of the design is that CRK is not derivable), and no server copy. B keeps their own — or deletes those too and takes the shared history with them. This is strictly worse than today's bug, because today the loss is accidental; here it is a one-request weapon, and 'additive-only' is the invariant that was supposed to prevent exactly it.
fatal_flaws.repair: Split the tables. `key_wraps` gets `REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE FROM authenticated` unconditionally — it is append-only, full stop, and the invariant becomes enforceable rather than aspirational. Revocation becomes an append: insert a signed tombstone into a separate `key_revocations(couple_id, recipient_id, revoked_at, signed_by_device)` table, and have readers ignore wraps whose recipient has a tombstone. Scope every write policy to `recipient_id` belonging to `auth.uid()`, never to the couple — a partner has no business writing into your recipient slots at all, and the partner-assisted flow needs only INSERT into the requesting device's slot, which can be granted narrowly via the key_requests row.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Stage 2 gates a one-way, irreversible cliff ('When the counter hits zero, drop the legacy path') on `legacy_rows_remaining`, a per-couple counter decremented by clients. Two devices re-wrapping concurrently each decrement for the same row. This is precisely the class of bug the brief rules out: a mutable counter driven by client messages, where the correct construction is a server-evaluated predicate.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Both partners are on the new build. The couple has 400 legacy rows. Both devices run the background re-wrap, oldest-first, and overlap on roughly half of them. The counter reaches zero after ~270 real rows are converted. The build ships the flag that drops the legacy read path. The remaining ~130 rows — the oldest photos and notes, the ones a couple most wants — are still in the legacy envelope, no code path can read them, and the CryptoCore._sharedKey derivation has been deleted. Permanent, silent, and it lands on exactly the couples with the longest history.
fatal_flaws.repair: Delete the counter. 'Legacy remaining' is a server-side predicate over the row shape (e.g. rows with no epoch_id stamp), computed by `count(*) where epoch_id is null`, and the legacy path is dropped only when that count is zero as observed by the server, per couple, not per client. Make the re-wrap UPDATE conditional (`where epoch_id is null`) so a concurrent second writer is a no-op rather than a competing write, and never let a client's local progress state gate a destructive migration.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Stage ordering reconstructs the original total-loss bug. Stage 2 ends with 'drop the legacy path'. Stage 3 — the first stage that creates any recovery credential — ships after it. Between the two, CRK's only copies in existence are wraps to the two live device keys, both of which die on reinstall (`allowBackup="false"` is explicitly retained). The design asserts Stage 2 is 'the only remaining window in which the old loss bug applies, and it shrinks monotonically'; the opposite is true — the window opens wider when the legacy fallback is removed and no recovery tier has landed.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Stage 2 completes for a couple in March; the legacy path is dropped in the April build. Stage 3a ships in June. In April, A drops their phone in a lake. A's DK is gone, A's wrap of CRK is unopenable, and there is no recovery credential, no partner-assisted flow, and no legacy derivation to fall back on. B still has CRK, so the design's own matrix says 'partner-assisted: readable' — but partner-assisted does not exist yet. A is locked out with no path, and the app now has a wrapped-key architecture that made the promise and cannot keep it.
fatal_flaws.repair: Reorder: Stage 3a (partner-assisted) and 3c (Recovery Key) must ship BEFORE Stage 2's cliff, and the cliff must additionally be gated per-couple on 'this couple has at least one non-device wrap of CRK'. A couple with zero enrolled recovery credentials keeps the legacy dual-read path indefinitely — that is the correct trade, because the legacy path is a worse bug than a longer migration but a better one than a keyless lockout.

fatal_flaws.flaw: `key_requests.expires_at ... default now()+15min` is irreconcilable with the same section's stated design goal — 'designed to work when the socket does not, when the app is backgrounded, and on OEM ROMs that defer wakeups indefinitely'. Fifteen minutes is a foreground-realtime timeout wearing a row-driven costume, and `purge_expired()` will reap the row on the hour.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A's phone is replaced. A registers a pending device and inserts a key_request at 21:04. B's phone is the Vivo, force-stopped by the OEM battery manager after an overnight idle; it receives no FCM data message and holds no socket. B picks the phone up at 08:30 the next morning and opens the app. The request row expired at 21:19 and was purged at 22:00. B sees nothing at all — not even 'a request expired', because the row is gone. A sees a timeout with no information about when to retry, and no way to schedule a retry for a moment B will be looking. The tier recommended to ship first cannot complete against the phone the app is actually installed on.
fatal_flaws.repair: Set `expires_at` to `now() + 7 days` and make expiry a display state, not a purge trigger — a pending request is a durable, visible item in B's app with its own inbox entry, surviving app kills, reinstalls of B's app, and OEM wakeup suppression. Bound the security instead by the PAKE attempt limit and by requiring A's pending device to still be present and unrevoked at approval time, not by a wall clock. Keep the FCM message and the channel as hints exactly as designed; delete the assumption that anyone sees them.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The partner-assisted handshake is protocol-incoherent and its rate limit sits in the one place the design's own invariant forbids. CPace takes a pre-shared low-entropy secret as INPUT; the design describes a 6-digit code that 'both screens show' as an OUTPUT to be compared, which is a short-authenticated-string comparison (Vaudenay SAS), not a PAKE. And the 3-attempt limit is backed by `key_requests.attempts int` — a Postgres row — while invariant 12 states 'There is no server-side guess counter anywhere in the design, because a Postgres row holding attempts_remaining is restorable from backup and provides zero cryptographic guarantee (research/e2ee.md:210)'.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Two failures, one root. (a) Implemented as written, the developer builds an unauthenticated X25519 exchange plus a derived 6-digit comparison string, and the approval UI reduces to a 'Yes, the codes match' button that users tap without reading — at which point a malicious server or an attacker who inserted a rogue device row can stand in the middle, which the design claims is impossible. (b) Implemented as CPace with the counter in `key_requests.attempts`, an attacker with A's session (a borrowed unlocked phone, a stolen refresh token) deletes the row and inserts a fresh one per guess. The 10^6 space is bounded only by B's willingness to keep tapping, and B is being told 'your partner is setting up a new phone' each time — a phishing prompt the design manufactures.
fatal_flaws.repair: Pick one and specify it. If PAKE: the code is generated on B's existing device and typed into A's new device (Labyrinth's shape, research/e2ee.md:123), it is never displayed on A's screen, and the attempt counter lives on B's device in local storage keyed to the requesting device's public key — client-side, on the approving side, which is the only party whose state an attacker does not control. Make the counter's key the pending device's x25519_pub so deleting and re-inserting the request row does not reset it. If SAS: say so, and make the UI require the user to type the partner's digits rather than confirm a match.

fatal_flaws.flaw: 'Destroying the wrapped DEK IS the delete ... independent of CDN caches, read replicas, WAL, and backups already taken' is false for backups, and the design cites the source that disproves it. The wrap is a Postgres row. Supabase daily backups and PITR restore Postgres rows. The design applies the 'restorable from a nightly backup' argument (research/e2ee.md:210) to reject server-side guess counters and then relies on the identical mechanism for its deletion guarantee.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A couple deletes an intimate photo. The wrap row is removed; the object bytes sit in a public bucket with a one-year TTL and an hourly purge job. Two hours later an unrelated incident triggers a PITR restore to a point three hours earlier. The wrap row is back. The object was never purged (the purge ran against a table state that no longer exists). The 'deleted' photo is readable again, and neither partner is told. Under any regime where a user asked for erasure, the design's honest-delete claim was the whole justification for accepting a one-hour byte-purge lag.
fatal_flaws.repair: Weaken the claim to what is true and add the mechanism that makes it true. Deletion must destroy key material that backups do not carry: on delete, the client re-wraps nothing and instead the DEK is discarded, but the object path is written to `storage_ledger` with `expires_at = now()` and purge runs on a short cycle; and the honest wording becomes 'unreadable within the hour, and irrecoverable once purged'. If immediacy is required, keep a per-item random `delete_salt` that is folded into the DEK derivation and stored in a table excluded from PITR retention — or accept and publish the backup window, as the design itself argues for publishing every other leak.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The imported Signal key-change state machine is inert in this domain. Invariants 5 and 6 gate SENDING, but Closer has no send path keyed to a peer's identity key — items are encrypted under EK_n, and a recovered device obtains EK_n through a wrap written by the partner's own device, not through anything the IK gate observes. Nothing is blocked by an UNVERIFIED status. Meanwhile the design's own recovery matrix says partner-assisted re-wrap issues a NEW IK and changes the safety number — and partner-assisted is the recommended-first, highest-coverage tier.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A replaces their phone, recovers via the partner-assisted path (the modal case). The safety number changes, a permanent in-thread event is written, VERIFIED collapses to UNVERIFIED, and a blocking send-gate raises. The user taps through it, because the alternative is not using the app, and because the event is factually routine. Nothing was ever actually protected: A's new device already received CRK for every epoch in step 4 of the handshake, before any verification event existed. The gate fires after the escrow has already been handed over, trains users to dismiss the one warning that would matter under a real substitution, and costs a full stage (Stage 6) to build.
fatal_flaws.repair: Move the gate to the only decision that matters here: approving a partner-assisted re-wrap. That is the moment key material crosses, it is the moment a human is present, and it is where the safety-number comparison belongs — show the safety number in the approval sheet, not in a settings screen afterwards. Keep the permanent transcript event (it is honest and cheap) and delete the send-side gate, which has no send to gate. Cross-signing should bind the requesting device's x25519_pub at approval time, not the IK afterwards.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The headline survivability number excludes PK_u. 'Roughly 1,000/mo -> 2/mo' is computed for couple history under CRK. PK_u — fantasy jar text and personal vault, the content the product promises is private even from the partner — is wrapped only to the user's own devices and own recovery credentials, so partner-assisted recovery loses it by construction. Under the recommended ship order (3a first, 3c last, and open_decision #1 leaves mandatory enrolment undecided), the modal recovery destroys PK_u at approximately the full phone-replacement rate the design quotes as ~2% monthly, i.e. ~1,000 users/month at 50k couples — the number it claims to have eliminated.
fatal_flaws.scenario: At 50k couples with partner-assisted shipped and Recovery Key optional at 40% enrolment, ~2,000 users/month replace a phone. ~60% have no Recovery Key. They recover through the partner, see 'your history is back', and their fantasy jar and personal vault are empty with no explanation — while the couple-shared timeline is intact, which makes it look like a bug rather than a designed outcome. Support has no reply, because by design there is none.
fatal_flaws.repair: State the PK_u loss rate alongside the CRK one in scale_ceiling — it is the number that decides open_decision #1, and stating it decides it. Then make Recovery Key enrolment a hard precondition for any feature backed by PK_u (fantasy jar, personal vault) rather than for Closer as a whole: the friction lands only on the content that cannot otherwise survive, and the couple-shared surface stays frictionless. Ship 3c before 3a, not after.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Encrypting storage objects removes server-side image transformation, which removes thumbnails, which makes egress a function of VIEWS rather than of uploads. The cost model prices only new media (270 GB/mo at 100k) and assumes the cached rate applies. It never prices the read amplification the encryption decision itself creates, and this is the one place where encrypting the bytes makes the bill worse, not better — directly contradicting 'the encryption choice saves ~$33/mo at this scale and grows'.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A couple with 200 vault photos opens the vault. Supabase's image transformer cannot decrypt, so there is no 200px variant to serve; the client must fetch each full 900 KB object to render a grid. One screen open is ~180 GB across 1,000 such couples. At 100k users the egress term is dominated by browsing, not uploading, and Poly1305 additionally forbids HTTP range requests and progressive decode — the whole object must land before any byte is trusted, so there is no cheap partial read either. On the IN2015 this is also a memory problem, not just a bill.
fatal_flaws.repair: Generate thumbnails client-side at write time and store each as its own object with its own DEK and ledger row — accept the doubled object count and say so in the cost model. Re-price egress on views/month, not uploads/month, and re-check the cached-vs-uncached claim: with ~2 readers per object, CDN hit rate cannot approach the level the $0.03/GB figure assumes. Then drop the cost argument for the public bucket entirely and keep it on the security argument, which stands on its own.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Stage 0 is presented as 'no crypto change, no data migration, ships alone ... every item here is independently revertible'. It is the largest change to Realtime authorization the app has ever had: 29 `.channel(` call sites across ~27 topics all flipped to `private: true`, each of which then requires a database authorization query at join, served from Realtime's `DB_POOL_SIZE=5` pool (supabase.md ENVS.md source), against Pro's 500 joins/sec ceiling — and supabase.md names 'rapid reconnection loops from failed authentication attempts' as a top cause of RealtimeDisabledForTenant project suspension. It also adds DDL for `couple_media`, `couple_intimate` and `chat-bg`, three buckets whose live policies exist only in the dashboard and are therefore unknown to the DDL author.
fatal_flaws.scenario: At 10k users (~800 peak devices) a carrier-side network event drops a large fraction of sockets simultaneously. Every device rejoins ~8 private channels: ~6,400 authorization queries funnelled through a 5-connection pool, above the joins/sec quota, producing `too_many_joins`, which the client retries, which is the reconnect loop the docs call out. Private-channel RLS execution time is a Pro/Team-only report, so the team cannot see the cause. Separately, the new bucket DDL replaces an unknown-but-working dashboard policy on `couple_intimate` and either locks users out of their own body photos or opens them up — and 'revertible' does not restore a policy nobody had written down.
fatal_flaws.repair: Split Stage 0. Ship `private: true` per-topic, highest-risk first (touch, touch_trace, capsule_proximity — the ones carrying intimate media and GPS), each behind a remote flag, and measure joins/sec and error rate between each. Before writing bucket DDL, dump the live policies from `storage.policies`/`pg_policies` and commit them verbatim as the baseline, then change them in a separate commit. Wire `realtime.setAuth()` on every token refresh in the same change — private channels disconnect on JWT expiry (supabase.md: 'Realtime's answer is to disconnect the client when the JWT expires'), which is the app's existing 'joined but dead channel' bug class that realtime_service.dart was written to fix.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The cost section misquotes its own source by 5-6x and omits the term that dominates the bill. supabase.md:271 states $500-560/mo at 10k users and :279 states $5,000-6,500/mo at 100k; the design cites 'research/supabase.md:267 puts [10k] at ~$70-110/mo' (line 267 is about connection overage, not the total) and '$700-1,100/mo band' for 100k. supabase.md:282 states cost is '~85-90% Realtime messages at every scale past 1,000 users' — Realtime messages appear nowhere in the design's cost model, and Stage 0's move to private channels plus 'a URL is never a capability' (broadcast id, then REST resolve, then Storage GET) touches exactly that path.
fatal_flaws.scenario: The design is used to justify a budget. At 10k users the team plans for ~$110/mo and receives ~$550. At 100k they plan for ~$1,000 and receive ~$6,000, and supabase.md:276 notes the 100k configuration is 5x past the 2,500 msg/s Team ceiling — a hard stop requiring Enterprise or a self-hosted Realtime cluster, not an overage. The crypto-attributable figures (~$5 and ~$85) are plausible on their own; the framing they sit in is not, and the '$33/mo saved by encrypting' argument is 0.5% of a bill the design has mis-stated by an order of magnitude.
fatal_flaws.repair: Re-cite lines 271 and 279, restate crypto-attributable cost as a fraction of the real totals (~1% at 10k, ~1.3% at 100k — which strengthens the design's actual argument), and add the two terms the crypto choices move: additional REST round trips introduced by 'a URL is never a capability', and PADMÉ padding at ~12% on storage and egress. Drop the cost justification for the public bucket.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Device revocation is cosmetic, and the one key that never rotates is the one used as a search index. The design deliberately declines epoch rotation on device removal, so a revoked device retains every EK it ever held — the `devices.state='revoked'` transition changes nothing cryptographically. Worse, the fantasy tag key is `HKDF(CRK,'fantasy-tags-v2')`, and CRK is minted once and never rotates; epoch rotation derives forward from EK_n and does not touch it.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A phone is stolen. The user taps 'remove device' and, per the design, is offered an explicit epoch rotation which they perform. New content is safe. But the thief's device still holds CRK, therefore still holds the tag-HMAC key, and the tag_hashes column is a plain text[] readable under couple-wide RLS to anyone holding the victim's session — which the thief has, on an unlocked phone, until the JWT is revoked and often after. The thief can enumerate every future fantasy tag both partners select. The design's own invariant 11 claims tag tokens 'cannot be enumerated by anyone without CRK'; it never says CRK is immortal.
fatal_flaws.repair: Derive the tag key from the CURRENT epoch key, not CRK, and accept that matching only works within an epoch (which is correct — 'reset shared history' should reset matching too). Rebuild tag tokens as part of the rotation the user just performed. Separately, either make 'remove device' force an epoch rotation (a couple always has a second EK holder, so it is always possible) or rename the state to `retired` and say in the UI that it does not revoke access to existing content.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The design claims 'it never re-encrypts in a batch' while specifying four separate touch-every-row client passes — Stage 2 (legacy -> CRK), Stage 4 (bytea -> Storage), Stage 5 (body-map x,y into ciphertext), Stage 5 (fantasy text CRK -> PK_u) — and one of them cannot be completed by any single device. It also contains an ordering contradiction: Stage 5 says old FNV tag tokens 'are recomputed during the Stage-2 re-wrap the device is already doing', but Stage 2 has completed and had its code path deleted several releases earlier.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Fantasy migration: A's device re-encrypts A's own entries from CRK to PK_u. It cannot touch B's entries, and it cannot know whether B's device has done the same. Meanwhile every pre-Stage-5 entry of A's was encrypted under CRK, which B has held all along and may have cached locally — so the retroactive privacy upgrade is unenforceable for existing content, and the UI now claims key-enforced privacy for a table containing both kinds of row. Separately, Stage 4's per-row sequence (decrypt, upload, write object id, null the bytea) is three non-atomic steps; on a train with 30-second gaps, an interruption between step 3 and step 4 leaves an orphan object that the nightly sweeper reaps, and an interruption between 2 and 3 leaves a row pointing at nothing.
fatal_flaws.repair: Say plainly that this is four migrations, each with its own server-side completion predicate, and give each one a stage. For fantasy: do not migrate — entries written before PK_u are permanently partner-readable, mark them in the UI, and let PK_u apply only to new entries. For Stage 4: reverse the order to upload, then a single UPDATE that sets object_id and nulls bytea in one statement, and insert the ledger row in the same transaction as the object_id write so the sweeper can never see an object without a ledger row it is about to gain.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The device state machine has no state for a device key that dies without the app being uninstalled, and the hardware verification plan omits the two events the entire recovery design exists for. The DK is sealed under an Android Keystore AES-GCM key; Keystore keys can be permanently invalidated by lock-screen credential changes and biometric re-enrolment (KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException), and the sketch's `absent -> pending -> active -> revoked` has no transition for 'active device, key gone'. The verification section's one hardware test covers app upgrade, force-stop and reboot — not uninstall/reinstall and not Android device-to-device transfer.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A user changes their screen lock PIN on the OnePlus 7. On next launch the app cannot unwrap its DK. The device row still says `active`, so the app is not in the pending/recovery flow, but every unwrap fails. Depending on the implementation it either loops on 'items couldn't be opened' — the exact misleading state the design set out to kill — or silently registers as a new device, burning one of the three device slots and firing the safety-number-changed event on a phone that never left the user's pocket. Neither outcome is tested, because the only hardware test listed does not include changing the lock screen.
fatal_flaws.repair: Add an `invalidated` state entered when the unwrap raises the Keystore invalidation error, distinct from `absent`; it must re-enter recovery without consuming a new device slot and with copy that names the cause ('your screen lock changed'). Do not set setUserAuthenticationRequired or setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment unless the product wants that behaviour. Extend the one-afternoon hardware matrix to: lock-screen change, biometric re-enrolment, uninstall/reinstall, and Android device-to-device transfer, on all three phones — that is six events, still one afternoon, still one phone at a time.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The schema sketch cannot hold the keys the prose requires. `pk(couple_id, epoch, key_kind, key_owner, recipient_id)` includes `key_owner uuid`, which is meaningless for `key_kind='crk'` — and Postgres forbids NULL in a primary key, so CRK rows need a sentinel that is never specified. `key_kind` is enumerated as `'crk'|'pk'`, but the prose states 'IK is itself wrapped into the recovery envelopes', and there is no `'ik'` kind. `epoch` is a required PK column but PK_u does not rotate with epochs, so PK wraps need a second sentinel.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Implemented literally, the first INSERT of a CRK wrap fails with a not-null violation on key_owner, and the developer picks a sentinel — probably the couple_id or a zero UUID — inconsistently between the mint path and the partner-assisted re-wrap path, which then produces wraps that do not collide when they should (defeating the epoch election) or collide when they should not. The IK wrap has nowhere to live, so recovery restores CRK and PK_u but not identity, and the design's claim that 'a recovered user keeps their identity and the safety number does not change' silently becomes false for every recovery path.
fatal_flaws.repair: Add `'ik'` to key_kind. Make `key_owner` NOT NULL and set it to the couple_id for CRK (or split couple-scoped and user-scoped wraps into two tables, which is cleaner). Replace `epoch int` with `epoch_id uuid` (see the glare repair) and use a fixed all-zero epoch_id for non-epoch-scoped kinds, documented in the DDL.

fatal_flaws.flaw: RLS on `devices` is never specified, and the metadata-exposure CI gate is scoped to 'Closer tables', which the four new key tables are not. `devices` carries `label` and `last_seen_at` per user.
fatal_flaws.scenario: `devices` inherits the permissive posture of `partner_keys` (which today is readable to publish/fetch a partner's key). Any authenticated stranger selects `devices` and gets, for every user in the system, a device count, human-written labels ('Sam - work phone'), and `last_seen_at` — a global presence and device-inventory oracle, which the design's accepted-leaks list does not include and the CI gate does not cover. It is also the cheapest possible input for the phishing version of the partner-assisted attack: knowing that a target just registered a pending device tells an attacker exactly when to call the partner.
fatal_flaws.repair: State the policies: SELECT on `devices` restricted to `user_id = auth.uid()` OR the requester's couple partner; INSERT/UPDATE restricted to `user_id = auth.uid()`; `label` client-encrypted or dropped; `last_seen_at` removed or coarsened to a day. Widen the CI gate from 'Closer tables' to a checked-in allowlist of every table the client can read, and add devices, key_wraps, recovery_credentials and key_requests to metadata-exposure.md.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The single asserted property in the verification plan is false under the design's own recovery matrix, so the property test would fail a correct implementation. Stated: 'for every item written at time t, and every device d that is a couple member at t\' > t holding at least one surviving recovery credential, read(d, item) succeeds.' Partner-assisted recovery is a recovery credential and does not restore PK_u.
fatal_flaws.scenario: The simulator random-walks to `{writeItem(A, kind=personal), loseDevice(A), recoverByPartner(A), readItem(A)}`. Under a correct implementation the read fails — that is the design working. The property test reports a violation. The team either weakens the property until it stops catching things, or 'fixes' the code by wrapping PK_u to the partner, silently deleting the product's only key-enforced privacy guarantee. Two related weaknesses: `information_schema.column_privileges` cannot detect whether a column is 'used in an expiry predicate' (the actual mechanism is per-column GRANT UPDATE, which does work), and the ciphertext-on-the-wire test samples one object from one writer, so a plaintext path introduced by the Stage-4 migration or by thumbnails passes.
fatal_flaws.repair: Split the property by key kind: couple-scoped items require any surviving credential; PK_u items require a credential of kind 'code' or 'platform_vault' specifically. Replace the column_privileges check with an assertion that `has_column_privilege('authenticated', t, c, 'UPDATE')` is false for every column in a checked-in list of server-owned timestamps. Assert the ciphertext property at every upload call site by construction (a single choke-point function, grep-enforced) rather than by sampling one object.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The residual-loss arithmetic assumes independent device loss within a couple, and the recommended-first recovery tier is unavailable in the scenario that generates the most support load.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Two cases the model does not cover. (a) Correlated loss: couples upgrade on a shared plan, travel together, are burgled together, and lose a bag together — dual loss is not 0.05% independent, and the 2/mo figure rests entirely on that unsourced number. (b) Breakup: the moment a user most urgently reinstalls to retrieve shared memories is the moment the partner will not approve a re-wrap — and 'breakup' is listed as an epoch-rotation trigger, so the ex-partner can also rotate them out of future content while holding the only approval that would restore the past. Partner-assisted, as the sole shipped tier, is unavailable exactly when it is most needed. Also unhandled: both partners replace phones in the same window, each pending, each waiting for the other to approve — a deadlock the matrix has no row for.
fatal_flaws.repair: Label the 0.05% as an assumption to be measured, not a result, and give the sensitivity (at 0.5% correlated loss the residual is 20/mo, not 2). Add the mutual-pending deadlock to the state machine explicitly: if both devices are pending, neither can approve, and the only exit is a Recovery Key — which is another argument for making it mandatory. Say in the setup copy that partner-assisted recovery requires a cooperative partner, before the fact.

verdict:
FAILS. The design is the best-argued of its kind for this repo, and its central move (dump production as the baseline rather than reconstructing it) is correct. But it rests its entire weight on one load-bearing claim — "the repo produces the database, or CI fails, and everything else is a consequence of that" — and that claim is false as specified, because `supabase db diff` compares DDL and every safety-critical fact in this design is a ROW: pg_cron job definitions, `retention_policy` entries, `storage.buckets.public`. The design says outright that a retention rule "is reviewed, diffed and rolled back like any other change." It is not diffed. Someone unschedules the outbox drain or re-publicises `couple_media` in the dashboard — the documented historical behaviour of this project — and the nightly check stays green forever while every push stops or all intimate media goes world-readable. Since staging, rollback, DR and drift detection are all derived as consequences of that one property, the hole propagates.

Three further breaks are self-inflicted and would ship:

(1) Stage 4 replaces `net.http_post` (fires at commit) with an outbox drained by pg_cron every 10 s, and asserts "the app behaves identically on the happy path." calls.md documents FCM `ttl:'30s'` for calls — FCM discards the ring rather than queueing it. Spending up to 10 of those 30 seconds in a poll queue before FCM sees the message converts marginal deliveries into silent losses on exactly the doze/MIUI devices the brief names. That is a regression in a domain the brief says is already broken.

(2) `push_outbox.state='sent'` transitions on the edge function's HTTP response, which is the same lie the design condemns `reach-notify` for. During a total delivery outage to force-stopped MIUI devices, `select state, count(*) from push_outbox` reads 100% healthy. Invariant 10 ("nothing observes success by the absence of an error") is violated by its own exemplar. And FCM `UNREGISTERED` — which every reinstall produces, since `profiles.fcm_token` is a single column — will retry, back off and dead-letter, so the one alert the design defines goes permanently red and gets muted.

(3) The proposed `presence(couple_id, updated_at desc)` index destroys HOT updates on the hottest-written table in the app. Verified: `presence_server_time.sql` sets `new.updated_at := now()` on EVERY write, and realtime.md puts that at ~18 writes/min/user. Indexing a column that changes on every write means no update can ever be HOT: an index insert plus a dead index tuple per heartbeat, ~3,000/s at 10k users, on a table already carrying REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, against 250 baseline IOPS. The index exists to serve `order by updated_at desc limit 1` over 2-3 rows per couple, where the sort is free. The design's headline optimisation makes its worst table worse.

Per scenario. Symmetric-NAT strangers: holds, nothing here depends on topology — except that `app_secrets` (Cloudflare TURN key + token) is one of five tables with no DDL and unknown RLS that Stage 0 blesses into the baseline unexamined. Clock 3 minutes wrong: holds for `now()`-based sweeps, breaks because retention keys off client-writable `created_at` (verified: `default now()`, and the repo contains no table-level grants, so Supabase's default full INSERT for `authenticated` stands — unlike `presence.updated_at`, which is trigger-stamped). A client writing `created_at` in the future is never swept, its `offer_sdp` never nulled, and the invite stays answerable forever — the exact bug the 10-minute null was added to fix. Force-stopped MIUI: breaks, flaws 2 and 3. Offline 3 days then a train: reads hold (genuinely nothing socket-dependent), but the 24 h `call_invites` sweep destroys the only record a call was attempted — there is no call-history table among the 35 and `answered_at` is never written. 10k on Pro: optimistic — 200 msgs/user/month (~7/day) is off by roughly 7x for a constant-contact app, the high-frequency event tables are absent from the volume model, and correcting the rate puts `messages` past the design's own 50M-row partitioning trigger inside a year at 10k, contradicting "partition at 100k". Partner reinstalls: breaks via UNREGISTERED dead-lettering, and catastrophically with a pending deletion — no `cancelled` state exists and `current_user_couple_id()` returns NULL, so the reinstalled app is an empty shell with no way back and the purge still fires on day 7. Both partners simultaneously: `data_subject_map` scope for couple-scoped rows is explicitly undecided (verification step 8 says the test "pins whichever behaviour is chosen") while the migration performing an irreversible purge is scheduled to ship. Malicious stranger with a couple UUID: breaks. Verified by grep — zero `realtime.messages` policies in any file, and calls.md confirms no channel uses `private: true`. Making `couple_media` private is obscurity, not a fix; the UUID leaks via invite codes, shared URLs, CDN entries the cited Smart CDN doc says revocation does not purge, and an ex-partner's memory. After all seven stages, a stranger can still join `call:<uuid>`, inject `hangup` to kill any call, inject `offer` to ring a phone, and read raw GPS every 4 s. The design claims the bucket change "closes the root cause"; it does not, and the fix that would (RLS on `realtime.messages`) is this domain's to write and is absent.

Big bang in disguise: yes, Stage 0+1. `migration repair --status applied` marks production before staging has ever replayed the baseline, and the append-only rule then forbids fixing it. With `--schema auth,storage` included, that replay is likely to fail on duplicate objects and `ALTER ... OWNER TO supabase_admin`. Correct order is dump → replay clean on staging → then repair prod.

Invariants depending on the client: three. Outbox `sent` is a proxy for client receipt. Retention correctness depends on client-written timestamps. `data_subject_map` completeness is scoped to "RLS-enabled tables", so a table with RLS off escapes both the security check and the export/deletion check at once — and all four `pg_policies` assertions are vacuously true for a table with zero policies. The first assertion must be over `pg_class.relrowsecurity`, not `pg_policies`.

Cost: omits database and Realtime egress entirely, which the design's own supabase.md says is billed. The 4-SELECT/min presence poll this domain indexes for returns a ~25-column row with GPS and photo URLs; at 10k users that is plausibly 200-400 GB/month against a 250 GB Pro allowance before chat loads and WAL fan-out — a $50-200/month line reading $0.

Everything above is checkable on one laptop with no phones, which is to the design's credit. Fix flaws 1-4 and the plan is shippable; ship it as written and the drift check gives false confidence while calls ring 10 seconds late.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The drift invariant covers DDL only. `supabase db diff` does not compare data, and the design's three most safety-critical runtime facts are rows, not schema: pg_cron job definitions in `cron.job`, `retention_policy` registry entries, and `storage.buckets.public`. The design explicitly claims the opposite — 'a registry entry is an INSERT in a migration, so adding a retention rule is reviewed, diffed and rolled back like any other change.' Since every other property (staging, rollback, DR, RLS conformance) is described as a consequence of the drift check, the hole propagates through the whole design.
fatal_flaws.scenario: The owner debugs at 2am in the dashboard and flips `couple_media` back to public, or disables the `miles_retention` cron job, or sets a `retention_policy` row `enabled=false`. Nightly `db diff --linked` returns empty. CI is green indefinitely. Intimate media is world-readable by couple UUID, or pushes silently stop, and the single mechanism the design says catches dashboard hand-edits within 24 hours never fires.
fatal_flaws.repair: Split the check in two and say so. Keep `db diff` for DDL. Add a separate nightly read-only CONFORMANCE job against production asserting checked-in expectations: every expected `cron.job` row exists with the expected schedule and `active=true`; `storage.buckets` flags (`public`, `file_size_limit`, `allowed_mime_types`) match a committed expected table; `retention_policy` rows match the repo registry exactly; every table in `public` has `relrowsecurity=true` unless allowlisted. Fail on any mismatch. Stop describing row-level configuration as 'diffed'.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Stage 4 moves push egress from a commit-time `net.http_post` to an outbox drained by pg_cron every 10 seconds, and asserts 'NO CLIENT RELEASE NEEDED — the app behaves identically on the happy path.' False for calls. calls.md documents FCM `android {priority:'high', ttl:'30s'}` for the ring — FCM DISCARDS rather than queues a call message it cannot deliver inside 30 s. Adding up to 10 s of queue latency before FCM even sees the message consumes a third of the ring window.
fatal_flaws.scenario: MIUI phone in doze. Caller taps Call at t=0. The outbox row waits up to 10 s for the next cron tick, so FCM receives it at t=10 with a 30 s TTL now effectively expiring at t=40 relative to the tap. The device's doze window opens at t=32. Under the old path the ring sat in FCM's queue from t=0.5 with until t=30.5; the extra 10 s is the difference between a delivered ring and a discarded one. Nothing is logged: the outbox row reads `sent`.
fatal_flaws.repair: Make the outbox the RETRY owner, not the primary path. The trigger both inserts the outbox row and issues the immediate `net.http_post` (or `pg_notify` to a LISTEN-driven worker) in the same statement; the cron drain claims only rows still `pending` after N seconds. Latency unchanged, retry and countability gained. Separately raise the call TTL above 30 s now that a retry owner exists.

fatal_flaws.flaw: `push_outbox.state='sent'` transitions on the edge function's HTTP response — the identical proxy the design condemns `reach-notify` for ('returns HTTP 200 on every error path so the invocation metric reads 100% healthy during a total delivery outage'). FCM accepting a message says nothing about delivery to a force-stopped app, and calls.md documents that `ttl:30s` messages are discarded outright. The stated SLI, '0 rows in state=dead', therefore reads healthy during exactly the outage it exists to catch. Compounding: FCM `UNREGISTERED` is a permanent failure the design's backoff will retry then dead-letter, and `profiles.fcm_token` is a single scalar column (calls.md), so every reinstall and every second device produces permanent dead rows.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A MIUI OEM update starts force-stopping the app for an entire population. FCM returns 200 for all of them. `select state, count(*) from push_outbox group by 1` shows 100% sent, 0 dead. The owner's dashboard is green for weeks while nobody receives a message or a call. Meanwhile one partner reinstalls, their old token returns UNREGISTERED on every push, those rows retry-and-dead-letter, the dead-letter alert fires continuously for a benign cause and gets muted — so the one alarm that could catch a real outage is already off.
fatal_flaws.repair: Three terminal states, not one: `accepted` (FCM 200), `delivered` (client wrote an ack/receipt row keyed to the outbox id), `invalidated` (UNREGISTERED/NOT_FOUND → null the token, terminal, never retried, never dead-lettered). The SLI becomes 'accepted but not delivered within N minutes', segmented by manufacturer. This requires a per-device token table rather than a single column — state it as a dependency rather than letting the outbox launder a lie.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The proposed index `presence(couple_id, updated_at desc)` destroys HOT updates on the most-written table in the app. Verified: `presence_server_time.sql` sets `new.updated_at := now()` in a BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE trigger on EVERY write, and realtime.md documents ~18 writes/min/user (30 s heartbeat, 5 s chat_last_read, 15 s location, typing, screen). A B-tree index containing `updated_at` means every write changes an indexed column, so no update can be HOT — each heartbeat costs an index insert plus a dead index tuple, on a table already carrying REPLICA IDENTITY FULL. The index exists to serve `fetchPartner`'s `order by updated_at desc limit 1` over 2-3 rows per couple, where the sort costs nothing.
fatal_flaws.scenario: 10,000 users, ~3,000 presence upserts/sec. Index bloat on `presence` grows continuously; autovacuum on a Small instance with 250 baseline IOPS cannot keep pace with an update rate that now dirties two pages instead of one. Within weeks the index scan the change was meant to speed up is reading bloated pages, and the symptom is 'presence feels broken again' with no error logged anywhere — the same shape as every previous failure in this app.
fatal_flaws.repair: Index `presence(couple_id)` only. `couple_id` is stable so HOT updates survive; the 2-3-row sort is free. Verify locally with no phones: `pg_stat_user_tables.n_tup_hot_upd / n_tup_upd` on `presence` before and after under a synthetic heartbeat loop, asserting the HOT ratio stays above ~0.9. Add that ratio as a standing SLI — it is the cheapest early warning for this whole class of index mistake.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Stage 0's `supabase db dump --schema public,storage,auth` produces a baseline that cannot be replayed and permanently poisons the drift check, and `migration repair` marks it applied on production BEFORE anything has proven it replays. `supabase db reset` runs the local stack's own gotrue/storage migrations first, so an auth/storage baseline collides on duplicate objects and on `ALTER ... OWNER TO supabase_admin` (the `postgres` role is not superuser on a Supabase project). Once `storage` is in diff scope, every Supabase-side storage-api or gotrue upgrade produces a non-empty nightly diff. The append-only rule then forbids amending the baseline, and `supabase_migrations.schema_migrations` carries no checksum (unlike Flyway), so ledger and repo can diverge with nothing to notice.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Day 1: dump, repair, prod ledger says baseline applied. Day 3: Stage 1 step 5 pushes to staging and fails on `relation "auth.users" already exists`. The design says 'that failure IS the finding', but it is unfixable under its own rules — prod already claims the baseline is applied. Weeks later Supabase upgrades storage-api; the nightly diff goes non-empty for a reason nobody controls, fires again the next night, and gets muted — leaving no drift detection at all.
fatal_flaws.repair: Baseline `public` only. Capture `storage.objects` policies and `storage.buckets` rows as committed expectations asserted by the conformance job, not by `db diff`. Reorder: dump → replay clean on staging (amending the baseline freely, since it has been applied nowhere) → only then `migration repair` production. Add a checksum side table if append-only is to be enforced rather than hoped for.

fatal_flaws.flaw: All four `pg_policies` assertions quantify over rows in `pg_policies`, so a table with RLS disabled or zero policies passes every one vacuously. The `data_subject_map` completeness check is scoped to 'RLS-enabled tables', so the same table escapes the export/deletion check too. The population at risk is exactly the five tables with no DDL anywhere — verified: `cycle_events`, `cycle_settings`, `love_reasons`, `app_secrets` appear in zero .sql file and `care_nudges` is referenced but never created. The repo contains no table-level GRANT statements at all (verified: only function EXECUTE grants), so Supabase's default `grant all ... to anon, authenticated` stands. Stage 0 blesses whatever state those tables are in into the baseline and calls it reviewed.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A malicious signed-up stranger issues `GET /rest/v1/cycle_events?select=*` with their own JWT. If RLS is off on that table — and nobody can currently say whether it is, which is the point — they receive every user's menstrual-cycle history. `app_secrets` holds the Cloudflare TURN key id and API token (calls.md); the same query returns a relay credential with no revocation and no per-call scoping. Every check in the design stays green, because none of them can see a table with no policies.
fatal_flaws.repair: Make the first assertion over `pg_class`, not `pg_policies`: every table in `public` has `relrowsecurity = true` AND at least one policy, with a committed allowlist for deliberate exceptions. Run it against production BEFORE Stage 0's `migration repair`, so the baseline is inspected rather than adopted blind. Source `data_subject_map` completeness from all tables in `public`, not from RLS-enabled ones.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Retention keys off timestamps the client can write. Verified: `messages.created_at` and `call_invites.created_at` are `timestamptz not null default now()` — a DEFAULT, not a trigger — and the repo grants no table-level privileges, so `authenticated` retains Supabase's default full INSERT including those columns. Contrast `presence.updated_at`, which IS trigger-stamped. The sweeper predicate `ts < now() - keep` is therefore under client control, and the design states no invariant requiring `ts_column` to be server-set.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A modified client (or anyone with the shipped anon key and their own JWT) inserts a `call_invites` row with `created_at = now() + interval '10 years'`. The 24 h purge never touches it and the 10-minute `offer_sdp` null never fires, so the invite stays answerable forever — exactly calls.md weakness 4, the defect the SDP-nulling entry was introduced to fix. The same trick makes any row in any swept table immortal, defeating the retention design for the actor most likely to abuse it.
fatal_flaws.repair: Require every `ts_column` named in `retention_policy` to be stamped by a BEFORE trigger and column-level revoked from `authenticated`, asserted in CI by joining `retention_policy` against `information_schema.column_privileges` and `pg_trigger`. Refuse to enable a registry entry whose timestamp column fails that join. Apply the same rule to `account_deletions.requested_at` and `purge_after`.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The sweep is bounded in rows deleted, not in work done, and no index is required. `delete ... where ts < now() - keep and ctid in (select ctid ... limit n)` re-runs the inner scan on every batch. The registry is generic over `(table_name, ts_column)`, so nothing guarantees an index on `ts_column` — and the design's own indexing rule ('one index per named query, added in the migration that needs it') never lists one for any retention column. Because the sweeper is dynamic SQL, `supabase db lint` cannot see the problem.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A registry entry is added for a table whose timestamp column is unindexed. The hourly sweeper does a sequential scan per batch, N batches per run, on a growing table. On Nano's 250 baseline IOPS this saturates the disk for the whole hour, every hour. The design's own invariant 9 names an unbounded DELETE as 'an outage' — this is that outage with a LIMIT clause on it, and the row-count bound makes it look safe in review.
fatal_flaws.repair: CI assertion: every `retention_policy` row must have a matching btree index whose LEADING column is `ts_column`. The sweeper refuses to process an entry without one and writes an `ops_event` at severity='page' instead of silently scanning. Add the per-entry index in the same migration that inserts the registry row, per the design's own rule.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The design claims making `couple_media` private 'closes the root cause of couple_id being guessable, which is what makes every unauthenticated broadcast topic in the app exploitable.' That is security by obscurity and it is wrong on the design's own evidence. Verified by grep: ZERO `realtime.messages` policies in any file, and calls.md confirms no channel anywhere uses `RealtimeChannelConfig(private: true)`. The anon key ships in the APK. The couple UUID also leaks via invite codes, any URL a user has shared, an ex-partner's memory, and CDN entries which the design's own cited Smart CDN doc says revocation does not purge. The actual fix — RLS on `realtime.messages` — belongs to this domain and is absent from all seven stages.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A malicious signed-up stranger obtains one couple UUID. After the entire plan lands, they join `call:<uuid>` with the shipped anon key, broadcast `{kind:'hangup'}` to terminate any call in progress, broadcast `{kind:'offer'}` to make the phone ring at will, and subscribe to `capsule_proximity:<uuid>` to read raw GPS every 4 seconds. Nothing in the design's CI, conformance queries or SLIs registers any of it. Separately, Stage 6 step 16 keeps the old public bucket 'as a fallback for 30 days', so all historical intimate media stays world-readable for a month after the change advertised as fixing it.
fatal_flaws.repair: Add `realtime.messages` RLS policies as a Stage 3 migration, using the same `couple_id = (select public.current_user_couple_id())` shape and the same TO authenticated / InitPlan / WITH CHECK conformance assertions, and require `private: true` topics. Stop presenting the bucket change as a root-cause fix; it is defence in depth. For Stage 6, empty the public bucket at cutover rather than leaving it readable, and state the CDN residue as a time-bounded exposure.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The account-deletion state machine has no cancel path, and revoking through the tenancy helper takes the partner down with the user. States are `requested|purging|done|error`. `current_user_couple_id()` returns NULL from the instant of the request, so the app is an empty shell for the entire 7-day grace with no in-app route back. Separately, `data_subject_map(scope)` for couple-scoped tables governs an irreversible purge whose semantics the design leaves undecided — verification step 8 says the partner-rows assertion 'pins whichever behaviour is chosen', while Stage 7 step 18 ships the purge.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A user rage-taps delete during a fight. Their partner talks them down that evening. They reinstall next morning, sign in with the same email — same auth user, same pending `account_deletions` row — and get a blank app with no explanation and no undo. On day 7 the sweeper purges. If `scope='couple'` is chosen, the partner, who requested nothing and was never notified, loses the entire chat history, every capsule and every memory thread. If both partners request deletion in the same week, purge ordering across two rows is undefined and one member's grace is silently consumed by the other's purge.
fatal_flaws.repair: Add `cancelled` to the state machine and a `cancel_my_deletion()` SECURITY DEFINER RPC reachable while revoked (it must not route through the couple-scoped helper), surfaced on the empty-shell screen. Decide `scope` per table BEFORE step 18 ships, and default couple-scoped rows to survive until every member is purged. Notify the partner on `requested`, not on `done`.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The cost model omits database and Realtime egress entirely, and the volume model underestimates message rate by roughly an order of magnitude. The design's own supabase.md is explicit that Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions and Realtime all count toward egress and that 'data pushed to clients via Supabase Realtime for subscribed events' is billed at $0.09/GB uncached. The cost section counts only storage-object reads. It also assumes 200 messages/user/month (~7/day) for an app whose product premise is constant contact, and models zero volume for `body_touches`, `breath_events`, `intimacy_signals`, `reach_events`, `dice_rolls` and `prompt_responses`.
fatal_flaws.scenario: 10,000 users on Pro. The presence poll this design indexes for runs 4 unconditional SELECTs/min/user (realtime.md:35) returning a ~25-column row with GPS and photo URLs; a few app-open hours a day puts that alone in the 200-400 GB/month range against a 250 GB Pro allowance, before the 300-message catch-up on every resume and REPLICA-IDENTITY-FULL WAL fan-out to 5-10 always-on channels per user. A $50-200/month line reads $0. Correcting messages to a defensible ~50/user/day also pushes the table past the design's own 50M-row partitioning trigger inside a year at 10k — contradicting the stated 'partition at 100,000 users'.
fatal_flaws.repair: Cost egress as its own line per source (PostgREST responses, Realtime frames, Storage) using the poll and channel counts already measured in realtime.md. Restate the partitioning trigger as row-count-only and note it will most likely fire at 10k, not 100k — the row count is the honest trigger, the user count is not.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The static column-level GRANT on `public.profiles` is a landmine the baseline freezes into place, and the design adds no check for it. `hardening_2026_08.sql:43-45` and `newuser_fixes.sql:170-172` revoke table-level UPDATE on `profiles` and re-grant a column list computed at apply time. `pg_dump` captures the RESULT — a fixed column ACL. Under the design's own rules (append-only, no guards, never re-run), the next migration that adds a column to `profiles` produces a column `authenticated` cannot UPDATE. The design claims to have deleted this problem by deleting the 42-file ordering problem; it has moved it from apply order to every future ADD COLUMN.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A future migration adds `profiles.chat_theme_id` (a column the client already writes and which exists in zero .sql file today — verified). The migration is reviewed, CI is green: schema builds, diff empty, every pg_policies assertion passes. In production the client's update fails with `permission denied for column chat_theme_id`. This is byte-for-byte the /role-setup dead end that `newuser_fixes.sql:142-173` exists to document, reintroduced by a design that cites that comment as its motivating example.
fatal_flaws.repair: CI assertion: for every column of `public.profiles` outside a committed protected set, `has_column_privilege('authenticated','public.profiles',<col>,'UPDATE')` is true. Better, drop the column-ACL approach entirely — the `guard_couple_id` trigger already prevents the transition the ACL was defending — and re-grant table-level UPDATE so the trap has no surface.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Verification never exercises the Realtime RLS evaluation path, which the inventory names as the actual ceiling. The EXPLAIN-based InitPlan assertion validates the PostgREST path only. realtime.md:124 states the same couple-scoped policy is evaluated by `realtime.apply_rls` per subscriber per WAL row, and supabase.md:300 records that Realtime uses a separate DB_POOL_SIZE=5 pool for those checks. A policy InitPlan-hoisted for PostgREST is not necessarily hoisted the same way in Realtime's evaluation context, and the pool is five connections wide.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Stage 3 lands; CI proves an Index Scan with InitPlan 1 for `select * from presence where couple_id = $1`. In production at 10k users, 8 postgres_changes subscriptions per user across thousands of subscribers still saturate a 5-connection pool doing per-subscriber RLS on every presence WAL record. The design declares the RLS work done and the symptom appears in a domain nobody is looking at.
fatal_flaws.repair: Add a local test that subscribes N synthetic clients to `presence:<coupleId>` against the local stack, drives a write loop, and asserts delivery latency and Realtime pool wait — all on one laptop. If that cannot be instrumented locally, say so explicitly rather than letting the PostgREST EXPLAIN stand in for it.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Two smaller gaps in the operational surface. (a) The nightly `db diff --linked` against production requires the production database password as a CI secret; nothing addresses that this extends the blast radius of a compromised GitHub Actions runner to the entire database, including `app_secrets`. (b) The 24-hour `call_invites` retention entry, shipped in Stage 5 step 13 as one of the 'safe entries', destroys the only record that a call was ever attempted — there is no call-history table among the 35, and `answered_at` is declared and never written.
fatal_flaws.scenario: (a) A compromised or malicious CI dependency reads the prod DB secret and dumps every table. (b) A user offline for three days opens the app on a train and has no evidence their partner tried to call eleven times — the rows were swept on schedule and there is nowhere else that fact was ever recorded.
fatal_flaws.repair: (a) Run the nightly diff with a dedicated read-only role restricted to catalogue access, IP-allowlisted, or from a machine the owner controls; never give CI the owner password. (b) Before enabling the `call_invites` sweep, add a narrow `call_history(couple_id, caller_id, callee_id, started_at, outcome)` row written by the same trigger and retain that instead. Nulling the SDP at 10 minutes already removes the bulk of the row.

verdict:
The core idea (local SQLite as the app, one generic sync engine, one generic outbox, doorbell-only transport) is right and is the correct answer for this codebase. The execution has four defects that cause permanent data loss or a non-terminating loop as written, and three of them are introduced by migration step 4 — the step that deletes the 300-row-refetch-on-tab-switch. That refetch is currently the only thing masking them.

The pattern is consistent: the design NAMES the correct primary source, then implements the anti-pattern the source warns about. It quotes Synapse on published-position, then never schedules the nextval→counter conversion. It quotes Telegram's `differenceTooLong` and Matrix's `M_UNKNOWN_POS` as SERVER-declared, then implements client-inferred page counting — which makes bootstrap loop forever above 4,000 messages. It quotes Signal's `recipient.id.toQueueKey(hasMedia)`, then drops the hasMedia split, so in a one-conversation app a stuck video blocks every text. It writes the `on conflict ... do update set body = messages.body returning *` idiom into research/delivery.md and then states the invariant as `do nothing returning *`, which returns zero rows and breaks the retry path it exists to enable.

VERIFIED AGAINST CODE, not inferred: `messages.seq` default is `nextval('public.messages_seq_seq')` (receipts_v2.sql:31) — a single GLOBAL sequence, not per-couple. `clear_conversation_everyone` does `delete from public.messages where couple_id = v_couple_id` (chat_media_cleanup.sql:53) — a hard delete no cursor can see. `delete_message_for_everyone` is `update ... set deleted_for_everyone = true` (settings_and_delete.sql:46) — an UPDATE that does not touch seq. So classifying `messages` as an append-only log collection is factually wrong about this app, and step 4 silently kills three shipped destructive features.

The scale ceiling is honest about storage and dishonest by omission about connections: the design's own cited figure is a 10,000-connection hard cap on Pro-no-spend-cap, and it then projects "~10k peak at 100k users" as a $100/mo line item rather than as the wall it is. The cost model contradicts its own open decision 4 — "under 2,000 messages/user/month" is arithmetically impossible while keeping Heartbeat (70-90 broadcasts/user/MINUTE) and Watch-Together (24/min).

Migration honesty: steps 0, 1, 2, 3 and 6 are genuinely incremental and well-ordered — step 2's shadow writer is the right call and step 3-before-4 (stop the bleeding before optimising) is correct. Step 5 is a whole-codebase refactor wearing a lint's clothing, and it is claimed as parallelisable with the steps that rewrite the same files. Steps 3/4/7 all depend on a kill-switch that is an open decision, in an app with no Play Store distribution channel.

Fix flaws 1-4 (all server-side, all landable in step 1 before any client change) and this design is sound. Ship step 4 as written and you convert three self-healing bugs into permanent ones.

fatal_flaws.flaw: `messages.seq` is a Postgres `nextval` sequence (verified: receipts_v2.sql:31, a single GLOBAL sequence for the whole table). The design correctly names the Synapse/nextval commit-order hazard and specifies an in-transaction per-conversation counter — but NO migration step converts it. Step 1 covers `on conflict`, `greatest()`, `updated_at` and tombstones only. Step 4 then persists a durable cursor over the unconverted column AND deletes `ChatRepository.fetch()`'s 300-rows-on-open, which is currently the only thing that re-surfaces a skipped row.
fatal_flaws.scenario: 10k users. Couple X's message A is assigned seq 4001; its transaction is still open because the AFTER INSERT `notify_message` trigger is doing a `net.http_post` pg_net enqueue (message_push.sql) under contention. Message B is assigned 4009 and commits first. The partner's client runs a catch-up in that window, sees only B, and commits cursor=4009 in the same transaction as the row (invariant 3 holds perfectly — and is irrelevant). No query the client will ever issue again includes seq 4001. Today this self-heals on the next tab switch; after step 4 it is permanent. Probability rises with concurrency and with pg_net queue latency, i.e. it gets worse exactly at the scale this design targets.
fatal_flaws.repair: Move the counter conversion into step 1, server-only, invisible to clients: add `couples.last_seq`, backfill `last_seq = max(seq) per couple`, and mint seq via `update couples set last_seq = last_seq + 1 where id = $1 returning last_seq` inside the insert RPC — the row lock serialises writers so seq N+1 cannot be assigned until N has committed. Make step 4 refuse to ship until this is live in production, not just in migrations. Add a belt-and-braces lag window: catch-up queries `seq > cursor - K` and relies on idempotent upsert, so a single skip is recovered on the next round rather than never.

fatal_flaws.flaw: `messages` is classified as an append-only log collection with cursor = `seq`. It is not append-only in this app. Three shipped features mutate or remove existing rows without advancing `seq`: `hide_message` appends to `deleted_by uuid[]`; `delete_message_for_everyone` is `update ... set deleted_for_everyone = true, deleted_at = now()` (settings_and_delete.sql:46); `clear_conversation_everyone` is `delete from public.messages where couple_id = v_couple_id` (chat_media_cleanup.sql:53). A `seq > cursor` cursor is structurally blind to all three. The design declares tombstones 'mandatory' — but only for LWW collections, and it puts messages in the other class.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Partner taps the sweep icon and confirms 'Clear chat'. Their entire history is hard-deleted server-side and locally. Your client's cursor is already past every deleted seq, so no catch-up will ever return anything about them; your local SQLite retains the full conversation forever, and the design provides no mechanism that can ever reconcile it — not the doorbell, not the generation bailout (which only triggers on a server-rejected cursor). Same for delete-for-everyone: your partner un-sends an intimate photo, the row is tombstoned, and it stays on your screen permanently. Today all three half-work because ChatScreen refetches 300 rows on every tab switch; step 4 deletes that. This is a user-visible destruction-of-trust regression shipped by the step billed as the first big win.
fatal_flaws.repair: Messages need a mutation cursor, in step 1, before step 4: add `rev bigint` bumped from the same per-couple in-transaction counter on every UPDATE, and give the collection two cursors — `seq > seq_cursor` for inserts and `rev > rev_cursor` for mutations — applied in the same round and the same transaction. Replace the hard DELETE in `clear_conversation_everyone` with a tombstone sweep (`deleted_for_everyone = true, deleted_at = now()`) plus a server-side reaper that only removes rows both participants' `rev_cursor` has passed. Until then, step 4 must keep a bounded periodic reconciliation read.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The LWW cursor is `(updated_at, id)` with `updated_at` maintained by a BEFORE trigger on the server clock. Postgres `now()` is TRANSACTION START time, so a row's `updated_at` is always strictly earlier than its commit — this is the same commit-order hole as nextval, and strictly worse. The design names the hazard for `seq` and does not name it here at all, while step 7 puts presence, profiles, receipts, reasons, care, capsules, cycle and settings behind exactly this cursor.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Two presence writes overlap (trivially common — the app writes presence on typing, navigation, heartbeat, location and chat_last_read). T1 begins at 10:00:00.000, T2 at 10:00:00.005; T2 commits at .010, T1 at .020. A catch-up between the two commits reads T2, advances the cursor to (10:00:00.005, id2), and T1's row — stamped .000 — is below the cursor and is never returned again. The partner's location or read watermark is silently a version behind, forever, until something else touches that row. On `chat_receipts` this means the seen-tick regresses and never recovers; on `profiles` it means a display name or avatar change is lost.
fatal_flaws.repair: Pick one and state it in step 1. Either (a) give LWW collections the same per-couple in-transaction `rev` counter as messages and cursor on `rev`, or (b) exploit the fact that LWW apply is idempotent: query `updated_at > cursor - safety_window` (safety_window > max transaction duration, e.g. 60s) and accept redundant rows. Option (b) is three characters of SQL and is correct for every collection in step 7. Option (a) is correct and also cheap once the counter exists for messages. Shipping step 7 with neither is silent, unattributable state divergence across eight collections.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Bootstrap does not terminate. Section G: catch-up pages at 200 with 'a hard per-round cap (20 pages) before declaring "too far behind" and re-bootstrapping.' Section B: too-far-behind → increment generation, delete the collection's local rows, re-bootstrap. A fresh install has cursor 0. Separately, `seq > 0 order by seq` pages OLDEST-first, so even without the loop the reinstalling partner watches an empty chat fill forward from the couple's first message.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Partner reinstalls (the brief's own scenario). Their couple has 6,000 messages. Round one pages 20 × 200 = 4,000 rows, hits the cap, declares 'too far behind', increments generation, deletes the 4,000 rows it just wrote, and restarts at cursor 0. Round two does the same. The app burns battery and egress in a tight loop and never shows a message. This is not a 100k-user ceiling as the design claims — it fires on the developer's own device the day step 4 ships, since this couple's chat is already well past 4,000 messages. The design cites Telegram's `differenceTooLong` and Matrix's `M_UNKNOWN_POS` — both SERVER-declared — and then implements client-inferred page counting, which is the precise anti-pattern those exist to avoid.
fatal_flaws.repair: Bootstrap is a distinct phase, not a catch-up with a big gap. Fetch newest-first (`order by seq desc limit N`, N≈500), set cursor = max(seq) in that transaction, and let the existing keyset scroll-back backfill older history lazily and on demand — which the design already has in section G and which makes the server-side snapshot endpoint unnecessary. The 20-page cap applies only to INCREMENTAL catch-up. 'Too far behind' must be a server response (a 4xx when the presented cursor precedes retention), never a client page count — retention here is unbounded, so the condition should essentially never fire, and a client that can trigger a wipe by counting pages is a self-inflicted data-loss lever.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Invariant 12 states 'No device clock participates in any ordering, gating, or freshness decision... expiry is evaluated server-side.' This is false for the outbox, which is the component the invariant most needs to cover. `created_at`, `next_attempt_at` and `expires_at` are all local wall-clock; the state machine's `now > expires_at → failed_permanent` transition is a device-clock comparison. The property test in verification layer 2 generates ±1h clock jumps — precisely the magnitude that does NOT find this.
fatal_flaws.scenario: A cheap Android (the IN2015/Vivo test set) loses power; the RTC resets to the ROM build date. The user opens the app and sends a message. `created_at` is stamped 2023; `expires_at` = 2023 + 24h, which is already in the past, so the drainer marks it `failed_permanent` before the first attempt and the UI shows a failed bubble for a message typed one second ago with a Retry that fails identically. The mirror case — clock set forward — leaves every op's `next_attempt_at` in the past, so the drainer busy-loops on a dead network with no backoff. Two NTP-synced phones on one wifi will never show either.
fatal_flaws.repair: Backoff and lifespan run on monotonic time (Android `elapsedRealtime` equivalent) plus a persisted boot epoch, not wall clock. Persist `attempts` and `monotonic_enqueued_at`; express lifespan in elapsed monotonic time across boots by summing per-boot deltas. Clamp defensively: never expire an op whose `created_at > now()`. Change the property test's clock-jump generator to ±10 years and ±1 boot, not ±1h — the design's own claim is that this is the one thing two phones can never test, so the generator has to actually generate it.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Invariant 2 specifies `on conflict (id) do nothing returning *`. `DO NOTHING` returns ZERO rows on conflict. The outbox's whole retry story depends on learning the server-assigned `seq` back from the write, and on distinguishing 'landed' from 'did not land' after an ambiguous timeout. research/delivery.md gives the correct idiom verbatim (`on conflict ... do update set body = messages.body -- no-op, forces RETURNING`) and the design paraphrased it into the broken form.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Send on a train. The insert commits server-side; the response is lost in a tunnel. The drainer retries with the same op_id. The server hits the conflict, does nothing, and returns an empty result set. The drainer now has an unrepresentable outcome: if it treats empty-as-failure it retries until the 24h lifespan expires and then marks a message the partner already received as `failed_permanent` with a Retry chip — the exact ghost-state class the design was built to delete, inverted. If it treats empty-as-success it never learns `seq`, so the row stays `pending` with seq unset and the receipt comparison `msg.seq <= peer_read_seq` is undefined for it.
fatal_flaws.repair: State the invariant as `on conflict (id) do update set <col> = excluded.<col> returning *` where the update is a no-op on an immutable column, so RETURNING always yields the authoritative row (and its seq) whether the write was the first or the fifth attempt. Add the ambiguous-timeout case to verification layer 1 as a named test asserting a non-empty response on retry, not just 'assert one row'.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The outbox queue_key for `msg.send` is `chat:<couple>`. This app has exactly ONE conversation, so the 'one undeliverable photo blocks exactly its own conversation' invariant is vacuous — it blocks the only conversation. Signal's cited source splits on media: `queue = recipient.id.toQueueKey(hasMedia)`. The design quotes that line in why_top_tier and drops the hasMedia split.
fatal_flaws.scenario: User shoots a 30MB video on a train (rapid_camera → outbox), then types three texts. The video's upload fails repeatedly with Full Jitter backoff up to 30s, unlimited attempts, 24h lifespan. All three texts sit behind it in the serial queue for hours. Today text bypasses ChatSendQueue entirely, so it sends immediately — step 3 makes this strictly worse than the status quo for the most common message type, in the exact network conditions the design exists to survive.
fatal_flaws.repair: Two queue keys: `chat:<couple>:text` and `chat:<couple>:media`. Ordering is preserved where it is observable (within each) and head-of-line blocking is scoped where it matters, which is what the cited source actually does. Add 'a stuck media op does not delay a subsequent text op' as a named case in the property test — the current invariant list would let this ship as correct.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The doorbell is a free request-amplification lever for any stranger who knows a couple_id. The design's answer to forged CONTENT is correct and elegant. But the doorbell TRIGGERS A QUERY issued with the victim's own JWT, and no migration step makes the channel private — `private: true` and `realtime.messages` RLS appear in none of steps 0-8, and step 7's per-collection PRs are explicitly client-side. Coalescing is keyed `collection:scope:cursor` behind a 250ms debounce; after an empty catch-up the cursor is unchanged, so the key is immediately reusable.
fatal_flaws.scenario: couple_id is not secret — it is the first path segment of every never-expiring public couple_media URL, which hardening_2026_08.sql:25 admits. A signed-up stranger joins the topic and broadcasts doorbells at 4 Hz across the 15 registered collections. The victim's phone issues ~60 PostgREST requests/second, indefinitely, all passing RLS because they are the victim's own reads. Battery drains, mobile data burns, the project's compute and egress bill rises, and nothing anywhere logs it as abnormal — it is indistinguishable from an active user. The design's rejected_alternatives assumes 'an authorised private channel'; the migration never builds one.
fatal_flaws.repair: Two changes. (1) A token bucket per collection that is independent of doorbell arrival — at most one catch-up per collection per N seconds no matter how many doorbells land; the doorbell may only advance a 'dirty' bit, never schedule work directly. (2) Add 'private channel + realtime.messages RLS' as an explicit named prerequisite of step 4 in the migration table, so the security property the invariants assume is something the plan actually ships rather than something it inherits.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The design has no place for calls, games, heartbeat, touch, watch-together, proximity or together — and read literally it FORBIDS them. Invariant 5 ('nothing arriving over a peer-writable channel is ever stored'), invariant 13 ('no screen may issue a network request') and section E's lint (`_c.from(...)` banned outside `lib/data/remote/`) are incompatible with WebRTC signalling, TURN credential fetch, and every ephemeral broadcast feature in the inventory. Calls are one of the three things the brief states are still broken; the client architecture mentions them zero times.
fatal_flaws.scenario: An engineer implements this literally. Call signalling must consume SDP and ICE from `call:<coupleId>` — a peer-writable broadcast channel — and must act on it within seconds. Under the doctrine there is no legal path: it cannot be stored (invariant 5), it cannot be fetched by the screen (invariant 13), and there is no third class. Either the engineer carves an undocumented exception (and the doctrine's value — that the shape is uncompilable — evaporates on first contact), or calls stay broken. Same for the 12+ ephemeral modules: heartbeat's per-beat haptic cannot round-trip through SQLite and a catch-up query.
fatal_flaws.repair: Name a third data class explicitly, alongside log and LWW: SESSION TRANSPORT — ephemeral, never persisted, never a source of durable rows, exempt from the outbox and the cursor, with its own liveness/glare rules and an explicit lint allowlist. State that its failure mode is 'the interaction did not happen' and that it may never write to an entity table. Without this the design is silent on a third of the app's realtime surface and actively blocks the domain the brief calls broken.
