fatal_flaws.flaw: Step 5 is a whole-codebase refactor presented as a 3-day lint, and it is claimed to be parallelisable with steps 3, 4 and 7 — which rewrite the same files. `lib/data/remote/` does not exist. 52 `.select(` call sites (verified) call `_c.from(...)` directly from feature code across roughly 30 files. `Result<T>` 'at the repository boundary' changes every repository signature in the app. The lint cannot be enabled until all of that has moved, or the build is red.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Step 5 is handed to a second engineer 'in parallel' as the plan suggests. They must touch chat_repository.dart, presence_service.dart, supabase_repository.dart, care_repository.dart, reasons_repository.dart and ~25 more — the exact files steps 3, 4 and 7 are simultaneously rewriting. Every day is a merge conflict; the 68 empty catches get migrated by whoever wins the rebase. The 'independently shippable, individually revertible' property that the migration section rests on is false for this step.
fatal_flaws.repair: Ship the lint as a warning with a per-directory allowlist seeded with every current offender, and delete exactly one allowlist entry per step-7 PR — so the lint becomes an enforced ratchet rather than a flag day, and it inherits step 7's natural sequencing. Apply `Result<T>` only to the paths the outbox already owns; do not change signatures the other steps are rewriting. Re-estimate: this is 2-3 weeks trailing step 7, not 3 days in parallel.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Steps 3, 4 and 7 each say 'behind a kill-switch'; open decision 6 admits no remote config exists and proposes building one. And this is a private, deliberately non-Play-Store app (disguised launcher, sideloaded) — so 'revert' means rebuilding an APK and getting it onto each device by hand. The migration's revertibility claim has no delivery channel behind it at any user count.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Step 4 ships with the nextval cursor unfixed (flaw 1). Messages start going missing at a low background rate on flaky networks. There is no flag to turn it off, so the fix is a new build. At 2 users that is an evening. At 1,000 sideloaded users with no update channel, a permanent-data-loss bug is live until every device is manually updated, and the design's own telemetry (step 8) has not shipped yet, so nobody knows the rate.
fatal_flaws.repair: Make `couples.client_flags jsonb`, read at boot and on resume with absent = safe path, a step-0 deliverable — it is pure SQL with zero client risk and it is the cheapest insurance in the plan. Gate steps 3, 4 and 7 on it explicitly. Separately, state the distribution constraint in the migration section: with no store channel, the blast radius of a bad step is bounded by manual reinstall, which is an argument for landing the telemetry of step 8 EARLIER, not last.

fatal_flaws.flaw: The cost model contradicts open decision 4, and the largest claimed saving is scheduled last. 'Realistic post-change volume is under 2,000 messages/user/month' (a ~9× reduction) is asserted while the same document recommends KEEPING Heartbeat and Watch-Together. Heartbeat is 70-90 broadcast messages per user per MINUTE; Watch-Together is 24/min. Separately, the entire 100k-user media saving ($80-110/mo) comes from step 8 thumbnails, which is deliberately scheduled last, and adding a ≤512px thumb alongside every ≤1920px original INCREASES stored bytes by roughly 12%.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Ten minutes of Heartbeat a week is ~3,600 broadcast messages/user/month on its own — 1.8× the entire claimed post-change budget, from one optional feature, before a single chat message. The 9× figure and the $25-30/mo saving at 1k users are therefore not what the design as specified produces. At 100k the egress line the design flags as 'the largest bill in the project' is untouched until the final step, which is exactly the point at which it has already been the largest bill for months.
fatal_flaws.repair: Re-derive the message budget with Heartbeat and Watch-Together included at their measured rates, or move the hard client-side rate limit (≤4 msgs/sec) out of open-decision territory and into step 7 as a committed deliverable with a number. Move thumbnail generation forward — it is server-side, independent of every client step, and can ship alongside step 0/1 where it starts saving immediately. Add stored-bytes growth to the cost table; the thumb tier is a net storage increase traded for an egress decrease, which is the right trade but should be stated.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Swapping `Expanded(child: bodies[bodyIndex])` (verified, app_shell.dart:240) for `IndexedStack` keeps every tab mounted, so under the current one-channel-per-feature model per-user always-on topics go from 5-8 to the union of all tabs. The design asserts 'zero channel churn (IndexedStack + sync scopes)' but never defines sync scopes and never states the invariant that would make it safe. inventory/realtime.md rates per-subscriber RLS evaluation as the binding constraint, and postgres_changes evaluates RLS per subscriber per change.
fatal_flaws.scenario: Step 4 lands IndexedStack for the ≤100ms tab-switch budget. Chat's three channels, Home's cycle channel and Touch's two now coexist permanently instead of alternating. Per-user subscription count roughly doubles, and at 10k users that doubles the tenant-wide per-row RLS evaluation load — trading measurable client jank for the server ceiling the phase-1 research identifies as the one that actually breaks first.
fatal_flaws.repair: Add the missing invariant: exactly ONE realtime channel per device, carrying only `{collection, scope_id}` doorbells, with tab visibility affecting nothing about the socket. Make it a step-4 acceptance criterion measured by asserting channel count == 1 in the lab. With it, IndexedStack is free and the smoothness claim holds; without it, the smoothness claim is paid for by the constraint that is already binding.

fatal_flaws.flaw: Verification layer 3 — the deterministic two-engine simulator, described as 'strictly stronger' than two phones — is structurally incapable of finding flaws 1, 2 or 3. An in-memory fake server written the obvious way assigns seq in commit order, stamps updated_at monotonically, and never hard-deletes rows behind a cursor. The golden assertion ('after reconnect B's rows are byte-identical to A's') passes trivially under those assumptions.
fatal_flaws.scenario: All five verification layers go green. The engine ships. In production, seq 4001 is skipped because pg_net widened a transaction; a partner clears the chat and the other side keeps it forever; a presence row is silently a version behind. Every one of these is invisible to the test suite by construction, which reproduces exactly the failure history the brief describes: the fix passed, then failed in production.
fatal_flaws.repair: The fake server must be adversarial by construction, and its hostile behaviours must be enumerated as generator inputs, not left to the implementer: reveal seq N+1 before N; stamp updated_at at transaction START and commit out of order; hard-delete rows below the cursor; mutate rows without advancing any cursor; return an empty RETURNING on conflict. Each maps 1:1 to a flaw above. This is an afternoon's work and it is the difference between the suite proving the design and merely confirming it.
